**〜方面 is what you want.** 新宿方面 means "towards Shinjuku" and is on every platform sign.

**Other signs:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 番線(ばんせん) | platform number |
| 乗(の)り換(か)え | transfer |
| 出口(でぐち) | exit |
| 改札(かいさつ) | ticket gate |
| 東口(ひがしぐち) | east exit |
| 車両(しゃりょう) | carriage |
| 優先席(ゆうせんせき) | priority seat |
| 女性専用(じょせいせんよう) | women only |

**The announcements** follow a fixed pattern: まもなく〜番線に、〜行きの電車が参ります — shortly, on platform ~, the train bound for ~ will arrive. 参ります is humble 来る, from the keigo lesson.

**〜行(ゆ)き** is "bound for" and is written on the front of the train and on every sign.

**Practice.** Read: 急行 新宿方面 · 各駅停車 3番線 · 東京行き · 乗り換え. Then say: Does this train stop at Shibuya? Answer: この電車は渋谷に止まりますか。
IC cards:
A rechargeable card that replaces tickets and much small cash. Getting one is the first thing to do on arrival.

**The cards:** Suica and PASMO in Tokyo, ICOCA in Osaka, and eight others regionally. **They are all mutually compatible** — a Suica works in Osaka and an ICOCA works in Tokyo. The choice does not matter.

**What they do:** trains, buses, convenience stores, vending machines, coin lockers, some taxis and many shops. Tap on, tap off; the fare is deducted automatically and is slightly cheaper than a paper ticket.

**Charging:** チャージ, at any ticket machine or convenience store. The button says チャージ and takes notes.

**The words:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| チャージ | top up |
| 残高(ざんだか) | balance |
| 履歴(りれき) | usage history |
| 入場(にゅうじょう) | entry |
| 払い戻し | refund (of the card itself) |

**残高不足(ざんだかぶそく)** — insufficient balance — is what the gate says when it refuses to open. Charge at the machine beside the gate; there is always one.

**Mobile Suica** works on an iPhone or an Android phone with FeliCa, and is better than the card: it charges from the phone and shows the balance without a machine. Setting it up requires a Japanese Apple or Google account for some of it, which is the usual friction.

**The deposit** is ¥500, returned when you hand the card back.

**Shinkansen is not included** on a basic IC card — that needs a separate ticket or a registered service.

**Practice.** Say: I'd like to charge this. · What's the balance? · Can I pay with Suica? Answers: チャージをお願いします。 · 残高はいくらですか。 · スイカで払えますか。
Asking for directions:
A question you can ask with stage 2 grammar, and an answer you need stage 3 to follow.

**Asking:**

すみません、〜はどこですか。 — Excuse me, where is ~?
〜はどうやって行きますか。 — How do I get to ~?
〜までどのくらいかかりますか。 — How long does it take to ~?
この近(ちか)くに〜はありますか。 — Is there a ~ near here?

**道(みち)に迷(まよ)いました。** — I'm lost. A complete and useful sentence.

**What you will hear**, and this is why the と conditional mattered:

まっすぐ行くと、右にあります。 — Go straight and it's on the right.
二つ目(ふたつめ)の角(かど)を左に曲(ま)がってください。 — Turn left at the second corner.
突(つ)き当(あ)たりを右です。 — Right at the end.

**〜目(め) makes an ordinal:** 一つ目 first, 二つ目 second, 三つ目 third.

**The vocabulary:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 角(かど) | corner |
| 信号(しんごう) | traffic light |
| 交差点(こうさてん) | intersection |
| 突き当たり | the end of the road |
| 曲がる | to turn |
| 渡(わた)る | to cross |
| まっすぐ | straight |
| 向(む)かい | opposite |
| 隣(となり) | next to |

**People will walk you there.** This happens often and is genuinely meant. Refusing twice and then accepting is the usual shape.

**交番(こうばん)**, the police box, exists partly for this. Asking at one is completely normal and they have maps.

**Practice.** Ask where the station is, how to get to the post office, and how long it takes. Then follow this aloud: 信号を渡って、二つ目の角を右に曲がると、左にあります。
Giving directions:
The other side of the same conversation. Worth practising, because you will be asked — usually by someone who assumes you live there.

**The pattern is a chain of て-forms ending in an instruction:**

まっすぐ行って、信号を渡って、二つ目の角を右に曲がってください。

**The useful verbs:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 行く | go |
| 曲がる | turn |
| 渡る | cross |
| 通(とお)る | pass through |
| 出る | exit |
| 進(すす)む | proceed |

**Landmarks are how directions are given in Japan**, because most streets have no names. コンビニの隣, 郵便局の向かい, 銀行の角 — next to the convenience store, opposite the post office, at the bank's corner. An address is a set of nested areas rather than a street and a number, which is why even locals use maps.

**Distance:**

ここから歩いて五分くらいです。 — About a five minute walk from here.
すぐそこです。 — It's just over there.
ちょっと遠(とお)いです。 — It's a bit far.

**If you do not know:**

すみません、分かりません。 — Sorry, I don't know.
この辺(へん)は詳(くわ)しくないんです。 — I'm not familiar with this area.

That second one uses んです from stage 3, and it is the natural way to say it — explaining rather than merely stating.

**Pointing at a phone map is a complete answer** and nobody minds.

**Practice.** Give directions from where you are to the nearest shop, as a chain of て-forms. Then say: it's about a ten minute walk, next to the convenience store. Answer: 歩いて十分くらいです。コンビニの隣です。
Taxis and buses:
Two systems that work differently from most countries in ways worth knowing before you need them.

**Taxis.**

The door opens **by itself** — the driver operates it. Do not touch it, and do not close it.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 〜までお願いします。 | To ~, please. |
| ここで止めてください。 | Stop here please. |
| 急(いそ)いでいます。 | I'm in a hurry. |
| 領収書をお願いします。 | Receipt, please. |

**Showing an address on a phone is normal** and often better than saying it, since addresses are hard to say and harder to hear.

**空車(くうしゃ)** in red means available; 賃走(ちんそう) means occupied.

**No tipping**, and payment is usually by card or IC card now.

**Buses.** The system varies by city and there are two kinds:

**Flat fare** (Tokyo): pay as you **board**, at the front.

**Distance fare** (most of the country): take a 整理券(せいりけん) — a numbered ticket — as you board at the **back**, watch the board at the front for the fare against your number, and pay as you **leave** at the front.

**整理券 is the thing to know.** Forgetting to take one means paying the maximum fare.

**Signalling to stop:** press the button. 次(つぎ)、止まります — "next stop" — lights up.

**両替(りょうがえ)** — the change machine on the fare box — breaks 1,000 yen notes. It does not give change from the fare; you insert the exact amount afterwards.

**Practice.** Say: To Tokyo Station, please. · Please stop here. · Receipt, please. Answers: 東京駅までお願いします。 · ここで止めてください。 · 領収書をお願いします。
Long distance: shinkansen and airports:
The vocabulary for travelling between cities, and the one decision that confuses everyone.

**A shinkansen needs two tickets**: the 乗車券(じょうしゃけん), the basic fare, and the 特急券(とっきゅうけん), the express supplement. Both go into the gate together. This is the thing that catches people out — one ticket is not enough.

**Seats:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 指定席(していせき) | reserved seat |
| 自由席(じゆうせき) | unreserved — first come, first served |
| グリーン車(しゃ) | first class |
| 禁煙(きんえん) | non-smoking (nearly all of it) |

**自由席 is cheaper and fine off-peak.** At New Year or Golden Week it means standing for three hours.

**Buying:** みどりの窓口 or the machine. 〜まで、指定席を一枚お願いします。

**On board:** a trolley, announcements in Japanese and English, and absolute quiet. Phone calls are made in the vestibule between carriages, never in the seat.

**Airports:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 出発(しゅっぱつ) | departures |
| 到着(とうちゃく) | arrivals |
| 搭乗(とうじょう)券(けん) | boarding pass |
| 手荷物(てにもつ) | hand luggage |
| 預(あず)ける | to check in (baggage) |
| 税関(ぜいかん) | customs |
| 入国(にゅうこく)審査(しんさ) | immigration |

**Luggage forwarding — 宅配(たくはい)便(びん)** — is worth knowing: send your suitcase from the airport to your hotel, or between hotels, for a few thousand yen, arriving next day. Almost everyone does it and it transforms travelling with luggage on trains.

**Practice.** Say: One reserved seat to Kyoto, please. · Is this the unreserved carriage? · I'd like to send this to my hotel. Answers: 京都まで指定席を一枚お願いします。 · これは自由席ですか。 · これをホテルまで送りたいです。
Reading signs: the kanji you must know:
A small set of characters carries nearly all public signage, and knowing them is disproportionately useful.

**Directions and places:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 入口(いりぐち) | entrance |
| 出口(でぐち) | exit |
| 非常口(ひじょうぐち) | emergency exit |
| 改札(かいさつ) | ticket gate |
| north 北 · south 南 · east 東 · west 西 | 北口 = north exit |
| 階(かい) | floor |
| 上(うえ) · 下(した) | up · down |

**Instructions and warnings:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 禁止(きんし) | prohibited |
| 立入(たちいり)禁止 | no entry |
| 禁煙 | no smoking |
| 注意(ちゅうい) | caution |
| 危険(きけん) | danger |
| 工事中(こうじちゅう) | under construction |
| 使用中(しようちゅう) | in use / occupied |
| 故障(こしょう)中 | out of order |
| 準備中(じゅんびちゅう) | preparing, not yet open |

**〜中 means "in the middle of"** and is everywhere: 営業(えいぎょう)中 open for business, 休憩(きゅうけい)中 on break, 清掃(せいそう)中 being cleaned.

**営業中 and 準備中 hang on restaurant doors** and are the ones that decide whether you can go in.

**Toilets:**

お手洗(てあら)い · トイレ · 化粧室(けしょうしつ) · 男(おとこ) men · 女(おんな) women · 多目的(たもくてき) accessible

**押(お)す push · 引(ひ)く pull** — on every door, and worth a second to learn.

**Practice.** Read: 立入禁止 · 準備中 · 故障中 · 非常口 · 北口 · 使用中. Then look at a photograph of any Japanese street scene and name every sign you can.
At the clinic: describing symptoms:
A conversation worth being able to have badly rather than not at all.

**The opening:**

どうしましたか。 — What's the matter?
今日はどうされましたか。 — (politer) What brings you in?

**The pattern: 〜が痛(いた)いです** — ~ hurts.

頭(あたま)が痛いです。 — I have a headache.
お腹(なか)が痛いです。 — My stomach hurts.
喉(のど)が痛いです。 — I have a sore throat.

**Other symptoms:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 熱(ねつ)があります | I have a fever |
| 咳(せき)が出ます | I have a cough |
| 鼻水(はなみず)が出ます | runny nose |
| 吐(は)き気(け)がします | I feel sick |
| めまいがします | I feel dizzy |
| 下痢(げり)をしています | I have diarrhoea |
| 体(からだ)がだるいです | I feel heavy / lethargic |
| 食欲(しょくよく)がありません | no appetite |

**〜がします is for sensations** — 吐き気がする, めまいがする — and is a fixed pattern worth taking whole.

**When and how long:**

三日前(みっかまえ)からです。 — Since three days ago.
昨日の夜(よる)からです。 — Since last night.

**They will ask:**

熱は何度(なんど)ですか。 — What's your temperature?
アレルギーはありますか。 — Any allergies?
薬(くすり)を飲んでいますか。 — Are you taking any medication?

**保険証(ほけんしょう)** — insurance card — is asked for first, every time. Without it you pay the full amount.

**Practice.** Say: I have a headache and a fever. · My stomach has hurt since last night. · I have no appetite. Answers: 頭が痛くて、熱があります。 · 昨日の夜からお腹が痛いです。 · 食欲がありません。
The body:
Vocabulary for the clinic, the gym and half the idioms in the language.

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 頭(あたま) | head | 髪(かみ) | hair |
| 顔(かお) | face | 目(め) | eye |
| 耳(みみ) | ear | 鼻(はな) | nose |
| 口(くち) | mouth | 歯(は) | tooth |
| 喉(のど) | throat | 首(くび) | neck |
| 肩(かた) | shoulder | 腕(うで) | arm |
| 手(て) | hand | 指(ゆび) | finger |
| 背中(せなか) | back | 腰(こし) | lower back |
| お腹(なか) | stomach | 胸(むね) | chest |
| 足(あし) | leg, foot | 膝(ひざ) | knee |

**足 covers both leg and foot**, and 手 covers hand and arm in some expressions. Japanese divides the body slightly differently, and 腰 — the lower back and hips — has no single English word.

**They appear in a great many idioms:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 頭がいい | clever |
| 目がない | mad about something |
| 耳が痛い | hard to hear (a criticism) |
| 口が軽(かる)い | indiscreet |
| 手が空(あ)く | to be free |
| 顔が広(ひろ)い | well connected |
| 足を運(はこ)ぶ | to make the trip |

**お世話(せわ)になる** and the body idioms are the part of the language that cannot be worked out from the parts, and they are learned as whole phrases.

**For the clinic**, the useful ones are 頭, 喉, お腹, 腰, 背中, 歯 and 熱.

**歯医者(はいしゃ)** is the dentist, 内科(ないか) general medicine, 外科(げか) surgery, 耳鼻科(じびか) ear nose and throat, 眼科(がんか) eyes.

**Practice.** Name ten body parts without looking. Then say: My shoulder hurts. · My knee hurts when I walk. Answers: 肩が痛いです。 · 歩くと膝が痛いです。
At the pharmacy:
薬局(やっきょく) and ドラッグストア — the dispensing pharmacy and the general one — and what to ask in each.

**With a prescription**, 処方箋(しょほうせん), from a clinic: hand it over with your insurance card, wait, and take the bag. The pharmacist will explain the dosage and ask whether you have taken it before.

**Without one**, at a drugstore:

風邪(かぜ)薬(ぐすり)はありますか。 — Do you have cold medicine?
頭痛(ずつう)に効(き)く薬はありますか。 — Something for a headache?

**〜に効く** — effective for ~ — is the pattern.

**The medicines:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 風邪薬 | cold medicine |
| 頭痛薬 | headache tablets |
| 胃腸薬(いちょうやく) | stomach medicine |
| 目薬(めぐすり) | eye drops |
| 絆創膏(ばんそうこう) | plaster |
| 湿布(しっぷ) | medicated patch |
| マスク | face mask |
| 消毒(しょうどく) | disinfectant |

**湿布 deserves a mention** — adhesive medicated patches for aches, used constantly in Japan and unfamiliar elsewhere. They work.

**Dosage instructions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 一日(いちにち)三回(さんかい) | three times a day |
| 食後(しょくご) | after meals |
| 食前(しょくぜん) | before meals |
| 食間(しょっかん) | between meals |
| 一回(いっかい)一錠(いちじょう) | one tablet per dose |

**食後 is the default** and appears on nearly everything.

**Japanese doses are often lower** than Western equivalents, and codeine-containing cold medicines are sold over the counter where they would not be elsewhere. Pseudoephedrine, conversely, is restricted — some common Western cold remedies are illegal to bring in.

**Practice.** Ask for: cold medicine · something for a sore throat · plasters. Then read: 一日三回 食後. Answers: 風邪薬はありますか。 · 喉に効く薬はありますか。 · 絆創膏はありますか。
Making an appointment:
Booking anything — a clinic, a restaurant, a haircut — runs on the same handful of sentences.

**Asking:**

予約(よやく)をお願いしたいんですが。 — I'd like to make a booking.
明日(あした)の三時は空(あ)いていますか。 — Is three tomorrow free?
何時(なんじ)が空いていますか。 — What times are free?

**んですが again** — the explanatory ending with a trailing が, which is how any request to a stranger opens.

**What they ask:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| お名前は？ | Your name? |
| お電話番号は？ | Your phone number? |
| 何名様ですか。 | How many people? |
| 何時がよろしいですか。 | What time would suit? |
| 初(はじ)めてですか。 | Is this your first visit? |

**Giving your name.** Foreign names are taken in katakana and you will be asked to repeat them. Spelling it out character by character is normal: ステファンです。ス、テ、フ、ァ、ン。

**Times:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 午前(ごぜん) / 午後(ごご) | am / pm |
| 〜時から | from ~ o'clock |
| 空いています | free, available |
| 満席(まんせき) / いっぱい | full |

**Changing or cancelling:**

予約を変更(へんこう)したいんですが。 — I'd like to change my booking.
予約をキャンセルしたいんですが。 — I'd like to cancel.

**Cancelling late is taken seriously**, more so than in many countries, and a no-show at a restaurant may be charged. Phoning to cancel, even at short notice, is strongly expected.

**Practice.** Book a table for two at seven tomorrow, giving your name. Answer: 予約をお願いしたいんですが。明日の七時、二人です。名前はステファンです。
Emergencies:
Short, and worth knowing before it is needed.

**The numbers:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **110** | police — 警察(けいさつ) |
| **119** | fire and ambulance — 消防(しょうぼう)・救急(きゅうきゅう) |

**119 covers both fire and ambulance.** The first question is 火事(かじ)ですか、救急(きゅうきゅう)ですか — fire or ambulance?

**The sentences:**

助(たす)けて！ — Help!
救急車(きゅうきゅうしゃ)を呼(よ)んでください。 — Call an ambulance.
事故(じこ)です。 — There's been an accident.
火事です。 — There's a fire.
病院(びょういん)に行きたいです。 — I want to go to a hospital.
englishを話せる人はいますか。 — Is there anyone who speaks English?

**They will ask for the address**, which is the hard part. 住所(じゅうしょ)が分かりません — I don't know the address — is an acceptable answer, followed by landmarks: 〜の前です.

**Ambulances are free** in Japan. Treatment is not, but the ride is.

**交番(こうばん)** — the police box — is on many corners and is staffed. Walking into one is the fastest route to help with anything from a lost wallet to directions.

**Earthquakes.** 地震(じしん). The advice is: get under something solid, stay away from windows, do not run outside. 津波(つなみ) warnings mean move to high ground immediately. Phone alerts come automatically and are extremely loud.

**避難所(ひなんじょ)** — evacuation centre — is signposted in every neighbourhood, usually a school. Knowing where the nearest one is, before anything happens, is worth ten minutes.

**Practice.** Say: Please call an ambulance. · There's been an accident. · Is there anyone who speaks English? Answers: 救急車を呼んでください。 · 事故です。 · 英語を話せる人はいますか。
Renting a flat:
The most paperwork-heavy thing in Japanese life, and a vocabulary that appears nowhere else.

**The up-front costs**, which are the shock:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 敷金(しききん) | deposit — one to two months, partly returned |
| 礼金(れいきん) | "key money" — one to two months, **not returned** |
| 仲介(ちゅうかい)手数料(てすうりょう) | agent's fee — one month |
| 前家賃(まえやちん) | first month's rent in advance |

Moving in typically costs four to six months' rent. 礼金なし properties exist and are worth looking for.

**Reading a listing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 家賃(やちん) | rent |
| 管理費(かんりひ) / 共益費(きょうえきひ) | building maintenance, monthly |
| 築(ちく)〜年 | ~ years old |
| 駅(えき)から徒歩(とほ)〜分 | ~ minutes' walk from the station |
| 〜畳(じょう) | size in tatami mats |
| 1K / 1DK / 1LDK | rooms + kitchen / dining-kitchen / living-dining-kitchen |

**畳 is the unit of room size** — about 1.65 square metres — and is used even in buildings with no tatami.

**1LDK means one bedroom** plus a combined living-dining-kitchen. The number is bedrooms only.

**保証人(ほしょうにん)** — a guarantor — is usually required, and a guarantor company (保証会社) can be paid instead, which is what most foreigners do.

**Things that are often not included:** 照明(しょうめい) light fittings, エアコン air conditioning in older places, and カーテン. An empty Japanese flat can be very empty.

**Practice.** Read this listing: 家賃8万円 管理費5千円 敷金1 礼金1 築15年 駅から徒歩7分 1DK 6畳. Then say what it costs to move in.
Utilities, bills and the paperwork:
Setting up a life, which is done by phone and by form.

**The utilities:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 電気(でんき) | electricity |
| ガス | gas |
| 水道(すいどう) | water |
| インターネット | internet |

**Gas requires someone to visit** and be present to open the supply — 開栓(かいせん) — and must be booked. Electricity and water usually just need a postcard or a phone call.

**Paying.** Three ways:

1. **口座(こうざ)振替(ふりかえ)** — direct debit, set up at the bank.
2. **クレジットカード払い** — by card.
3. **コンビニ払い** — take the paper bill to a convenience store and pay cash.

The third is why convenience stores matter: a bill arrives, you hand it over with cash, done.

**The words on a bill:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 請求書(せいきゅうしょ) | invoice |
| 使用量(しようりょう) | amount used |
| 今月(こんげつ) / 先月(せんげつ) | this month / last month |
| 支払期限(しはらいきげん) | payment deadline |
| お客様番号(きゃくさまばんごう) | customer number |

**住民票(じゅうみんひょう)** — residence registration — is done at the ward office within 14 days of moving, and is the document everything else asks for. **マイナンバー**, the individual number, is needed for work and banking.

**判子(はんこ) / 印鑑(いんかん)** — a personal seal — is still asked for on some paperwork, though signatures are increasingly accepted. A cheap one with your name in katakana is available in any stationery shop.

**Practice.** Say: I'd like to start electricity service. · When is the payment deadline? · Can I pay at a convenience store? Answers: 電気の使用を開始したいんですが。 · 支払期限はいつですか。 · コンビニで払えますか。
Rubbish, recycling and the neighbours:
Two things that will make you unpopular faster than anything else if got wrong.

**Rubbish is sorted, and the categories vary by municipality.** The common split:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 燃(も)えるごみ / 可燃(かねん)ごみ | burnable |
| 燃えないごみ / 不燃(ふねん)ごみ | non-burnable |
| 資源(しげん)ごみ | recyclable |
| プラスチック / プラ | plastic packaging |
| ビン · カン · ペットボトル | bottles · cans · PET bottles |
| 粗大(そだい)ごみ | oversized — must be booked and paid for |

**Each type goes out on a different day**, early in the morning, in the designated bag, at the designated spot. The calendar comes from the ward office and is also on its website.

**Designated bags.** Many areas require specific paid bags — 指定(してい)ごみ袋 — sold in convenience stores. Using the wrong bag means the rubbish is left with a sticker on it.

**PET bottles are three separate items**: cap, label, bottle. Rinsed.

**粗大ごみ** — furniture, appliances — is collected by appointment, with a sticker bought in advance. Fly-tipping is taken seriously.

**Neighbours.** 引越(ひっこ)しの挨拶(あいさつ) — greeting the neighbours when you move in, with a small gift — is traditional and still common in houses, less so in flats. 隣に引っ越してきた〜です。よろしくお願いします。

**Noise.** Walls are thin, and expectations about quiet after about 10pm are firm. The washing machine at night is a common complaint.

**Practice.** Say: Which day is burnable rubbish? · Where do I put the plastic? · I've just moved in next door. Answers: 燃えるごみは何曜日ですか。 · プラスチックはどこに出しますか。 · 隣に引っ越してきました。よろしくお願いします。
The post office and the bank:
Two institutions with fixed scripts and a lot of forms.

**The post office — 郵便局(ゆうびんきょく)**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 切手(きって) | stamp |
| 封筒(ふうとう) | envelope |
| 葉書(はがき) | postcard |
| 小包(こづつみ) | parcel |
| 速達(そくたつ) | express |
| 書留(かきとめ) | registered |
| 航空便(こうくうびん) / 船便(ふなびん) | air mail / sea mail |
| 送料(そうりょう) | postage |

これを南アフリカまで送りたいんですが。 — I'd like to send this to South Africa.

They will ask 中身(なかみ)は何ですか — what's inside — and you fill in a customs form.

**Japan Post is also a bank**, ゆうちょ, and its ATMs are the most foreigner-friendly in the country.

**The bank — 銀行(ぎんこう)**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 口座(こうざ) | account |
| 口座を開(ひら)く | to open an account |
| 通帳(つうちょう) | passbook |
| 暗証番号(あんしょうばんごう) | PIN |
| 振込(ふりこみ) | bank transfer |
| 引(ひ)き出(だ)す | to withdraw |
| 預(あず)ける | to deposit |
| 残高 | balance |

**振込 is how everything is paid** — rent, bills, salaries. Bank transfer, not cheque and often not card.

**Opening an account** needs a residence card, an address, a phone number and usually a hanko. Some banks will not open one until you have been resident six months, which is a known obstacle; ゆうちょ is usually the easiest.

**ATMs close.** Many stop at 9pm and charge outside business hours. Convenience store ATMs run 24 hours and accept foreign cards.

**Practice.** Say: I'd like to send this to South Africa by air mail. · I'd like to open an account. · What's the balance? Answers: これを南アフリカまで航空便で送りたいんですが。 · 口座を開きたいんですが。 · 残高はいくらですか。
Phones, contracts and the internet:
Signing up for things, which in Japan means a shop visit and a stack of paper.

**The words:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 契約(けいやく) | contract |
| 料金(りょうきん) | charges, fee |
| 月額(げつがく) | monthly amount |
| 解約(かいやく) | cancellation |
| 違約金(いやくきん) | cancellation penalty |
| 格安(かくやす)SIM | budget SIM |
| データ | data |
| 通話(つうわ) | calls |
| 乗(の)り換(か)え | switching provider |
| 本人確認(ほんにんかくにん)書類(しょるい) | proof of identity |

**Contracts are long and penalties are real.** Two-year contracts with automatic renewal were standard; they have loosened, but 違約金 still exists and 解約 often has a window.

**格安SIM** — MVNOs on the big three networks — are far cheaper and are what most people recommend now. Setting one up is largely online, which avoids the shop.

**What you need:** residence card, Japanese bank account or credit card, and a Japanese address. A foreign card is often refused for monthly billing, which is the usual blocker.

**Prepaid SIMs and pocket wifi** avoid all of it for short stays.

**Internet at home** takes two to four weeks to install, needs the landlord's permission in some buildings, and 工事(こうじ) — the installation visit — must be booked.

**Useful sentences:**

一番安(やす)いプランはどれですか。 — Which is the cheapest plan?
月にいくらかかりますか。 — How much per month?
解約金はかかりますか。 — Is there a cancellation fee?

**Practice.** Ask: Which plan is cheapest? · How much is it a month? · Is there a cancellation fee? Then read: 月額2,980円（税別）・2年契約・違約金9,500円.
Job interviews and first meetings:
The most ritualised conversation in Japanese, and one where the form matters as much as the content.

**The arrival:**

失礼(しつれい)します。 — Excuse me. (said entering a room, every time)
よろしくお願いします。 — On being introduced.

**失礼します is said on entering and leaving** any room where someone senior is, and 失礼しました on the way out of an interview.

**The self-introduction** is the 自己紹介 from stage 2, lengthened:

本日(ほんじつ)はお時間(じかん)をいただき、ありがとうございます。
[name]と申します。
[background]。
よろしくお願いいたします。

**本日 rather than 今日**, いただく rather than もらう, いたします rather than します — formal registers of words you already know.

**Questions you will be asked:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 志望(しぼう)動機(どうき)は？ | Why do you want this job? |
| 自己PRをお願いします。 | Tell us about your strengths. |
| 長所(ちょうしょ)と短所(たんしょ)は？ | Strengths and weaknesses? |
| 何か質問(しつもん)はありますか。 | Any questions? |

**Business cards — 名刺(めいし)** — are exchanged with both hands, received with both hands, read, and placed on the table rather than pocketed. Writing on someone's card in front of them is rude.

**Bowing** rather than handshaking, and a deeper bow to the more senior person.

**Modesty is expected** in answers about yourself, which cuts against Western interview habits. まだまだ勉強中です is a normal thing to say about a skill you are good at.

**Practice.** Write and rehearse a three-sentence answer to 志望動機は？ Then practise 失礼します on entering a room and 失礼しました on leaving.
In the office:
The phrases that structure a Japanese working day, almost none of which translate.

**Arriving and leaving:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| おはようございます | Good morning — used all day on first meeting |
| お疲(つか)れさまです | The all-purpose greeting and farewell |
| お先(さき)に失礼します | Said when leaving before others |
| お疲れさまでした | Said in reply to the above |
| 行ってきます / 行ってらっしゃい | Leaving the office / seeing someone off |
| ただいま戻(もど)りました | I'm back |

**お疲れさまです is the single most used phrase in Japanese working life.** It means roughly "you must be tired" and functions as hello, goodbye, thank you, well done, and acknowledgement of someone's existence in a corridor.

**ご苦労(くろう)さまです is the same thing downward** — from a superior to a subordinate — and using it to your boss is a mistake.

**Working phrases:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| お願いします | Please / over to you |
| 承知(しょうち)しました | Understood. (to a superior) |
| かしこまりました | Understood. (to a customer) |
| 확認(かくにん)します | I'll check |
| 少々お待ちください | One moment please |
| すみません、質問があるんですが | Sorry, I have a question |

**報連相(ほうれんそう)** — 報告 report, 連絡 contact, 相談 consult — is the stated expectation: tell your superior what is happening, early and often. Solving something quietly and reporting the result can be received badly, which surprises people from cultures that reward autonomy.

**残業(ざんぎょう)** is overtime, and 有給(ゆうきゅう) is paid leave — the next lesson.

**Practice.** Say: Good morning. · I'm leaving before you. · Understood. · Sorry, I have a question. Answers: おはようございます。 · お先に失礼します。 · 承知しました。 · すみません、質問があるんですが。
Email and messages:
Written Japanese for work has a fixed shape, and following it matters more than elegance.

**The skeleton:**

```
[会社名] [名前]様

お世話になっております。
[your company] の [your name] です。

[the actual message]

よろしくお願いいたします。

――――――――――
[your signature block]
```

**お世話になっております** — "thank you for your continued support" — opens essentially every business email and means nothing in particular. Leaving it out reads as abrupt.

**様(さま)** after a name, 御中(おんちゅう) after a company name. 殿(どの) is older and used downward.

**The closings:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| よろしくお願いいたします | The standard close |
| ご確認よろしくお願いいたします | Please check |
| お忙(いそが)しいところ恐縮(きょうしゅく)ですが | Sorry to trouble you when you're busy |
| ご返信(へんしん)お待ちしております | Looking forward to your reply |

**Keep it short.** Japanese business email is formulaic and brief; the formality is in the frame, not the body.

**Messages — LINE** is what people actually use for everything informal, including with colleagues. Far more casual: short, plain form, stickers, no openings.

**了解(りょうかい)です is casual "got it"**; 承知しました is the polite version. Using 了解 to a superior is a small error people do notice.

**Practice.** Write an email to a colleague asking them to check a document by Friday, using the skeleton. Then write the same thing as a LINE message, in two lines.
Telephone Japanese:
The hardest listening there is — no face, no context, and a script you must know to survive.

**Answering at work:**

はい、[会社名]でございます。 — Yes, [company] speaking.

**Calling:**

お世話になっております。[会社名]の[名前]と申します。
[相手の名前]様はいらっしゃいますか。 — Is Mr/Ms ~ there?

**いらっしゃいますか** is honorific いる, from the keigo lesson, and this is where it first becomes compulsory rather than optional.

**What you will hear:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 少々お待ちください | One moment |
| ただいま席(せき)を外(はず)しております | He's away from his desk |
| 외出(がいしゅつ)しております | He's out |
| 折(お)り返(かえ)しお電話いたしましょうか | Shall we call you back? |
| お電話番号をお願いします | Your number, please |

**おります and しております are humble** — the company lowers itself when speaking to an outsider, even about the person you want. Your own boss is referred to without 様 or さん to an outsider: 田中はただいま外出しております.

**That in-group rule is the one to absorb.** Inside the company, 田中さん. To a customer, just 田中.

**When you cannot follow:**

すみません、もう一度お願いします。
少しゆっくりお願いできますか。
メールでお送りいただけますか。 — Could you send it by email?

That last one is a legitimate escape and is used by native speakers too.

**Practice.** Rehearse: calling a company, giving your name, asking for someone, and asking them to call back. Answer: お世話になっております。[name]と申します。田中様はいらっしゃいますか。…では、折り返しお電話いただけますか。
Making plans and invitations:
Arranging to meet, and the shape of a Japanese refusal.

**Inviting:**

今度(こんど)、飲みに行きませんか。 — Shall we go for a drink sometime?
よかったら、一緒にどうですか。 — If you like, shall we go together?
映画でも見に行きませんか。 — Shall we go and see a film or something?

**でも after a noun softens it** — "a film or something" — and makes the invitation less of a demand. It is used constantly: お茶でも, ご飯でも.

**ませんか and ましょう** from stage 2 are the engine here, and ませんか is the invitation.

**Fixing the details:**

いつがいいですか。 — When suits you?
金曜日はどうですか。 — How about Friday?
何時にしますか。 — What time shall we make it?
どこで会(あ)いますか。 — Where shall we meet?
駅の東口で七時に。 — East exit of the station at seven.

**Refusing.** This is the part worth learning properly, because a direct no is rare:

すみません、その日はちょっと…。 — Sorry, that day is a bit…
行きたいんですが、予定(よてい)があって…。 — I'd like to, but I have plans…
また今度(こんど)お願いします。 — Another time, please.

**The sentence is not finished**, and that is the refusal. Completing it would be blunter than necessary. ちょっと on its own, with a slight intake of breath, is a complete and understood no.

**また今度 usually means no**, not "let's do it later". Reading it as a firm plan is a common misunderstanding.

**Practice.** Invite someone for a drink on Friday, fix a time and place, then refuse the same invitation politely. Answers: 今度、飲みに行きませんか。金曜日はどうですか。 · すみません、金曜日はちょっと…。また今度お願いします。
Small talk: weather and seasons:
The default opening of any conversation, and more load-bearing in Japanese than in English.

**The weather openers:**

いい天気(てんき)ですね。 — Nice weather, isn't it.
暑いですね。 — Hot, isn't it.
寒くなりましたね。 — It's got cold, hasn't it.
よく降(ふ)りますね。 — It's been raining a lot.

**ね is compulsory here.** The point is agreement, not information — 暑いです without ね states a fact at someone, which is not what small talk is for.

**Seasonal vocabulary:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 春(はる) | spring — 桜(さくら), 花見(はなみ) |
| 梅雨(つゆ) | rainy season, June |
| 夏(なつ) | summer — 蒸(む)し暑い, 花火, お盆(ぼん) |
| 秋(あき) | autumn — 紅葉(こうよう), 涼(すず)しい |
| 冬(ふゆ) | winter — 雪(ゆき), お正月(しょうがつ) |

**蒸し暑い — humid** — is the summer word and you will hear it constantly. Japanese summers are the thing everyone complains about, and joining in is good small talk.

**Weather words:**

晴(は)れ sunny · 曇(くも)り cloudy · 雨 rain · 雪 snow · 風(かぜ) wind · 台風(たいふう) typhoon · 気温(きおん) temperature · 湿度(しつど) humidity

**The seasons are a serious topic.** Seasonal food, seasonal menus, seasonal greetings in letters. Asking 好きな季節は何ですか is an entirely normal question and produces a real conversation.

**Beyond weather:** 出身(しゅっしん)はどちらですか (where are you from), 日本はどのくらいですか (how long have you been in Japan), 仕事は何ですか. These three carry the first five minutes of most conversations a foreigner has.

**Practice.** Open a conversation about the weather three ways. Then answer: 出身はどちらですか。 · 日本語はどのくらい勉強していますか。
Compliments, and how to accept one:
Receiving a compliment is where Western instincts go most obviously wrong.

**The compliment you will get constantly:**

日本語が上手ですね。 — Your Japanese is good.

**The answer is not ありがとう.** It is a denial:

いいえ、まだまだです。 — No, I've a long way to go.
いいえ、そんなことないです。 — No, not at all.
いいえ、全然です。 — No, not at all.

**Accepting a compliment directly reads as immodest.** The convention is to deflect it, and the deflection is not false modesty — it is the expected move, and both parties know it.

**まだまだです is the all-purpose one** and works for any skill.

**Deflecting to someone or something else** also works:

先生がいいんです。 — I have a good teacher.
運(うん)が良(よ)かっただけです。 — I was just lucky.

**Giving a compliment:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| すごいですね | That's impressive |
| さすがですね | Just what I'd expect from you |
| 上手ですね | You're good at it |
| お似合(にあ)いですね | It suits you |
| おいしそうですね | That looks delicious |

**さすが is worth having** — it means the person has lived up to their reputation, and it is warm without being gushing.

**Do not compliment a superior's work directly.** 勉強になりました — "that was instructive" — is the form it takes upward.

**Praising someone's family, home or food is safe and welcome.** Praising their appearance is more constrained than in English and is best kept to clothes rather than the person.

**Practice.** Respond to 日本語が上手ですね three ways. Then compliment someone's cooking and their new shirt. Answers: いいえ、まだまだです。 · おいしいですね、すごいです。 · そのシャツ、お似合いですね。
Apologising:
Japanese apologises more often, more readily, and with more gradations than English.

**The ladder, light to heavy:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| すみません | Excuse me / sorry — the everyday one |
| ごめんなさい | Sorry — personal, to someone close |
| 申し訳(もうしわけ)ありません | I'm very sorry — formal |
| 申し訳ございません | The most formal |
| 失礼(しつれい)しました | Sorry for the rudeness / excuse me |

**すみません covers an enormous range** — bumping someone, interrupting, being late by a minute, and thanking someone for trouble they took. It is the single most useful word in the language.

**ごめんなさい is warmer and more personal**, and ごめん alone is casual. Using ごめん at work is too casual; using 申し訳ございません to a friend is strange.

**For something real:**

遅(おく)れてすみません。 — Sorry I'm late.
ご迷惑(めいわく)をおかけして、申し訳ありません。 — I'm sorry for the trouble I've caused.

**ご迷惑をおかけして** is the standard formula for having inconvenienced someone, and it appears in every apology announcement on every delayed train.

**Apologising is not admitting fault** in the way it can be in English. It acknowledges that something has gone wrong and that you are part of the situation, which is why both parties often apologise.

**What not to do:** explaining at length before apologising. The apology comes first, the reason second, and the reason should be short. でも at the start of a response to a complaint is received badly.

**Thanking with an apology:** すみません、ありがとうございます — both, for a favour that cost someone something.

**Practice.** Apologise for: being late to meet a friend · being late to a meeting · causing a colleague extra work. Answers: 遅れてごめん。 · 遅れて申し訳ありません。 · ご迷惑をおかけして、申し訳ありません。
Giving and receiving gifts:
A structured practice with its own vocabulary and a reliable script.

**The occasions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| お土産(みやげ) | a souvenir from a trip — expected |
| お中元(ちゅうげん) | mid-year gift, July |
| お歳暮(せいぼ) | year-end gift, December |
| お年玉(としだま) | New Year money for children |
| 手土産(てみやげ) | a small gift when visiting |
| お返(かえ)し | a return gift |

**お土産 is close to compulsory** after any trip, for colleagues especially. Boxed individually-wrapped sweets from the place you went, to be shared out in the office.

**Giving:**

つまらないものですが…。 — It's nothing much, but…
ほんの気持(きも)ちです。 — Just a small token.
皆(みな)さんでどうぞ。 — Please share it.

**つまらないものですが is the classic formula** and is literally "it's a boring thing" — self-deprecation about the gift, which is the convention. It is becoming less common among younger people but is still safe.

**Receiving:**

ありがとうございます。 — Thank you.
わあ、嬉(うれ)しいです。 — Oh, I'm delighted.
よろしいんですか。 — Are you sure?

**よろしいんですか is a light protest** before accepting, and is expected.

**Both hands**, a small bow, and traditionally not opening it in front of the giver — though that has relaxed and 開けてもいいですか is fine.

**お返し is real.** A significant gift creates an obligation to return roughly half the value, which is why large gifts can be a burden rather than a pleasure.

**Avoid:** sets of four (四 sounds like 死, death), clocks, knives, and anything in white-and-black wrapping.

**Practice.** Give a souvenir to a colleague and receive one. Answers: これ、お土産です。皆さんでどうぞ。 · わあ、ありがとうございます。よろしいんですか。
Visiting someone's home:
A rarer event than in many countries, and correspondingly more formal.

**At the door:**

こんにちは。お邪魔(じゃま)します。 — Hello. Sorry to intrude.

**お邪魔します is said on entering** — literally "I will be a nuisance" — and お邪魔しました on leaving. It is not optional.

**Shoes come off in the 玄関(げんかん)**, the entrance, which is a step below the floor level. Turn them to face the door after taking them off. Slippers are usually provided.

**Slippers come off on tatami.** Tatami rooms are socks only. There are also separate toilet slippers — wearing them back into the living room is the classic foreigner's mistake.

**The gift** is handed over at this point: つまらないものですが。

**どうぞお上(あ)がりください** — please come up — is the invitation to step up into the house proper.

**Inside:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 失礼します | Said on sitting, entering a room |
| いただきます | Before eating or drinking what you are given |
| ごちそうさまでした | After |
| そろそろ失礼します | I should be going |

**そろそろ** — "it's about that time" — is how you begin to leave, well before actually leaving. Announcing departure abruptly is abrupt.

**Being offered more** will happen repeatedly, and declining once is not taken as final. もう十分(じゅうぶん)です — I've had plenty — is the polite stop.

**Leaving:** お邪魔しました。ありがとうございました。 And a message afterwards thanking them again is normal.

**Practice.** Walk through: arriving, handing over a gift, being invited in, and leaving. Answers: こんにちは、お邪魔します。これ、つまらないものですが。 · …そろそろ失礼します。お邪魔しました。
Holidays and the calendar:
The year's shape, which structures when things are busy, closed, or impossible to book.

**The big three:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| お正月(しょうがつ) | New Year, 1–3 January. Everything closes. |
| ゴールデンウィーク | late April to early May, a run of holidays |
| お盆(ぼん) | mid-August, when people return to their home towns |

**During all three, travel is full and expensive** and much of the country is shut or elsewhere. Booking anything months ahead is normal.

**Other holidays worth knowing:**

成人(せいじん)の日 Coming of Age Day, January · 春分(しゅんぶん)の日 and 秋分(しゅうぶん)の日, the equinoxes · こどもの日 5 May · 海(うみ)の日 July · 敬老(けいろう)の日 September · 文化(ぶんか)の日 November · 勤労(きんろう)感謝(かんしゃ)の日 November

**振替(ふりかえ)休日(きゅうじつ)** — if a public holiday falls on a Sunday, the Monday is taken instead.

**Seasonal events** that are not holidays but structure the year: 花見(はなみ) cherry blossom viewing in late March and April, 花火大会(はなびたいかい) firework festivals in summer, 紅葉(こうよう) autumn leaves in November, クリスマス which is a couple's evening rather than a family day.

**大晦日(おおみそか)** — New Year's Eve — is spent at home, with 年越(としこ)しそば and a long television programme. 初詣(はつもうで), the first shrine visit of the year, follows in the first days of January.

**The era system.** Years are also counted by imperial era: 令和(れいわ) began in 2019, so 2026 is 令和8年. Official forms use it and it appears on every document.

**Practice.** Say which months hold New Year, Golden Week and Obon. Then convert: 令和8年 is which Western year? And say: I'm going home for Obon. Answer: お盆に実家(じっか)に帰ります。
Talking about what you did:
Narrating the past, which is the commonest thing you will be asked to do in conversation.

**The question:**

週末(しゅうまつ)は何をしましたか。 — What did you do at the weekend?
昨日は何をしましたか。
日本はどうでしたか。 — How was Japan?

**The answer needs sequencing**, and stage 3 gave the tools:

朝(あさ)起きて、友達と会って、映画を見ました。
午前中(ごぜんちゅう)は勉強して、午後は買い物に行きました。
本を読んだり、散歩(さんぽ)したりしました。

**て-form for a sequence, たり for examples.** That distinction is what makes the account sound deliberate rather than listed.

**Time words:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 昨日(きのう) | yesterday |
| 一昨日(おととい) | the day before yesterday |
| 先週(せんしゅう) | last week |
| 先月(せんげつ) | last month |
| 去年(きょねん) | last year |
| この前(まえ) | the other day |
| 〜前(まえ)に | ~ ago |

**三日前に** — three days ago. **一週間前に** — a week ago.

**Giving an impression**, which is what どうでしたか asks for:

楽(たの)しかったです。 — It was fun.
面白かったです。 — It was interesting.
疲(つか)れました。 — I was tired out.
思ったより〜でした。 — It was more ~ than I expected.

**思ったより is worth having** — 思ったより寒かったです, colder than I expected — and it makes an answer sound like an opinion rather than a report.

**Practice.** Answer 週末は何をしましたか in four sentences using て-form, たり, a time word and an impression.
Talking about what you will do:
Plans, intentions and predictions — the forms from stage 3 put to their everyday use.

**The question:** 週末は何をしますか。 · 今度の休みは？ · 将来(しょうらい)どうしますか。

**The ladder of certainty:**

| Form | Certainty |
| --- | --- |
| 〜ます | plain future — I'm doing it |
| 〜予定です | it's scheduled |
| 〜つもりです | I intend to |
| 〜ようと思っています | I'm thinking of |
| 〜かもしれません | I might |
| 〜たいです | I want to |

来週、東京に行きます。 — I'm going to Tokyo next week.
来週、東京に行く予定です。 — I'm scheduled to.
いつか日本に住みたいです。 — I'd like to live in Japan one day.

**Japanese hedges more than English.** Stating a plan flatly can sound like a commitment you are making to the listener, so 〜と思います and 〜予定です soften it. たぶん and 〜かもしれません soften it further.

**Time words:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 明日(あした) | tomorrow |
| 明後日(あさって) | the day after tomorrow |
| 来週(らいしゅう) | next week |
| 再来週(さらいしゅう) | the week after next |
| 来月(らいげつ) · 来年(らいねん) | next month · next year |
| そのうち | sometime, eventually |
| いつか | someday |

**まだ決(き)めていません** — I haven't decided yet — is a complete and common answer, and uses the ている form correctly from stage 2.

**Practice.** Answer 週末は何をしますか with a plan, an intention and a possibility. Example: 土曜日は友達と会う予定です。日曜日は勉強しようと思っています。天気がよかったら、散歩するかもしれません。
Asking for time off, and sick days:
A short conversation with real consequences for how you are perceived.

**The vocabulary:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 有給(ゆうきゅう)休暇(きゅうか) | paid leave — usually shortened to 有給 |
| 休(やす)みを取(と)る | to take time off |
| 早退(そうたい) | leaving early |
| 遅刻(ちこく) | being late |
| 欠勤(けっきん) | absence |
| 代休(だいきゅう) | a day off in lieu |
| 申請(しんせい) | application |

**Asking:**

来週の金曜日、有給を取りたいんですが、よろしいでしょうか。 — I'd like to take leave next Friday; would that be all right?

**んですが、よろしいでしょうか** is the formula. The explanatory ending plus a deferential question.

**Calling in sick:**

おはようございます。[name]です。
申し訳ありませんが、熱があるので、今日は休ませていただきます。

**休ませていただきます** is the causative plus humble receiving — "I will humbly receive permission to rest" — and is the standard phrasing. It is not asking; it is announcing while sounding like asking.

**Giving a reason is expected** for sickness and is not expected for 有給 — paid leave is an entitlement and you do not have to justify it, though in practice many people do. 私用(しよう)で — "for personal reasons" — is a complete answer.

**Taking leave is culturally fraught** in some workplaces despite being a legal right, and a law since 2019 requires employees to take at least five days a year. The expectation of apology around it is real.

**On returning:** ご迷惑をおかけしました — sorry for the trouble.

**Practice.** Ask for next Friday off. Then call in sick with a fever. Answers: 来週の金曜日、有給を取りたいんですが、よろしいでしょうか。 · 申し訳ありませんが、熱があるので、今日は休ませていただきます。
Hobbies and free time:
The second thing anyone asks you, after where you are from.

**The question:** 趣味(しゅみ)は何ですか。 — What are your hobbies?

**The answers:**

趣味は読書(どくしょ)です。 — My hobby is reading.
ゲームをするのが好きです。 — I like playing games.
絵(え)を描(か)くのが趣味です。 — Drawing is my hobby.

**〜のが好きです** uses the nominaliser from stage 3 and is the natural pattern: verb + のが + 好き.

**Common hobbies:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 読書 | reading |
| 映画(えいが)を見ること | watching films |
| 音楽(おんがく)を聞くこと | listening to music |
| 料理(りょうり) | cooking |
| 旅行(りょこう) | travel |
| 写真(しゃしん) | photography |
| 絵を描くこと | drawing |
| ゲーム | games |
| 散歩(さんぽ) | walking |
| 筋(きん)トレ | weight training |

**Sports take する or やる:**

サッカーをします · テニスをします · 泳(およ)ぎます · 走(はし)ります

**How long and how often**, which is what the follow-up question asks:

三年前から始(はじ)めました。 — I started three years ago.
週に二回(しゅうににかい)くらいです。 — About twice a week.
たまにやります。 — I do it occasionally.

**週に〜回** — ~ times a week — is the frequency pattern: 月に一回, 年に二回.

**Modesty applies here too.** 下手ですけど、好きです — "I'm bad at it, but I enjoy it" — is the normal register for talking about something you do well.

**Practice.** Answer 趣味は何ですか with three sentences: what it is, how long you have done it, how often. Then ask it back.
Hair, nails and the barber:
A short errand that is surprisingly hard without the vocabulary, because it is all specifics.

**The shops:** 美容院(びよういん) a salon, 床屋(とこや) or 理髪店(りはつてん) a barber, 1000円カット the quick-cut chains.

**The sentences:**

カットをお願いします。 — A cut, please.
短(みじか)くしてください。 — Shorter, please.
あまり短くしないでください。 — Not too short.
〜センチ切(き)ってください。 — Take off ~ centimetres.
そろえるだけでいいです。 — Just a trim.
前(まえ)は切らないでください。 — Don't cut the front.

**The vocabulary:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 前髪(まえがみ) | fringe |
| 横(よこ) | sides |
| 後ろ(うしろ) | back |
| 毛先(けさき) | the ends |
| すく | to thin out |
| 刈(か)り上(あ)げる | to clip short, fade |
| シャンプー | shampoo |
| ブロー | blow dry |
| 染(そ)める | to dye |
| パーマ | perm |

**Showing a photograph works** and is what most people do, including Japanese customers.

**What they will ask:**

今日はどうされますか。 — What are we doing today?
このくらいですか。 — About this much?
いかがですか。 — How does that look? (at the end)

**いかがですか at the end** expects だいじょうぶです or ありがとうございます, not a critique.

**Shampoo is usually included** and happens lying back, and a head massage often comes with it. 1000円カット chains skip all of it and take ten minutes.

**Practice.** Ask for a cut, two centimetres off, not too short at the front. Answer: カットをお願いします。二センチくらい切ってください。前髪はあまり短くしないでください。
Set phrases you will hear constantly:
A collection of fixed expressions that are everywhere and that cannot be worked out from their parts.

| Japanese | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| お疲れさまです | Hello, goodbye, well done, acknowledgement |
| よろしくお願いします | Over to you, nice to meet you, please handle this |
| お世話になっております | Opening any business contact |
| 失礼します | Entering, leaving, interrupting, hanging up |
| 恐(おそ)れ入(い)ります | Sorry to trouble you / thank you (formal) |
| 大丈夫です | I'm fine / no thanks / that's OK |
| とりあえず | For now, to start with |
| やっぱり | As I thought / actually, on reflection |
| なるほど | I see / that makes sense |
| そうですね | Yes, indeed / let me think |
| ちょっと… | No. (unfinished) |
| お待たせしました | Sorry to have kept you waiting |
| いただきます / ごちそうさま | Before and after eating |
| どうぞ | Please, go ahead, here you are |
| どうも | Thanks / hello — context decides |

**そうですね does two opposite jobs.** With falling intonation it agrees; drawn out with rising intonation it is "hmm, let me think" and often precedes a disagreement. The intonation carries the whole meaning.

**やっぱり is one of the most used words in the language.** It covers "I knew it", "after all", and "actually, on second thoughts" — やっぱりやめます, I'll pass after all.

**どうも is a shortening of several things** — どうもありがとう, どうもすみません — and on its own is a light, slightly casual thanks or greeting.

**なるほど is for peers and downward**, not to a superior, where it can read as evaluating what they said. そうなんですね is safer upward.

**Practice.** Use five of these in sentences today, aloud. Then listen for そうですね in anything you watch and decide each time which of its two jobs it is doing.
Numbers in the wild: phones, addresses a:
Reading and saying the numbers that appear on forms, which behave differently from counting.

**Phone numbers** are read digit by digit, with の for the hyphen:

090-1234-5678 → ゼロきゅうゼロ の いちにさんよん の ごろくななはち

**ゼロ or れい for 0.** ゼロ in speech, 零 in formal writing. **4 is よん, 7 is なな, 9 is きゅう** — the unambiguous readings, always, because し and しち are confusable over a line.

**Addresses run largest to smallest**, the opposite of Western order:

〒150-0001
東京都渋谷区神宮前1-2-3 マンション名 405号室

Postcode, prefecture, city, ward, district, block numbers, building, room. The 〒 symbol marks a postcode.

**The administrative words:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 都(と) · 道(どう) · 府(ふ) · 県(けん) | the four kinds of prefecture |
| 市(し) | city |
| 区(く) | ward |
| 町(ちょう・まち) | town |
| 丁目(ちょうめ) | district number |
| 番地(ばんち) | block number |
| 号(ごう) | building number |

**1-2-3 is 一丁目二番三号** spoken in full, and 1の2の3 informally.

**Dates** are year, month, day — 2026年10月13日 — and official forms also take the era: 令和8年.

**Money** past ten thousand uses 万: ¥25,000 is 二万五千円.

**Counting people in a form** uses 名(めい): 2名様.

**Practice.** Say your phone number aloud in Japanese. Then read: 〒160-0022 東京都新宿区新宿3-1-1. Then write today's date in both Western and era form.
Irodori Elementary 2:
The third of Irodori's four levels, and the one that matches this stage.

**What it covers.** Eighteen lessons of more complex situations: workplace conversation, explaining a problem in detail, giving opinions, making arrangements, dealing with trouble. The Can-do statements get longer and involve more turns.

**Why it fits here.** Stage 4 has given you the vocabulary for each of these situations and stage 3 gave the grammar to connect sentences. Elementary 2 is where both get used at conversational length rather than in single exchanges.

**The method does not change:**

1. Listen before reading.
2. Read, check what you missed.
3. Shadow it.
4. Do the worksheet.
5. Read the Can-do and ask honestly whether you can do it.

**What to add at this level: role-play both sides.** Record yourself as the customer and the staff member. Producing the staff keigo is useful even though you will not need it, because it is what you will *hear*, and producing something is the fastest way to recognise it.

**Mine the word lists.** By now mining should be a habit, and Irodori's lists come with audio. Ten words a lesson is plenty.

**After Elementary 2** comes Pre-Intermediate, which belongs to stage 5. At that point Irodori runs out and the functional strand becomes native material — which is the whole point of the arrangement.

**Practice.** Do Elementary 2 lesson 1 today by the five steps, including role-playing both sides.
Reading: Tadoku level 3:
Thirty-nine booklets, and the level where graded readers stop feeling graded.

**What changes.** Longer texts, chapters, and subjects rather than scenes — biographies, folk tales, explanations of how things work. The vocabulary is no longer controlled as tightly, and you will meet words that are simply unknown.

**The rules still hold**, and the third one matters more now than it did:

1. No dictionary.
2. Skip what you do not understand.
3. **Put it down if it is not working.** With 39 to choose from, there is no reason to push through one that is a slog.
4. Go down a level rather than struggle.

**What to watch at this level: whether you are hearing it.** Reading Japanese fluently means the words sound in your head as you go. If you are decoding — working out each kanji, then assembling — you are still below the level. Going back to level 2 and reading ten more is the fix, and it is a faster fix than struggling upward.

**Reading aloud occasionally helps here**, which contradicts the extensive-reading rule and is worth the exception once a week: it forces the sounding-out that silent reading can skip.

**After level 3.** Level 4 is 24 booklets and level 5 is four, including a Sherlock Holmes story. Past that is native material for children — 絵本, then 児童書(じどうしょ) — and NHK News Web Easy should by now be comfortable.

**Practice.** Read three level 3 booklets this week. For one of them, read a page aloud and notice how much slower it is than reading it silently. That gap is the thing closing.
Listening: real news:
The step from material made for learners to material made for Japanese people, taken on the easiest available ground.

**NHK's news is the right first native listening** because it is read slowly, in standard Tokyo Japanese, with no slang, and because the vocabulary repeats every day.

**Three sources, in order of difficulty:**

1. **NHK News Web Easy** — the articles have audio, read slowly. Start here.
2. **NHK ラジオニュース** — the real thing, free, updated hourly, about five minutes.
3. **NHK ニュース7** — television news, with pictures, which carry a lot.

**The method:**

- Listen once without the text.
- Listen again with the transcript, if there is one.
- Listen a third time without it.

**The third listen is the one that counts.** The gain is in hearing something you could not hear twenty minutes earlier, and it is immediate and measurable in a way most listening practice is not.

**News vocabulary is a closed set** and learning two hundred words unlocks most of it: 政府(せいふ), 発表(はっぴょう), 影響(えいきょう), 対応(たいおう), 可能性(かのうせい), 増加(ぞうか), 減少(げんしょう). They recur constantly, which is exactly what makes news a good place to start.

**Do not expect to follow a drama yet.** Scripted entertainment is far harder than news — fast, overlapping, slangy, full of implication. It comes in stage 6.

**Practice.** Listen to one NHK Easy article's audio three times, as above. Write down three words you heard repeatedly and mine them.
Writing: a longer text:
From a paragraph to a page, and from describing to arguing.

**The step up.** A paragraph says what happened. A longer text needs structure: an opening, points in order, and a close. Japanese has conventions for all three.

**Connectives for structure**, from stage 3 and extended:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| まず | first |
| 次(つぎ)に | next |
| それから | after that |
| また | also |
| 一方(いっぽう) | on the other hand |
| しかし | however |
| そのため | therefore |
| 最後(さいご)に | finally |

**Written Japanese uses the plain form**, not ます — the だ・である style. A text addressed to nobody in particular takes plain form, which was the point of the plain-and-polite lesson. Mixing the two in one text is the commonest error.

**Keep sentences short.** Japanese allows enormous sentences and good modern writing does not use them. One idea per sentence, joined by the connectives above.

**What to write.** A description of your town, an argument for something you believe, a summary of a Tadoku book you read, an account of a trip. Three hundred characters is a sensible target — about a screen.

**Getting it corrected.** HelloTalk works for a paragraph and is thin for a page. Lang-8's successor **HiNative** takes longer texts, and a tutor on italki will correct writing between lessons.

**Keep them.** Six months of these read back is the measure of the whole stage.

**Practice.** Write 300 characters in plain form about your home town, using at least four of the connectives above.
Speaking: a transaction from start to fi:
The test of this stage: a complete real-world exchange, unscripted, without switching to English.

**Pick one and do it entirely in Japanese:**

- Order a meal, ask a question about the menu, and pay.
- Buy something, ask whether they have another size or colour, and pay.
- Ask for directions and follow them.
- Book a table by phone.
- Buy a train ticket to somewhere you have not been.

**The rules you set yourself:**

1. **No English**, even if they switch to it. 日本語で大丈夫です is a complete and polite way to say so.
2. **Ask for a repeat** rather than nodding: すみません、もう一度お願いします。
3. **Finish the exchange**, however badly it goes.

**What will go wrong.** You will miss the question about bags or heating. You will not catch a number. Someone will speak at full speed and you will get nothing. All of that is normal and none of it matters — the exchange still completes, because the script is doing most of the work.

**The one phrase that saves everything:** ゆっくりお願いします。

**Why this is the test.** Reading, listening and writing can all be done alone, at your own pace, and they improve steadily and invisibly. Speaking is the one that cannot, and the gap between what you know and what you can produce under pressure is only closed by being under pressure.

**If you are not in Japan**, the equivalent is a 30-minute italki conversation lesson, or a voice call on HelloTalk. Not text — the pressure is the point.

**Practice.** Do one of the five above this week. Afterwards, write down the one sentence you wished you had been able to say, and learn it.
Review: the everyday can-do list:
The end of stage 4. A checklist of things you should now be able to do rather than know.

**Go down the list and, for each, say the Japanese aloud.** Anything you cannot produce in one go is a lesson to revisit.

**Shops and money**
- Ask whether they have something, in another size or colour
- Answer every question at a convenience store till
- Ask how much, and understand the answer
- Return something that is broken

**Food**
- Enter a restaurant, be seated, order, and pay
- Read a menu and order a set meal
- Say what you cannot eat, and ask what is in something
- Order the first round at an izakaya

**Transport**
- Buy a ticket from a machine and adjust the fare at the other end
- Read a platform board and tell an express from a local
- Ask for directions and follow the answer
- Take a bus with 整理券

**Living**
- Describe a symptom at a clinic
- Buy medicine for a specific complaint
- Make, change and cancel a booking
- Ask about rubbish day

**Work and people**
- Introduce yourself formally
- Ask for a day off
- Answer a phone call and take a message
- Invite someone out, and refuse an invitation politely
- Receive a compliment, apologise properly, and give a gift

**What stage 5 does.** Intermediate grammar — the forms that let you say complicated things rather than correct ones — and the move from graded material to native. The functional ground is covered; what follows is depth.

**Practice.** Work down the list honestly. Then pick the three weakest and do something about each this week.
Kanji 6 · 今 先 来 毎 週 午 間 何:
Eight more, continuing down the frequency list. Each is given with the readings it takes and the words those readings appear in — a character on its own has a meaning and no pronunciation.

Time and frequency — the characters behind the words stage 2 and 4 used for saying when.

| Kanji | Strokes | Readings | In words |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 今 | 4 | コン / いま | 今 ima · 今日 kyō · 今週 konshū · 今年 kotoshi |
| 先 | 6 | セン / さき | 先生 sensei · 先週 senshū · 先に saki ni |
| 来 | 7 | ライ / く-る | 来る kuru · 来週 raishū · 来年 rainen |
| 毎 | 6 | マイ | 毎日 mainichi · 毎週 maishū · 毎朝 maiasa |
| 週 | 11 | シュウ | 今週 konshū · 週末 shūmatsu · 一週間 isshūkan |
| 午 | 4 | ゴ | 午前 gozen · 午後 gogo · 正午 shōgo |
| 間 | 12 | カン・ケン / あいだ・ま | 時間 jikan · 間 aida · 人間 ningen · 一週間 isshūkan |
| 何 | 7 | カ / なに・なん | 何 nani / nan · 何時 nanji · 何人 nannin |

**先 and 来 are opposites in time.** 先週 is last week and 来週 is next week — "ahead" is the past and "coming" is the future, which is the reverse of the English metaphor and worth a moment's thought.

**今 has four readings in four very common words**: 今 いま, 今日 きょう, 今週 こんしゅう, 今年 ことし. Only 今週 is regular. The other three are learned whole.

**間 is both かん and あいだ**, and the difference is grammatical: 時間 and 一週間 use かん for a span of time; 間 alone is あいだ, the gap between two things, as in 銀行と郵便局の間.

**何 is なん before です and before counters**, なに otherwise — the rule from stage 2, now in its character.

**Writing.** Watch each on Jisho once, trace it, then write it from memory before checking. The cards ask for exactly that, and the panel beside the card keeps what you wrote, so the previous attempt is there to compare against.

**Practice.** Write every word in the table by hand, then cover the readings and read them back.
Kanji 7 · 口 目 耳 手 足 力 心 体:
Eight more, continuing down the frequency list. Each is given with the readings it takes and the words those readings appear in — a character on its own has a meaning and no pronunciation.

The body, which is also a large share of the idioms in the language.

| Kanji | Strokes | Readings | In words |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 口 | 3 | コウ・ク / くち | 口 kuchi · 入口 iriguchi · 出口 deguchi · 人口 jinkō |
| 目 | 5 | モク / め | 目 me · 一つ目 hitotsume · 目的 mokuteki |
| 耳 | 6 | ジ / みみ | 耳 mimi |
| 手 | 4 | シュ / て | 手 te · 上手 jōzu · 手紙 tegami · 切手 kitte |
| 足 | 7 | ソク / あし・た-りる | 足 ashi · 足りる tariru · 一足 issoku |
| 力 | 2 | リョク・リキ / ちから | 力 chikara · 体力 tairyoku · 努力 doryoku |
| 心 | 4 | シン / こころ | 心 kokoro · 安心 anshin · 心配 shinpai |
| 体 | 7 | タイ / からだ | 体 karada · 体力 tairyoku · 体育 taiiku |

**口 is in 入口 and 出口**, the signs from stage 4 — entrance and exit, literally "entering mouth" and "exiting mouth". It is also 人口, population.

**目 makes ordinals**: 一つ目, 二つ目, 三つ目 — the first, second and third one — which is how directions are given.

**足 is both "foot/leg" and "to suffice"**: 足りる, to be enough. 足りない is "not enough" and is extremely common.

**心配(しんぱい) is "worry"** and 安心(あんしん) is "relief" — literally scattered heart and settled heart. 心配しないで is "don't worry".

**口 the character and ロ the katakana** are a pair to keep apart: the kanji is wider and sits heavier on the line.

**Writing.** Watch each on Jisho once, trace it, then write it from memory before checking. The cards ask for exactly that, and the panel beside the card keeps what you wrote, so the previous attempt is there to compare against.

**Practice.** Write every word in the table by hand, then cover the readings and read them back.
Kanji 8 · 子 女 男 父 母 友 名 私:
Eight more, continuing down the frequency list. Each is given with the readings it takes and the words those readings appear in — a character on its own has a meaning and no pronunciation.

People, and the family words from stage 2 in the characters they are written with.

| Kanji | Strokes | Readings | In words |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 子 | 3 | シ / こ | 子供 kodomo · 女の子 onna no ko · 椅子 isu |
| 女 | 3 | ジョ / おんな | 女 onna · 女性 josei · 彼女 kanojo |
| 男 | 7 | ダン / おとこ | 男 otoko · 男性 dansei |
| 父 | 4 | フ / ちち | 父 chichi · お父さん otōsan · 父親 chichioya |
| 母 | 5 | ボ / はは | 母 haha · お母さん okāsan · 母親 hahaoya |
| 友 | 4 | ユウ / とも | 友達 tomodachi · 友人 yūjin |
| 名 | 6 | メイ / な | 名前 namae · 有名 yūmei · 何名 nanmei |
| 私 | 7 | シ / わたし | 私 watashi · 私立 shiritsu |

**男 is 田 over 力** — a field and strength — and is one of the clearer pictographic compounds.

**父 and 母 take two readings each, and both are needed**: ちち and はは for your own, とう and かあ inside お父さん and お母さん. That is the humble/polite split from stage 2, visible in the characters.

**友達(ともだち) is irregular** — だち rather than たち — and is one of the first irregular compounds anyone meets.

**名 appears in three very different words**: 名前 a name, 有名 famous, 何名 how many people. The last is the polite counter from the restaurant lesson.

**私 is read わたし here and し in compounds**, and in formal speech it is わたくし. It is also one of several words for "I" — 僕(ぼく), 俺(おれ) and others carry gender and register, which stage 5 covers.

**Writing.** Watch each on Jisho once, trace it, then write it from memory before checking. The cards ask for exactly that, and the panel beside the card keeps what you wrote, so the previous attempt is there to compare against.

**Practice.** Write every word in the table by hand, then cover the readings and read them back.
Kanji 9 · 学 校 生 字 読 書 聞 語:
Eight more, continuing down the frequency list. Each is given with the readings it takes and the words those readings appear in — a character on its own has a meaning and no pronunciation.

School and language — including the characters for the thing you are doing right now.

| Kanji | Strokes | Readings | In words |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 学 | 8 | ガク / まな-ぶ | 学校 gakkō · 大学 daigaku · 学生 gakusei · 学ぶ manabu |
| 校 | 10 | コウ | 学校 gakkō · 高校 kōkō · 校長 kōchō |
| 生 | 5 | セイ・ショウ / い-きる・う-まれる・なま | 学生 gakusei · 先生 sensei · 生まれる umareru · 生ビール nama bīru |
| 字 | 6 | ジ | 漢字 kanji · 文字 moji · 字 ji · ローマ字 rōmaji |
| 読 | 14 | ドク / よ-む | 読む yomu · 読書 dokusho |
| 書 | 10 | ショ / か-く | 書く kaku · 辞書 jisho · 図書館 toshokan |
| 聞 | 14 | ブン / き-く | 聞く kiku · 新聞 shinbun |
| 語 | 14 | ゴ / かた-る | 日本語 nihongo · 英語 eigo · 単語 tango · 語る kataru |

**生 is the hardest-working character in the language**, with a dozen readings. The four here are the common ones: セイ in 学生, 先生; ショウ in 一生(いっしょう); う-まれる to be born; なま raw, as in 生ビール, draught beer. A character with this many readings is learned purely through its words.

**聞 is 門 with 耳 inside** — an ear in a gate — and means both "to hear" and "to ask". 聞く does both jobs, and which is meant comes from the particle: 音楽を聞く is listening, 先生に聞く is asking.

**書 appears in 図書館(としょかん), the library** — "picture-book hall" — and in 辞書, a dictionary.

**語 is the "language" suffix**: 日本語, 英語, フランス語, 中国語. Attach it to a country and you have the language.

**漢字 is "Han characters"** — 漢 is the Han dynasty, and the whole writing system is named after where it was borrowed from.

**Writing.** Watch each on Jisho once, trace it, then write it from memory before checking. The cards ask for exactly that, and the panel beside the card keeps what you wrote, so the previous attempt is there to compare against.

Kanji 10 · 見 言 話 食 飲 買 出 入:
Eight more, continuing down the frequency list. Each is given with the readings it takes and the words those readings appear in — a character on its own has a meaning and no pronunciation.

The commonest verbs, in the characters they are written with. Every one of these has been used since stage 2 in kana.

| Kanji | Strokes | Readings | In words |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 見 | 7 | ケン / み-る | 見る miru · 意見 iken · 見せる miseru |
| 言 | 7 | ゲン・ゴン / い-う・こと | 言う iu · 言葉 kotoba · 方言 hōgen |
| 話 | 13 | ワ / はな-す・はなし | 話す hanasu · 話 hanashi · 電話 denwa · 会話 kaiwa |
| 食 | 9 | ショク / た-べる | 食べる taberu · 食事 shokuji · 和食 washoku · 食堂 shokudō |
| 飲 | 12 | イン / の-む | 飲む nomu · 飲み物 nomimono · 飲食 inshoku |
| 買 | 12 | バイ / か-う | 買う kau · 買い物 kaimono |
| 出 | 5 | シュツ / で-る・だ-す | 出る deru · 出す dasu · 出口 deguchi · 出発 shuppatsu |

**出 and 入 are the transitive/intransitive pair from stage 3**, each with both verbs in one character: 出る it comes out, 出す to take it out; 入る to go in, 入れる to put in. The okurigana — the kana after the character — is what tells them apart, and that is what okurigana is for.

**話 contains 言**, which is the "speech" radical and appears in 語, 読, 記 and dozens more. Spotting a radical is how an unknown character stops being completely unknown.

**言葉(ことば) is "word" or "language"** — literally "speech leaves" — and is one of the more attractive compounds in the language.

**入 and 人 differ by which stroke is longer**, and they are easy to confuse written small. 入 has the right stroke crossing over the top; 人 does not.

**That is seventy-nine characters**, and roughly 40% of the characters in ordinary running text. The curve is steep at the start by design.

**Writing.** Watch each on Jisho once, trace it, then write it from memory before checking. The cards ask for exactly that, and the panel beside the card keeps what you wrote, so the previous attempt is there to compare against.

**Practice.** Write every word in the table by hand, then cover the readings and read them back.
～ところ — the point in time:
ところ means "place" and, attached to a verb, means a **point in a process**. Which point depends on the form of the verb, and the three are worth learning together.

| Form | Means |
| --- | --- |
| 〜る**ところ** | about to |
| 〜ている**ところ** | in the middle of |
| 〜た**ところ** | just finished |

今から出かける**ところです**。 — I'm just about to go out.
今、食べている**ところです**。 — I'm in the middle of eating.
今、終わった**ところです**。 — I've just finished.

**It is narrower than the plain forms.** 食べています is "I'm eating" generally; 食べているところです is "right now, at this moment, I am in the middle of eating" — and it is the natural answer to 今何をしていますか.

**〜たところ versus 〜たばかり.** Both are "just did", and they differ in what "just" measures:

- 今来**たところです**。 — I arrived just now. (clock time, minutes)
- 去年日本に来**たばかりです**。 — I only came to Japan last year. (subjective, any span)

ばかり is about how recent it *feels*; ところ is about how recent it *is*.

**ところ with を or に continues the sentence:**

出かけるところ**を**友達に会った。 — Just as I was leaving, I met a friend.
いいところ**に**来たね。 — You've come at a good moment.

**ところで, as a sentence opener, means "by the way"** — a different word with the same spelling, and extremely common in conversation.

**Practice.** Answer 今何をしていますか three ways: about to eat, in the middle of eating, just finished eating. Answers: 今から食べるところです。 · 今、食べているところです。 · 今、食べたところです。
～はじめる, ～だす, ～つづける, ～おわる:
Four verbs that attach to a ます stem and mark the phase of an action. They are compound verbs, and they conjugate as ordinary group 2 or group 1 verbs once formed.

| Ending | Means |
| --- | --- |
| 〜はじめる | to start doing |
| 〜だす | to suddenly start doing |
| 〜つづける | to keep doing |
| 〜おわる | to finish doing |

日本語を勉強し**はじめました**。 — I started studying Japanese.
急(きゅう)に雨が降り**だしました**。 — It suddenly started raining.
三時間走り**つづけました**。 — I kept running for three hours.
本を読み**おわりました**。 — I finished reading the book.

**はじめる and だす both mean "start" and are not interchangeable.**

- **はじめる** is deliberate and often planned: 勉強しはじめる.
- **だす** is sudden, unexpected, and often outside your control: 泣(な)きだす, 降りだす, 笑(わら)いだす.

So 赤ちゃんが泣きだした — the baby burst into tears — takes だす. 来年から勉強しはじめます takes はじめる. Using だす for something you chose sounds like it happened to you.

**〜おわる versus 〜てしまう.** おわる is neutral completion; しまう from stage 3 carries thoroughness or regret. 読みおわりました is "I finished it"; 読んでしまいました is "I got through it" or "I read it, more fool me".

**They stack with other grammar normally:** 読みはじめたばかりです — I've only just started reading it.

**Practice.** Say: I started learning Japanese two years ago. · It suddenly started raining. · He kept talking for an hour. · I finished writing the email. Answers: 二年前に日本語を勉強しはじめました。 · 急に雨が降りだしました。 · 一時間話しつづけました。 · メールを書きおわりました。
～きる, ～きれない, ～かける:
Three more compound endings, about completeness and its absence.

**〜きる — to do completely, to the end.**

本を読み**きりました**。 — I read the book right through.
使い**きる** — to use up entirely.

It carries effort or exhaustiveness beyond おわる: 走りきる is to run the whole way, not merely to finish running.

**〜きれない — cannot finish, too much to.**

食べ**きれません**。 — I can't eat it all.
数(かぞ)え**きれない**ほどあります。 — There are more than you could count.

This is the more common of the pair, and it is the polite way to leave food.

**〜かける — half-done, or on the point of.**

言い**かけて**やめました。 — I started to say something and stopped.
読み**かけ**の本 — a book I'm part-way through.
死に**かけた**。 — I nearly died.

**〜かけ as a noun** is useful: 食べかけ (partly eaten), 書きかけ (half-written).

**The distinction between かける and はじめる:** はじめる starts and continues; かける starts and does *not* continue, or has not yet. 言いかける is to begin a sentence you then abandon.

**〜ぬく — to do through to the end, against difficulty:**

最後(さいご)までやり**ぬきました**。 — I saw it through to the end.

ぬく is rarer and carries real determination. 生きぬく, 戦(たたか)いぬく.

**Practice.** Say: I can't eat it all. · I read it right through. · It's a half-finished book. · I nearly forgot. Answers: 食べきれません。 · 読みきりました。 · 読みかけの本です。 · 忘れかけました。
～なおす, ～あう, ～こむ:
Three more compound verbs, each very productive.

**〜なおす — to redo, to do again properly.**

書き**なおして**ください。 — Please rewrite it.
考(かんが)え**なおしました**。 — I reconsidered.
やり**なおす** — to start over.

It implies the first attempt was unsatisfactory, which is why 見なおす means both "to look again" and "to reassess, to think better of".

**〜あう — to do to each other, mutually.**

話し**あう** — to discuss (talk with each other)
愛(あい)し**あう** — to love each other
助(たす)け**あう** — to help each other
知り**あう** — to get to know each other

**知り合い(しりあい)** — an acquaintance — is this ending frozen into a noun, and so is 話し合い, a discussion.

**〜こむ — inward, or thoroughly.**

**Inward:** 飛(と)び**こむ** to jump in · 乗(の)り**こむ** to board · 持ち**こむ** to bring in · 書き**こむ** to write in

**Thoroughly:** 考え**こむ** to think deeply · 眠(ねむ)り**こむ** to fall fast asleep · 話し**こむ** to talk at length

**Compound verbs are how Japanese extends its verb vocabulary** without borrowing, and there are thousands. Recognising the second half is most of the work: a verb ending in こむ is going inward or going deep; one ending in あう is mutual; one ending in なおす is a second attempt.

**That recognition is the point of this lesson.** You will meet compound verbs you have never seen, constantly, and being able to read them from their parts is worth more than memorising a list.

**Practice.** Guess the meaning of: 読みなおす · 言いあう · 払(はら)いこむ · 思いこむ. Answers: to reread · to argue · to pay in · to be convinced of something (wrongly).
～がち, ～ぎみ, ～っぽい:
Three endings for tendencies and leanings, all slightly negative.

**〜がち — tends to, is prone to.** Attaches to a ます stem or a noun:

忘(わす)れ**がち**です。 — I tend to forget.
曇(くも)り**がち** — tending to be cloudy
病気(びょうき)**がち** — sickly

It is nearly always about something unwanted. 遅れがち, 休みがち, 忘れがち.

**〜ぎみ — a touch of, slightly.** A ます stem or a noun:

風邪(かぜ)**ぎみ**です。 — I've got a bit of a cold.
疲(つか)れ**ぎみ**です。 — I'm feeling a bit worn out.
太(ふと)り**ぎみ** — a bit on the heavy side

ぎみ is milder than がち and is about a current state rather than a tendency.

**〜っぽい — -ish, having the quality of.** Attaches to nouns, adjective stems and ます stems:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 子供(こども)っぽい | childish |
| 忘れっぽい | forgetful |
| 怒(おこ)りっぽい | quick-tempered |
| water っぽい → 水っぽい | watery |
| 安っぽい | cheap-looking |

**っぽい is casual and usually critical.** 子供っぽい is not a compliment, where 子供らしい — using らしい from stage 3 — means childlike in a good way. That contrast is worth holding: っぽい says it resembles the thing unflatteringly, らしい says it is a good example of the thing.

**In very casual speech っぽい attaches to whole clauses** and means "seems like": 雨が降るっぽい — looks like rain. This is recent and informal.

**Practice.** Say: I tend to be late. · I've got a bit of a cold. · He's quick-tempered. · That's childish. Answers: 遅れがちです。 · 風邪ぎみです。 · 怒りっぽいです。 · 子供っぽいです。
～はずだ and ～はずがない:
はず expresses expectation based on reason — "it should be the case" — and is one of the most useful intermediate forms.

今日は休みの**はずです**。 — It should be a holiday today.
田中さんは来る**はずです**。 — Tanaka is supposed to be coming.

**It is not probability.** はず means you have grounds: a schedule, an arrangement, a rule. でしょう is a guess; はず is an inference.

**It attaches to the plain form.** Nouns take の, な-adjectives take な:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| verb | 来るはず |
| い-adj | 寒いはず |
| な-adj | 静か**な**はず |
| noun | 休み**の**はず |

**〜はずがない — "there's no way".**

彼(かれ)が知っている**はずがありません**。 — There's no way he knows.

Stronger than ないはずです, which is "he's probably not supposed to". はずがない denies the possibility.

**〜はずだった — it was supposed to be, and was not.**

三時に来る**はずだった**んですが…。 — He was supposed to come at three, but…

This carries disappointment and is usually followed by an explanation, or trails off.

**はず versus べき.** はず is what you expect to happen; べき is what *ought* to happen morally. 行くはずです — he's expected to go. 行くべきです — he should go, it is right that he does.

**Practice.** Say: The shop should be open today. · There's no way he's forgotten. · She was supposed to come at six. Answers: 今日は店が開いているはずです。 · 忘れたはずがありません。 · 六時に来るはずだったんですが…。
～に違いない and ～おそれがある:
Two ways of stating near-certainty, one personal and one institutional.

**〜に違(ちが)いない — "must be", "I'm sure".**

彼は知っている**に違いない**。 — He must know.
これは田中さんの傘(かさ)**に違いありません**。 — This must be Tanaka's umbrella.

It attaches to the plain form; nouns and な-adjectives take nothing extra: 学生に違いない.

**It is a conclusion, not evidence.** You have reasoned your way there and are confident. It is stronger than でしょう, stronger than はず, and weaker than a flat statement.

**きっと pairs with it** and often appears in the same sentence: きっと忘れたに違いない.

**〜おそれがある — "there is a risk that".**

台風(たいふう)が来る**おそれがあります**。 — There is a risk of a typhoon.
事故(じこ)の**おそれがあります**。 — There is a danger of an accident.

**It is only for bad outcomes**, and it is the register of news and official warnings. You will hear it in every weather bulletin. A good outcome takes 可能性(かのうせい)がある — there is a possibility.

**可能性がある is neutral** and covers both: 雨の可能性があります.

**The ladder of certainty**, assembled from this stage and the last:

| | Roughly |
| --- | --- |
| かもしれない | might — 50% |
| でしょう / だろう | probably — 70% |
| はずだ | should be, by reason |
| に違いない | must be — near certain |
| 〜 | flat statement |

**Practice.** Say: He must be tired. · There's a risk of rain tomorrow. · She might not come. Answers: 疲れているに違いありません。 · 明日は雨のおそれがあります。 · 来ないかもしれません。
～わけだ, ～わけではない, ～わけがない:
わけ means "reason" and forms three expressions that look alike and mean very different things. This is the set that most often goes wrong.

**〜わけだ — "so that's why", a conclusion that now makes sense.**

寒い**わけだ**。窓が開いている。 — No wonder it's cold. The window's open.
三年住んでいたんですか。日本語が上手な**わけです**ね。 — You lived there three years? That explains your Japanese.

It is the sound of something clicking into place. なるほど often precedes it.

**〜わけではない — "it's not that…", a partial denial.**

嫌(きら)いな**わけではない**んですが、あまり食べません。 — It's not that I dislike it, I just don't eat much of it.

**It denies an inference, not a fact.** The listener has concluded something and you are correcting the degree, not the substance. This is an extremely useful hedge and is common in real speech.

**〜わけがない — "there's no way", a flat denial.**

そんなこと、ある**わけがない**。 — There's no way that's true.

Same force as はずがない.

**〜わけにはいかない — "I can't very well", for social or moral reasons.**

今日は休む**わけにはいきません**。 — I can't very well take today off.

Not inability — the potential form would be that — but impossibility given the circumstances. You could stay home; you cannot justify it.

**Summary:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| わけだ | that explains it |
| わけではない | it's not that… |
| わけがない | no way |
| わけにはいかない | I can't very well |

**Practice.** Say: No wonder you're tired — you worked all night. · It's not that I don't want to go. · There's no way he'd say that. · I can't very well refuse. Answers: 一晩中働いたんですか。疲れているわけですね。 · 行きたくないわけではありません。 · そんなことを言うわけがありません。 · 断(ことわ)るわけにはいきません。
～べきだ and ～ものだ:
Two ways of saying how things ought to be, differing in whether the obligation is moral or customary.

**〜べきだ — "should", morally or properly.**

もっと勉強す**べきです**。 — You should study more.
約束(やくそく)は守(まも)る**べきだ**。 — Promises ought to be kept.

**It attaches to the dictionary form.** する is irregular: す**べき** or するべき, both accepted, すべき more formal.

**It is strong.** べき carries real judgement and is not the everyday "should" — that is ほうがいい from stage 3. 休んだほうがいいですよ is advice; 休むべきです is closer to a reprimand.

**〜べきではない — "shouldn't", prohibitively.**

そんなことを言う**べきではありません**。 — You shouldn't say such things.

**〜ものだ — "that's how it is", a general truth.**

子供は遊(あそ)ぶ**ものだ**。 — Children are meant to play.
時間が経(た)つのは早い**ものです**ね。 — Time really does fly, doesn't it.

It states something as a universal, often with a slightly sententious or nostalgic air.

**〜たものだ — "used to", recalling the past fondly:**

子供のころ、よくここで遊んだ**ものです**。 — I used to play here as a child.

**〜ものではない — a soft prohibition**, close to "one doesn't do that":

人を指(ゆび)さす**ものではありません**。 — One doesn't point at people.

This is how a grandparent corrects a child, and it is gentler than べきではない while being just as clear.
