**Practice.** Say: You should see a doctor. · Promises ought to be kept. · I used to come here often. · One doesn't say such things. Answers: 医者に行くべきです。 · 約束は守るべきだ。 · よくここに来たものです。 · そんなことを言うものではありません。
～しかない and ～ざるを得ない:
Two ways of saying there is no alternative, differing in how reluctant they sound.

**〜しかない — "there's nothing for it but".**

歩く**しかありません**。 — There's nothing for it but to walk.
待つ**しかない**。 — We can only wait.

It attaches to the dictionary form, and it is the everyday version. It is matter-of-fact rather than bitter.

**しか with a noun** is the "only" from stage 3, and it is the same word: 千円しかない — I only have a thousand yen. Here it is attached to a verb instead.

**〜ざるを得(え)ない — "cannot but", formal and reluctant.**

認(みと)め**ざるを得ません**。 — I have no choice but to admit it.
中止(ちゅうし)せ**ざるを得なかった**。 — We had no choice but to cancel.

**Formation:** the ない form, with ない replaced by ざるを得ない. する is irregular: **せ**ざるを得ない.

**It is written and formal**, and it carries genuine reluctance — you are doing something against your will. News and essays use it; conversation rarely does.

**〜ほかない / 〜ほかはない** sits between the two in register and means the same as しかない.

**〜わけにはいかない, from the previous lesson, is the mirror image**: there is something you cannot do. しかない is something you must.

**Practice.** Say: There's nothing for it but to wait. · We had no choice but to cancel. · I can only do my best (頑張る). Answers: 待つしかありません。 · 中止せざるを得ませんでした。 · 頑張るしかありません。
～ば～ほど — the more, the more:
A fixed construction: the ば conditional, then the dictionary form, then ほど.

考(かんが)えれ**ば**考える**ほど**、分からなくなります。 — The more I think about it, the less I understand.
安けれ**ば**安い**ほど**いいです。 — The cheaper the better.

**The verb or adjective is repeated**, once in ば form and once plain. That repetition is the construction.

**With な-adjectives and nouns**, なら replaces ば:

便利(べんり)**なら**便利な**ほど**いい。 — The more convenient the better.

**The shorter form drops the first half** and is common in speech:

考える**ほど**分からなくなる。

**〜ほど on its own, after a noun**, compares:

彼**ほど**上手な人はいません。 — There's nobody as good as him.

That is the negative comparison from stage 3, and it is the same ほど.

**〜につれて and 〜にしたがって** express a parallel change without the repetition:

年を取る**につれて**、時間が早く感(かん)じます。 — As you get older, time feels faster.
技術(ぎじゅつ)が進(すす)む**にしたがって**、生活(せいかつ)が変わりました。 — As technology advanced, life changed.

**につれて is for gradual, natural change**; にしたがって is slightly more formal and can also mean "in accordance with".

**Practice.** Say: The more you study, the more you understand. · The cheaper the better. · As it gets warmer, there are more people. Answers: 勉強すればするほど分かります。 · 安ければ安いほどいいです。 · 暖かくなるにつれて、人が増(ふ)えます。
～ても and ～でも — even if:
The concessive: something is true regardless.

**Formation: the て-form, plus も.**

雨が降っ**ても**行きます。 — I'll go even if it rains.
高く**ても**買います。 — I'll buy it even if it's expensive.
学生**でも**できます。 — Even a student can do it.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| verb | 降って**も** |
| い-adj | 高く**ても** |
| な-adj | 静か**でも** |
| noun | 学生**でも** |

**い-adjectives take くても**, which is the く form plus ても — the same く as in the adverb and the negative.

**With a question word, it means "no matter what":**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 何を食べても | whatever I eat |
| どこに行っても | wherever I go |
| いくら高くても | however expensive |
| 誰が来ても | whoever comes |

いくら explain しても分かりません。 — However much I explain, he doesn't understand.

**いくら〜ても is the standard "no matter how much"** and is very common.

**〜としても — "even supposing", hypothetical:**

本当だ**としても**、関係(かんけい)ありません。 — Even if it's true, it doesn't matter.

**〜ても versus 〜のに.** ても is forward-looking and hypothetical; のに from stage 3 is backward-looking and about something that actually happened, with complaint attached.

- 雨が降っ**ても**行きます。 — I'll go even if it rains. (it may or may not)
- 雨が降っている**のに**行きます。 — I'm going even though it's raining. (it is)

**Practice.** Say: I'll go even if it rains. · However much I study, I forget. · Even a child can do it. · Wherever you go, it's the same. Answers: 雨が降っても行きます。 · いくら勉強しても忘れます。 · 子供でもできます。 · どこに行っても同じです。
～について, ～に関して, ～に対して:
Three expressions for what a statement is about or aimed at, and they are not interchangeable.

**〜について — "about", "concerning".** The everyday one.

日本の文化(ぶんか)**について**話します。 — I'll talk about Japanese culture.
その件(けん)**について**は、後で説明(せつめい)します。 — I'll explain about that later.

**〜に関(かん)して — "regarding".** The formal equivalent, for writing and business.

この問題(もんだい)**に関して**、ご意見(いけん)をお願いします。 — Regarding this issue, your views please.

**They are nearly identical in meaning** and differ only in register. について in speech, に関して in documents.

**〜に対(たい)して — "towards", or "in contrast to".** A different thing entirely.

**Towards, directed at:**

学生**に対して**厳(きび)しいです。 — He's strict towards students.
質問(しつもん)**に対して**答(こた)えました。 — I answered the question.

**In contrast:**

去年は暑かった**のに対して**、今年は涼(すず)しいです。 — Whereas last year was hot, this year is cool.

**The test between について and に対して:** について introduces a topic; に対して names a target or an opposite. 日本について話す is talking about Japan; 日本に対して厳しい is being hard on Japan.

**〜にとって — "for", from the point of view of:**

私**にとって**、家族が一番大切(たいせつ)です。 — For me, family is most important.

にとって is about whose perspective the judgement is from, and it is the one that answers "to whom does this matter".

**Practice.** Choose: 日本の歴史__について/に対して__ 調(しら)べます。 · 子供__について/に対して__ 優(やさ)しいです。 · 私__にとって/について__ 難しいです。 Answers: について · に対して · にとって。
～によって and ～として:
Two more compound particles, both extremely common and both doing several jobs.

**〜によって — "by", "depending on", "due to".**

**1. Agent of a passive:**

この本は夏目漱石(なつめそうせき)**によって**書かれました。 — This book was written by Sōseki.

More formal than に for the passive agent, and standard in writing.

**2. Depending on, varying with:**

人**によって**違(ちが)います。 — It depends on the person.
地域(ちいき)**によって**ルールが違います。 — The rules differ by area.

**人によって違います is an extremely useful sentence** and is the natural answer to "is it like this in Japan?"

**3. Means or cause:**

話し合い**によって**解決(かいけつ)しました。 — It was resolved through discussion.

**〜による as a modifier:** 地震(じしん)**による**被害(ひがい) — damage caused by the earthquake.

**〜として — "as", in the capacity of.**

学生**として**日本に行きました。 — I went to Japan as a student.
趣味**として**やっています。 — I do it as a hobby.
日本語の先生**として**働いています。 — I work as a Japanese teacher.

**として names a role or category**, and it is the one you want for "as a ~". The common error is using で, which means by means of.

**〜としては adds a perspective:** 私**としては**反対(はんたい)です — speaking for myself, I'm against it.

**Practice.** Say: It depends on the person. · I went as a tourist (観光客, かんこうきゃく). · It was written by Murakami. · Speaking for myself, I agree. Answers: 人によって違います。 · 観光客として行きました。 · 村上(むらかみ)によって書かれました。 · 私としては賛成(さんせい)です。
～せいで and ～おかげで:
Two ways of attributing a result to a cause, and the choice says whether you are grateful or blaming.

**〜おかげで — "thanks to", for a good outcome.**

先生**のおかげで**合格(ごうかく)しました。 — I passed thanks to my teacher.
雨が降った**おかげで**涼しくなりました。 — Thanks to the rain, it's cooled down.

**〜せいで — "because of", for a bad one.**

雨**のせいで**行けませんでした。 — I couldn't go because of the rain.
彼**のせいで**遅れました。 — I was late because of him.

**The grammar is identical** — nouns take の, verbs and adjectives take the plain form — and only the attitude differs. Using せい about someone to their face is an accusation.

**おかげさまで** is a set phrase of its own: "thanks to you", used in reply to お元気ですか — おかげさまで、元気です. The "you" is not literal; it is a general acknowledgement, and the phrase is said constantly.

**〜せいにする — to blame:**

人**のせいにしない**でください。 — Don't blame other people.

**ため is the neutral one**, from stage 3: 雨のために中止になりました — cancelled due to rain. No attitude attached, which is why it is the register of announcements.

**Summary:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| おかげで | thanks to — good |
| せいで | because of — bad |
| ために | due to — neutral, formal |

**Practice.** Say: Thanks to you, I understood. · I was late because of the train. · The event was cancelled due to the typhoon. Answers: おかげで分かりました。 · 電車のせいで遅れました。 · 台風のためにイベントが中止になりました。
～うちに and ～間に:
Two ways of saying "while", differing in what they imply about the window closing.

**〜うちに — "while, before the opportunity passes".**

若(わか)い**うちに**旅行したほうがいい。 — You should travel while you're young.
温(あたた)かい**うちに**食べてください。 — Please eat it while it's hot.
忘(わす)れない**うちに**メモします。 — I'll make a note before I forget.

**うちに implies the state will end**, and that is the whole point of it. 忘れないうちに — while I still haven't forgotten — is the classic use, and that negative form is very common.

**〜間(あいだ)に — "during, at some point within".**

寝ている**間に**地震がありました。 — There was an earthquake while I was asleep.
留守(るす)の**間に**誰か来ました。 — Someone came while I was out.

**間 without に means throughout the whole period:**

- 寝ている**間に** — at some point during my sleep (one event)
- 寝ている**間** — the whole time I was asleep (continuous)

夏休みの**間**、ずっと働いていました。 — I worked the whole summer holiday.

**That に is the difference** and it is easy to miss: に picks a point inside the span, no に covers the span.

**うちに versus 間に.** 間に is neutral about the window; うちに says you should act before it shuts. 子供が寝ている間に掃除します is just when it happened; 子供が寝ているうちに掃除します implies seizing the chance.

**Practice.** Say: Please eat it while it's hot. · Someone called while I was out. · I studied the whole holiday. · I'll do it before I forget. Answers: 温かいうちに食べてください。 · 留守の間に電話がありました。 · 休みの間ずっと勉強しました。 · 忘れないうちにやります。
～たとたん, ～次第, ～たびに:
Three time expressions about the moment something happens.

**〜たとたん(に) — "the instant", with surprise.**

ドアを開けた**とたん**、猫が飛(と)び出しました。 — The instant I opened the door, the cat shot out.
立ち上がった**とたんに**めまいがしました。 — The moment I stood up I felt dizzy.

**It takes the た form** and the second clause must be something **unexpected and already past**. You cannot use it for a plan: 着いたとたんに電話します is wrong.

**〜次第(しだい) — "as soon as", for a plan.**

着き**次第**、電話します。 — I'll call as soon as I arrive.
分かり**次第**、ご連絡(れんらく)します。 — I'll let you know as soon as I know.

**It takes the ます stem** and the second clause is future and intentional — the exact opposite constraint to とたん. It is formal and very common in business.

**〜たびに — "every time".**

東京に行く**たびに**、あの店に寄(よ)ります。 — Every time I go to Tokyo I drop into that shop.
彼に会う**たびに**、同じ話をします。 — Every time I meet him he tells the same story.

**It takes the dictionary form**, or a noun with の: 試験(しけん)**のたびに**緊張(きんちょう)します.

**〜とすぐ is the plain "as soon as"** and works for both past and future: 着くとすぐ電話します。

**Summary:**

| | Form | Second clause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| たとたん | た | past, unexpected |
| 次第 | ます stem | future, intentional |
| たびに | dictionary | habitual |

**Practice.** Say: I'll contact you as soon as I find out. · The moment I got home, the phone rang. · Every time I come here I eat ramen. Answers: 分かり次第ご連絡します。 · 家に帰ったとたん、電話が鳴りました。 · ここに来るたびにラーメンを食べます。
～一方で, ～反面, ～ものの:
Three ways of setting two things against each other, more formal than けど.

**〜一方(いっぽう)で — "on the other hand", "while".**

仕事は大変(たいへん)な**一方で**、やりがいがあります。 — The work is hard, but on the other hand it's rewarding.
物価(ぶっか)が上がる**一方で**、給料(きゅうりょう)は変わりません。 — Prices rise while wages stay the same.

**〜一方だ is a different thing** — "keeps getting more and more":

物価は上がる**一方です**。 — Prices just keep going up.

That one has no contrast in it at all, and the two are easy to confuse.

**〜反面(はんめん) — "on the flip side".** Almost identical to 一方で, and slightly more pointed about the two sides being of one thing:

便利な**反面**、高いです。 — It's convenient, but on the other hand expensive.

**〜ものの — "although", formal and written.**

買った**ものの**、一度も使っていません。 — I bought it, but I've never used it once.
約束した**ものの**、守(まも)れませんでした。 — Although I promised, I couldn't keep it.

**ものの is literary.** It belongs in writing and formal speech; けど does the same job in conversation.

**〜とはいうものの** — "that said", at the start of a sentence — is a useful connector of the same family.

**〜くせに — "although", with contempt.**

知っている**くせに**、教えてくれません。 — He knows perfectly well and won't tell me.
子供の**くせに**生意気(なまいき)だ。 — He's cheeky for a child.

**くせに is rude** and carries real criticism of the subject. It is のに with an insult attached, and it is worth recognising long before using.

**Practice.** Say: The work is hard, but rewarding. · I bought it but never used it. · He knows and won't say. Answers: 仕事は大変な一方で、やりがいがあります。 · 買ったものの、使っていません。 · 知っているくせに言いません。
～ばかりか, ～だけでなく, ～上に:
Adding a second thing on top of the first, with increasing emphasis.

**〜だけでなく — "not only … but also".** The neutral one.

日本語**だけでなく**、中国語も話せます。 — He speaks not only Japanese but Chinese too.

**〜だけでなく〜も** is the full pattern, and the も in the second half is what completes it.

**〜ばかりか — "not only that, but".** Stronger, often surprised.

遅(おく)れた**ばかりか**、謝(あやま)りもしませんでした。 — Not only was he late, he didn't even apologise.

**〜上(うえ)に — "on top of that".** Adds something of the same kind.

安い**上に**おいしいです。 — It's cheap and on top of that delicious.
雨が降っている**上に**、風も強いです。 — It's raining, and windy on top of that.

**上に requires both halves to lean the same way** — both good or both bad. 安い上にまずい is wrong; that needs が or のに.

**〜に加(くわ)えて — "in addition to"**, formal and used in writing.

**〜はもちろん — "to say nothing of":**

漢字**はもちろん**、ひらがなも読めません。 — He can't read hiragana, let alone kanji.

**Note the order.** はもちろん takes the *more obvious* case first, which is the reverse of the English "let alone". Reading it backwards into English is the habit to build.

**Practice.** Say: It's cheap and delicious on top of that. · Not only is he late, he didn't call. · He speaks not only English but Japanese. Answers: 安い上においしいです。 · 遅れたばかりか、電話もしませんでした。 · 英語だけでなく日本語も話せます。
～ようがない and ～きれない:
Two ways of saying something cannot be done, beyond the plain potential form.

**〜ようがない — "there is no way to".** The ます stem plus ようがない:

連絡(れんらく)の**しようがありません**。 — There's no way to contact him.
直(なお)し**ようがない**。 — There's no fixing it.

**It is about the absence of a method**, not about your ability. 連絡できません means you cannot — maybe you are busy. 連絡のしようがありません means there is no means at all: no number, no address.

**する becomes しよう**, and the の before it is common: 〜のしようがない.

**〜きれない, from earlier in this stage**, is about quantity: too much to finish. 食べきれない — I can't eat it all.

**〜得(え)ない — "cannot possibly", formal:**

あり**得ません**。 — That's impossible / out of the question.

ありえない in casual speech is an extremely common exclamation meaning "no way" or "unbelievable".

**〜かねる — "cannot bring oneself to", very formal.** The ます stem plus かねる:

お答(こた)えし**かねます**。 — I'm unable to answer. (a polite refusal)

**かねる is a refusal dressed as inability** and is the register of customer service and officialdom. それはし**かねます** is a firm no.

**〜かねない is the opposite** — "might well", about something bad:

彼なら言い**かねない**。 — He's quite capable of saying that.

かねる and かねない look like a pair and mean nearly opposite things, which is the trap.

**Practice.** Say: There's no way to contact her. · I can't eat it all. · That's impossible. · I'm unable to answer that. Answers: 連絡のしようがありません。 · 食べきれません。 · ありえません。 · お答えしかねます。
～こそ, ～さえ, ～でも as emphasis:
Three particles that add emphasis, each in a different direction.

**こそ — "precisely this", "it is X that".**

今日**こそ**やります。 — Today's the day I'll do it.
あなた**こそ**。 — And you. / No, *you*.
こちら**こそ**。 — The pleasure is mine.

**こちらこそ is the standard reply** to ありがとうございます or よろしくお願いします, and it is said constantly.

**〜からこそ — "precisely because":**

好きだ**からこそ**、厳しく言うんです。 — It's precisely because I care that I'm being hard on you.

**さえ — "even", at the extreme end.**

子供**さえ**知っています。 — Even a child knows that.
水**さえ**飲めません。 — I can't even drink water.

**〜さえ〜ば — "if only":**

お金**さえ**あれ**ば**、買えます。 — If only I had the money, I could buy it.
これ**さえ**覚(おぼ)えれ**ば**大丈夫です。 — If you just remember this, you'll be fine.

That pattern is very common and worth having whole: X さえ〜ば means X is the single sufficient condition.

**でも — "even", softer and more common.**

子供**でも**できます。 — Even a child can do it.

**さえ versus でも.** さえ is stronger and more surprising. 子供でもできる is "it's easy enough for a child"; 子供さえできる implies astonishment that even a child manages it and you do not.

**でも after a question word means "any":**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 何でも | anything |
| 誰でも | anyone |
| どこでも | anywhere |
| いつでも | anytime |

**Practice.** Say: Even a child knows. · If only I had time. · The pleasure is mine. · You can come anytime. Answers: 子供でも知っています。 · 時間さえあれば。 · こちらこそ。 · いつでも来てください。
～ということ and ～というのは:
Two uses of という, both for talking about ideas rather than things.

**〜ということ — nominalising a whole statement.**

彼が来ない**ということ**は、知りませんでした。 — I didn't know that he wasn't coming.
日本語が難しい**ということ**が分かりました。 — I realised that Japanese is hard.

**It makes a clause into a noun** so it can be the object of 知る, 分かる, 聞く or 意味する. こと alone can often do the same job; ということ is more explicit and is required after a full sentence with its own です or だ.

**〜ということだ — "I hear that", at the end of a sentence:**

試験は来週だ**ということです**。 — I hear the exam is next week.

Same as そうです for hearsay, slightly more formal.

**〜というのは — "what X means is", a definition.**

「もったいない」**というのは**、どういう意味ですか。 — What does *mottainai* mean?
日本語が上手**というのは**、どのくらいですか。 — What counts as being good at Japanese?

**It introduces the thing being defined**, and the definition follows. This is how you ask what a word means, and it is more natural than 〜の意味は何ですか.

**〜とは is the formal version**, used in dictionaries and essays:

民主主義(みんしゅしゅぎ)**とは**、国民(こくみん)が主権(しゅけん)を持つ制度(せいど)である。 — Democracy is a system in which the people hold sovereignty.

**In speech, というのは contracts to っていうのは or just って:**

もったいない**って**どういう意味？

**って is everywhere in casual Japanese** and does the work of という, と, and は all at once. Recognising it is most of what makes casual speech parse.

**Practice.** Ask what a word means. Then say: I didn't know he was coming. · I hear the shop is closed. Answers: 〜ってどういう意味ですか。 · 彼が来るということを知りませんでした。 · 店は閉まっているということです。
～まま — leaving something as it is:
まま means a state continuing unchanged, usually when it should not.

**With the た form:**

電気(でんき)をつけた**まま**寝ました。 — I fell asleep with the light on.
靴(くつ)を履(は)いた**まま**入らないでください。 — Please don't come in with your shoes on.

**With a noun + の:**

昔(むかし)の**まま**です。 — It's just as it was.

**With an adjective:**

熱(あつ)い**まま**食べてください。 — Eat it while it's still hot.

**まま carries "and that's not right"** more often than not. 立ったまま食べる — eating standing up — carries a mild disapproval that 立って食べる does not.

**〜ないまま — without having done:**

何も言わない**まま**帰りました。 — He went home without saying anything.
分からない**まま**終(お)わりました。 — It ended with me none the wiser.

**そのまま — "as it is", is the frozen form** and is extremely useful:

そのままにしておいてください。 — Please leave it as it is.
そのままどうぞ。 — Please stay as you are. (don't get up)

**まま versus ながら.** ながら is two actions at once; まま is one action and one unchanged state. 歩きながら食べる is walking and eating; 立ったまま食べる is eating in a standing state.

**Practice.** Say: I slept with the TV on. · Don't come in with your shoes on. · Please leave it as it is. · He left without saying anything. Answers: テレビをつけたまま寝ました。 · 靴を履いたまま入らないでください。 · そのままにしておいてください。 · 何も言わないまま帰りました。
The causative-passive, in full:
"Was made to do something" — the causative and the passive stacked, and the most unpleasant-looking form in the language. It is also genuinely common, because being made to do things is a common experience.

**Formation: causative, then passive.**

| Group | Dictionary | Causative | Causative-passive |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 飲む | 飲ま**せる** | 飲ま**せられる** → **飲まされる** |
| 1 | 書く | 書か**せる** | 書か**せられる** → **書かされる** |
| 2 | 食べる | 食べ**させる** | 食べ**させられる** |
| 3 | する | **させる** | **させられる** |
| 3 | 来る | **来させる** | **来させられる** |

**Group 1 contracts** — せられる becomes される — and the short form is what is used in speech. Group 2 and する cannot contract, which is why 食べさせられる stays long.

**The exception:** verbs ending in す do not contract, because 話さされる would be unsayable. 話させられる stays.

**Use:**

部長(ぶちょう)にお酒(さけ)を飲ま**されました**。 — I was made to drink by my boss.
一時間待た**されました**。 — I was kept waiting an hour.
毎日練習さ**せられました**。 — I was made to practise every day.

**It always carries resentment.** The causative-passive is the grammar of complaint — you did something, you did not want to, and someone made you. There is no neutral version; for a neutral statement you would use the plain past.

**待たされる is worth knowing as a word.** "To be kept waiting" is one of the commonest uses and there is no shorter way to say it.

**Practice.** Convert and use: 飲む, 書く, 待つ, 食べる, する. Then say: I was made to wait two hours. · I was made to study every day. Answers: 二時間待たされました。 · 毎日勉強させられました。
～させていただく — the humble request:
The causative plus the humble "receive", and the politest way to say you will do something.

発表(はっぴょう)さ**せていただきます**。 — I will give the presentation. (with your permission)
休ま**せていただきます**。 — I'll be taking the day off.
使わ**せていただきました**。 — I made use of it, with thanks.

**Literally: "I humbly receive the favour of being allowed to do it".** It is not asking — the thing is going to happen — but it is framed as permission granted, which is what makes it polite.

**It appeared in stage 4** in the sick-day call: 今日は休ませていただきます。 That sentence is an announcement wearing the clothes of a request, and now you can see the machinery.

**〜させてください is the plainer version** — "please let me" — and is a genuine request. いただく is the formal one and does not really expect an answer.

**〜させていただけませんか is an actual request**, and is about as polite as Japanese gets:

質問さ**せていただけませんか**。 — Might I be permitted to ask a question?

**It is overused**, and that is worth knowing. Shop announcements and corporate language use させていただく for everything, including things that need nobody's permission — 本日休業させていただきます, "we will be closed today". Japanese speakers complain about it in the way English speakers complain about "reach out". Use it where permission is genuinely involved.

**The common ones**: 休ませていただきます, 失礼させていただきます, 使わせていただきます, 確認させていただきます.

**Practice.** Say: I'll be taking tomorrow off. · May I ask a question? · I'll check, if I may. Answers: 明日休ませていただきます。 · 質問させていただけませんか。 · 確認させていただきます。
～ていただく and the ladder of requests:
Every way of asking for something, from blunt to extremely deferential, collected in one place.

**The ladder, least to most polite:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 手伝(てつだ)って。 | Help. (plain, to a friend) |
| 手伝ってください。 | Please help. |
| 手伝ってくれませんか。 | Won't you help? |
| 手伝ってもらえませんか。 | Could I have you help? |
| 手伝っていただけませんか。 | Might I ask you to help? |
| 手伝っていただけないでしょうか。 | Would it be possible to ask you to help? |

**Three things make a request politer**, and they stack:

1. **Negative rather than positive** — くれませんか over ください. Asking in the negative leaves room to refuse.
2. **Potential rather than plain** — もらえる over もらう. Asking whether they *can* rather than whether they will.
3. **Humble rather than neutral** — いただく over もらう.

**ください is not impolite** but it is a directive. To a superior or a stranger, the くれませんか rung or above is the floor.

**〜ていただけると助(たす)かります — "it would help me if you could"** — is a softer alternative that avoids asking outright:

ご確認いただけると助かります。 — It would help if you could check.

**The opening matters as much as the verb.** Any of these preceded by すみません、〜んですが lands far better than the bare request, which is the pattern from stage 3 doing real social work.

**Refusing a request** uses the same indirection: ちょっと難しいですね, or 申し訳ありませんが…. A flat できません is rare.

**Practice.** Ask the same thing — check a document — at three levels: to a friend, to a colleague, to a client. Answers: ちょっと見て。 · 見てもらえませんか。 · ご確認いただけないでしょうか。
Male and female speech:
Japanese marks gender in speech more than most languages, and the differences are in pronouns, sentence-final particles and register rather than in grammar.

**Pronouns for "I":**

| | Who |
| --- | --- |
| 私(わたし) | anyone; the neutral and formal choice |
| 私(わたくし) | very formal, both |
| 僕(ぼく) | men and boys, soft |
| 俺(おれ) | men, casual to rough |
| あたし | women, casual |
| うち | women, casual, Kansai-leaning |

**わたし is correct for everyone in formal speech**, including men. 僕 and 俺 are casual only; using 俺 at work is a statement.

**Sentence-final particles:**

| | Leaning |
| --- | --- |
| よ · ね | neutral |
| わ | feminine (rising); masculine in Kansai |
| かしら | feminine, "I wonder" |
| な · なあ | masculine-leaning |
| ぜ · ぞ | strongly masculine, rough |
| だろ | masculine |
| のよ · のね | feminine |

**だ is often dropped by women:** 綺麗ね rather than 綺麗だね.

**The caveats, which matter.**

- **These are tendencies, not rules**, and they are loosening fast. Younger women use 僕 and plain だ; men use softer forms.
- **Fiction exaggerates them.** Anime and manga use 役割語(やくわりご) — role language — where a character's speech signals their type. Nobody actually talks like an anime old man. Learning speech patterns from fiction will make you sound like a character.
- **Politeness overrides gender.** In ます form the differences nearly vanish.

**What to do with this.** Recognise it when listening — it tells you something about who is speaking. Produce the neutral register: わたし, です・ます, よ and ね. Copying a specific speaker's gendered style is how learners end up sounding odd.

**Practice.** Listen to any Japanese conversation and note which pronouns and final particles each speaker uses. Then check your own: are you using anything you picked up from fiction?
Dialects, and Kansai-ben:
Standard Japanese — 標準語(ひょうじゅんご) — is the Tokyo dialect, and it is what everything so far has taught. The rest of the country does not speak it.

**The main dialect you will meet is 関西弁(かんさいべん)**, from Osaka, Kyoto and Kobe, because Kansai is large, confident about its speech, and heavily represented in comedy and television.

**The headline differences:**

| Standard | Kansai |
| --- | --- |
| です | **や** / やで |
| だ | **や** |
| ありがとう | **おおきに** |
| 違う | **ちゃう** |
| とても | **めっちゃ** |
| ばか | **あほ** |
| いくら | なんぼ |
| 〜ない | 〜**へん** (行かへん) |
| 〜ている | 〜**とる** |
| いい | **ええ** |

ほんまに — really (standard: 本当に)
なんでやねん — "what are you on about" — the standard comic retort

**あほ and ばか swap weight.** In Tokyo ばか is light and あほ is harsh; in Osaka it is the reverse, and あほ between friends is affectionate.

**Pitch accent differs systematically**, which is why Kansai speech sounds different even when the words are the same.

**Other dialects:** 東北弁 in the north, famously hard for Tokyo speakers; 博多弁 in Fukuoka; 沖縄 with its own language entirely, Okinawan, which Imabi covers.

**What to do.** Learn standard Japanese and recognise Kansai. Speaking Kansai-ben as a foreigner is charming to some and affected to others, and it is a long way down the list of useful things. But you will hear it in every comedy programme, so recognising や for だ and へん for ない is worth the ten minutes.

**Practice.** Translate into standard: これ、めっちゃええやん。 · なんでやねん。 · 分からへん。 Answers: これ、とてもいいね。 · 何を言っているの。 · 分からない。
Contractions in speech:
Spoken Japanese wears words down, and the result is unrecognisable to anyone who has only read. This lesson is a key to what you are hearing.

| Full | Spoken | From |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 〜ている | 〜**てる** | 食べてる |
| 〜ておく | 〜**とく** | やっとく |
| 〜てしまう | 〜**ちゃう** | 忘れちゃう |
| 〜でしまう | 〜**じゃう** | 読んじゃう |
| 〜なければ | 〜**なきゃ** | 行かなきゃ |
| 〜なくては | 〜**なくちゃ** | 行かなくちゃ |
| 〜という | 〜**って** | 田中って人 |
| 〜ではない | 〜**じゃない** | 学生じゃない |
| 〜ところ | 〜**とこ** | 今行くとこ |
| 〜ばかり | 〜**ばっか** | ゲームばっか |
| 〜のだ | 〜**んだ** | 行くんだ |
| すみません | **すいません** | |
| ありがとうございます | **あざっす** | very casual |

**The vowel drops are the hardest.** 〜ている losing its い is in nearly every sentence of casual speech, and a learner listening for ています will miss it entirely.

**って does four jobs** and is the single most common contraction:

- という — 田中って人 (a bloke called Tanaka)
- と言った — 行くって (he said he's going)
- は — それって何？ (what's that?)
- と — 明日って聞いた (I heard it's tomorrow)

**Particles drop entirely** in casual speech:

ご飯食べた？ — Did you eat? (を gone)
どこ行くの？ — Where are you going? (に gone)

**は and が are the ones that survive**; を, に and へ are the first to go.

**What to do.** Produce the full forms; recognise the short ones. Nobody will think less of you for saying 食べています, and you will understand nothing if you cannot hear 食べてる.

**Practice.** Expand these: やっとくね。 · 忘れちゃった。 · 行かなきゃ。 · それって本当？ · ご飯食べた？ Answers: やっておくね。 · 忘れてしまった。 · 行かなければならない。 · それは本当ですか。 · ご飯を食べましたか。
Onomatopoeia: 擬音語 and 擬態語:
Japanese has two large classes of sound-words, and they are not decoration — they are ordinary vocabulary that adults use constantly, in writing as well as speech.

**擬音語(ぎおんご) — words for actual sounds:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| ワンワン | a dog barking |
| ニャーニャー | a cat |
| ザーザー | heavy rain |
| ガタガタ | rattling |
| ドキドキ | a pounding heart |

**擬態語(ぎたいご) — words for states and manners**, which have no English equivalent at all:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| きらきら | sparkling |
| ぺこぺこ | ravenous (お腹がぺこぺこ) |
| くたくた | exhausted |
| さっぱり | refreshed; not at all |
| ゆっくり | slowly |
| しっかり | firmly, properly |
| ぼんやり | vaguely, absent-mindedly |
| びっくり | startled |
| そっくり | identical |
| ぐっすり | soundly (asleep) |
| ばらばら | scattered, in pieces |
| ぎりぎり | just barely |

**Several of these are words you already use** — ゆっくり, しっかり, びっくり — without having noticed they belong to this class.

**They attach in three ways:**

- **+ する**: どきどきする, びっくりする, さっぱりする
- **+ と**: ゆっくりと歩く, しっかりと持つ
- **directly as an adverb**: ぐっすり寝る

**The doubled ones are often repeated action** and the ～り ones often a single state: ばらばら (scattered about) versus ぴったり (exactly fitting).

**They are everywhere in real Japanese** — in manga obviously, but also in news, instructions and conversation. 雨がざあざあ降っている is normal adult speech, not baby talk.

**There are thousands**, and they cannot be learned as a list. Meet them in context, mine the ones that recur.

**Practice.** Use: I'm starving. · I slept soundly. · My heart is pounding. · They look identical. Answers: お腹がぺこぺこです。 · ぐっすり寝ました。 · どきどきしています。 · そっくりです。
Loanwords, and 和製英語:
Katakana words are not always the English word you think, and the gap is a reliable source of error.

**Shortened:**

| Japanese | From |
| --- | --- |
| パソコン | personal computer |
| エアコン | air conditioner |
| コンビニ | convenience store |
| スマホ | smartphone |
| アニメ | animation |
| リモコン | remote control |
| アポ | appointment |

**和製英語(わせいえいご) — English-looking words made in Japan**, which are not English at all:

| Japanese | Means | Not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| サラリーマン | office worker | "salaryman" |
| オーダーメイド | made to order | "order made" |
| ガソリンスタンド | petrol station | |
| コンセント | power socket | "consent" |
| マンション | a flat | a mansion |
| バイキング | buffet | viking |
| クレーム | a complaint | a claim |
| ナイーブ | sensitive, delicate | naive |
| テンション | energy, mood | tension |
| ペーパードライバー | someone with a licence who doesn't drive | |

**テンションが高い means cheerful and energetic**, not tense. This one causes genuine misunderstandings in both directions.

**クレーム is a complaint**, and クレーマー is a serial complainer. Using it for an insurance claim will not be understood.

**Words from other languages** are common and often mistaken for English: アルバイト (part-time job, German *Arbeit*), パン (bread, Portuguese *pão*), イクラ (salmon roe, Russian), カルテ (medical record, German), ズボン (trousers, French).

**アルバイト shortens to バイト** and is the normal word for a part-time job.

**The lesson for a learner:** do not assume a katakana word means what the English means, and do not invent katakana words from English — the odds are against you. Check.

**Practice.** What do these mean? マンション · コンセント · テンション · バイト · クレーム. Answers: a flat · a power socket · mood/energy · part-time job · a complaint.
Reading kanji you have not met: on'yomi:
A strategy rather than a vocabulary list: how to guess at a character you do not know.

**Most kanji contain a phonetic component.** Roughly 80% of characters are 形声(けいせい) — one part gives the meaning, another gives the sound. Spotting the sound part lets you guess the on'yomi.

**Example — 青(セイ):**

| | Reading |
| --- | --- |
| 青 | セイ |
| 晴 | セイ (晴天) |
| 清 | セイ (清潔) |
| 静 | セイ (静止) |
| 情 | ジョウ |
| 精 | セイ |

Five of six take セイ. Seeing 青 inside an unknown character is a strong bet on セイ.

**More of them:**

| Component | Usual reading | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 寺 | ジ | 時 持 待 詩 |
| 工 | コウ | 江 紅 功 |
| 分 | フン・ブン | 粉 紛 |
| 反 | ハン | 板 坂 飯 版 |
| 生 | セイ | 性 姓 星 |
| 可 | カ | 何 河 歌 |

**The meaning component narrows it.** 氵 is water, so 清 is about water and reads セイ: clean. 言 is speech, so 語 is about words. 木 is wood, 心 is feeling, 糸 is thread, 魚 is fish.

**Guessing is worth doing even when wrong**, because the attempt attaches the character to something. A character guessed at and then corrected sticks far better than one looked up cold.

**The limits.** The sound components reflect Chinese pronunciation of a thousand years ago, filtered through Japanese, and they have drifted. The hit rate is perhaps 60%, which is useful rather than reliable.

**Kun readings cannot be guessed at all.** They are native Japanese words attached to borrowed characters and have no relationship to the shape.

**Practice.** Guess the on'yomi of 晴, 持, 飯, 性 using the components above. Then check on Jisho. Answers: セイ, ジ, ハン, セイ.
Radicals, and looking a kanji up:
Every kanji is built from a small set of components, and knowing them turns a wall of strokes into a structure.

**The common radicals:**

| Radical | Means | In |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 氵 | water | 海 池 洗 酒 |
| 木 | tree, wood | 林 森 机 村 |
| 言 | speech | 話 語 読 記 |
| 人 / 亻 | person | 休 体 作 他 |
| 手 / 扌 | hand | 持 押 指 打 |
| 心 / 忄 | heart | 思 急 情 快 |
| 糸 | thread | 紙 細 絵 続 |
| 口 | mouth | 味 和 品 唱 |
| 日 | sun, day | 明 時 晴 曜 |
| 金 | metal | 銀 鉄 針 |
| 女 | woman | 好 始 姉 |
| 艹 | grass | 花 草 茶 薬 |

**休 is a person beside a tree** — rest. **明** is sun and moon — bright. **好** is woman and child — to like. Not all of them are this tidy, and the ones that are make excellent memory hooks.

**Looking a kanji up, three ways:**

1. **Handwriting input.** Draw it on a phone or on Jisho's drawing pad. This is now the fastest method for most people and is why stroke order matters.
2. **By radical.** Jisho's radical search: pick the components you recognise and it narrows the list. This works when you cannot draw it.
3. **By reading**, if you know one.

**Yomitan, in a browser**, removes the problem for anything on screen: hover over a word and the reading and meaning appear. For reading native material on a computer it is transformative and free.

**Stroke count** is the old way, used in paper dictionaries, and is rarely needed now.

**Practice.** Name the radical and guess the meaning of: 海 泳 村 語 持 思. Then look up one character you cannot read, by drawing it.
Irodori Pre-Intermediate:
The last of Irodori's four levels, and the end of the graded functional strand.

**What it covers.** Eighteen lessons of longer, less predictable situations: explaining a problem in detail, negotiating, giving reasons and opinions, describing experiences, and conversations that run several turns without a script.

**What makes it harder.** The dialogues stop being transactional. Earlier levels gave you a shop and a counter; this one gives you a conversation with an ending that depends on what you say.

**The method, with one addition:**

1. Listen before reading.
2. Read, check what you missed.
3. Shadow it.
4. Do the worksheet.
5. **Change it.** Take the dialogue and alter one thing — a refusal instead of an acceptance, a different reason — and say it through. The script is a frame, and the point is now to leave it.

**After this, Irodori ends.** There is no Intermediate level. The functional strand becomes native material: news, podcasts, television, conversation — which is exactly where stage 6 goes.

**That gap is deliberate in the plan.** Graded material takes you to the point where real material is possible, and then real material is the only thing that takes you further. The transition is uncomfortable and it is the point of stage 6.

**Before leaving Irodori**, go back through the Can-do statements of all four levels and mark the ones you cannot do. Those are the lessons to redo, and redoing a Starter lesson at this level takes twenty minutes and is worth it.

**Practice.** Do Pre-Intermediate lesson 1 by the five steps, including changing the dialogue.
～ないで and ～なくて — the two negative te-form:
There are two ways to make a negative て-form and they are not interchangeable. This is a point learners get wrong for years.

**〜ないで — without doing, or instead of doing.**

朝ご飯を食べ**ないで**学校に行きました。 — I went to school without eating breakfast.
電話し**ないで**、急に来ました。 — He came suddenly without calling.

**〜なくて — because not, a cause.**

お金が**なくて**買えませんでした。 — I couldn't buy it because I had no money.
分から**なくて**困(こま)りました。 — I was stuck because I didn't understand.

**The test: does the second clause happen *because* of the negative?**

- Cause → **なくて**
- Manner, or an action not done → **ないで**

バスが来**なくて**遅れました。 — I was late because the bus didn't come. (cause)
傘を持た**ないで**出かけました。 — I went out without an umbrella. (manner)

**なくて is also the only option for adjectives and nouns:**

高く**なくて**よかった。 — I'm glad it wasn't expensive.
学生じゃ**なくて**、社会人(しゃかいじん)です。 — Not a student — a working adult.

**ないで is required before ください**, which is the form you already know:

行か**ないで**ください。 — Please don't go.

**〜ずに is the formal written ないで:**

何も言わ**ずに**帰りました。 — He left without saying anything.

する becomes **せずに**, which is irregular and common: 何もせずに.

**Practice.** Choose: 朝ご飯を食べ__ないで/なくて__ 行きました。 · 時間が__ないで/なくて__ できませんでした。 · 傘を持た__ないで/なくて__ 出ました。 Answers: ないで · なくて · ないで。
～ように — manner, purpose and indirect spee:
ように does several jobs and they are related: all of them are about a manner or an aim.

**1. Like, in the manner of:**

鳥(とり)の**ように**飛びたい。 — I want to fly like a bird.
言われた**ように**やりました。 — I did it as I was told.

**2. So that, an aim** — from stage 3, with a non-volitional verb:

忘れない**ように**メモします。 — I take notes so I don't forget.
よく見える**ように**、前に座りました。 — I sat at the front so I could see well.

**3. Indirect commands and requests**, with 言う, 頼(たの)む, 伝(つた)える:

静かにする**ように**言ってください。 — Please tell them to be quiet.
早く来る**ように**頼みました。 — I asked him to come early.

**That third use is how you report an instruction**, and there is no neater way to do it. It takes the dictionary form for a positive and the ない form for a negative: 行かない**ように**言われました — I was told not to go.

**4. ようにする — to make a point of doing:**

毎日運動(うんどう)する**ようにしています**。 — I make a point of exercising every day.

**It implies effort and habit**, and is the natural answer to a question about your routine. ようにしています is "I try to", and it is softer and more honest than a flat 毎日運動します.

**5. ようになる — to come to be able to**, from stage 3:

日本語が話せる**ようになりました**。 — I've become able to speak Japanese.

**The whole family in one line:** ように (aim), ようにする (make a habit), ようになる (come to be).

**Practice.** Say: I take notes so I don't forget. · I try to study every day. · Please tell him not to come. · I've become able to read kanji. Answers: 忘れないようにメモします。 · 毎日勉強するようにしています。 · 来ないように伝えてください。 · 漢字が読めるようになりました。
～かどうか and embedded questions:
How to put a question inside a sentence — "I don't know whether", "I'll ask where".

**〜かどうか — whether or not.** For yes/no questions:

来る**かどうか**分かりません。 — I don't know whether he's coming.
正しい**かどうか**確認してください。 — Please check whether it's correct.

**It attaches to the plain form.** Nouns and な-adjectives drop だ: 学生**かどうか**, 静か**かどうか**.

**With a question word, use か alone** — どうか is not needed:

どこに行った**か**分かりません。 — I don't know where he went.
何を言っている**か**分かりません。 — I don't understand what he's saying.
誰が来る**か**聞いてください。 — Please ask who's coming.

**The question word carries the uncertainty**, so どうか would be redundant.

**The verbs that take these:** 分かる, 知る, 聞く, 覚えている, 確認する, 教える, 考える.

**Word order is the thing to get right.** English puts the question clause after the verb; Japanese puts it before, like everything else:

I don't know **where he is**. → **どこにいるか** 分かりません。

**〜か、〜かは topicalised:**

来るかどうか**は**、まだ分かりません。 — As for whether he's coming, I don't know yet.

**In casual speech the か is often dropped** with a question word: どこ行ったか知らない → どこ行ったか分かんない, or just どこ行ったんだろう.

**Practice.** Say: I don't know whether she's coming. · Please ask what time it starts. · I don't remember where I put it. Answers: 来るかどうか分かりません。 · 何時に始まるか聞いてください。 · どこに置いたか覚えていません。
～ばよかった and ～ところだった:
Regret, and near-misses.

**〜ばよかった — "I should have".**

もっと勉強すれ**ばよかった**。 — I should have studied more.
早く来れ**ばよかった**です。 — I should have come earlier.

**It is the ば conditional plus よかった** — "if I had done it, it would have been good" — and it always carries regret about something that did not happen.

**〜なければよかった — "I shouldn't have":**

あんなことを言わ**なければよかった**。 — I shouldn't have said that.

**〜たらよかった** means the same and is slightly softer.

**〜ばよかったのに** adds reproach, directed at someone else:

言ってくれ**ればよかったのに**。 — You should have told me.

That のに at the end is the complaint from stage 3, and it makes the sentence about their failure rather than your regret.

**〜ところだった — "nearly", a near miss.**

遅(おく)れる**ところでした**。 — I nearly was late.
忘れる**ところでした**。 — I almost forgot.
危(あぶ)ない**ところでした**。 — That was close.

**It takes the dictionary form** and describes something that was about to happen and did not. もう少しで often precedes it: もう少しで転(ころ)ぶところでした — I nearly fell over.

**This is ところ from earlier in the stage**, in the past: the point of being about to do something, now gone by.

**Practice.** Say: I should have studied more. · I shouldn't have eaten so much. · You should have said something. · I nearly forgot. Answers: もっと勉強すればよかった。 · あんなに食べなければよかった。 · 言ってくれればよかったのに。 · 忘れるところでした。
～たらいい, ～ばいい, ～たらどう:
Asking what to do, and suggesting what someone else should.

**どうすればいいですか — "what should I do?"** The single most useful sentence in this family, and worth knowing cold.

**〜たらいい / 〜ばいい — "you should", "it would be good if":**

早く寝**たらいい**ですよ。 — You should go to bed early.
この本を読め**ばいい**と思います。 — I think you should read this book.

**They are gentler than ほうがいい**, which is advice, and far gentler than べき, which is judgement. たらいい is closer to "it'd be good if you…".

**〜たらどうですか — "how about…?"** A direct suggestion:

医者に行っ**たらどうですか**。 — How about going to the doctor?

**It can sound pushy.** 〜たらどう is close to "why don't you just…", and to a superior it is too direct. 〜たらいかがですか is the polite version.

**〜ばいいのに — "I wish you would", with reproach:**

言ってくれ**ればいいのに**。 — I wish you'd just tell me.

**〜たらいいな / 〜ばいいな — "I hope":**

明日晴れ**ればいいな**。 — I hope it's fine tomorrow.
うまくいく**といいですね**。 — I hope it goes well.

**〜といい is the most common form of "I hope"** about someone else's situation, and うまくいくといいですね is what you say to someone facing something difficult. It is worth having as a unit.

**Practice.** Ask what you should do. Then: You should rest. · How about taking the train? · I hope it's sunny tomorrow. Answers: どうすればいいですか。 · 休んだらいいですよ。 · 電車で行ったらどうですか。 · 明日晴れるといいですね。
Giving an opinion, and softening it:
Japanese states opinions less directly than English, and the softening is not optional politeness — a flat assertion sounds like a claim to authority.

**The ladder:**

| | Strength |
| --- | --- |
| 〜です。 | flat — rare about opinions |
| 〜と思います。 | I think |
| 〜と思うんですが | I think, but… (softest common form) |
| 〜ような気(き)がします | I get the feeling |
| 〜かもしれません | it might be |
| 〜んじゃないでしょうか | isn't it the case that…? |

**と思います is the default** and Japanese uses it far more than English uses "I think". Saying 高いです about a price is a statement of fact; 高いと思います is an opinion, and the second is usually what you mean.

**〜と思う attaches to the plain form:** 高いと思います, 行くと思います, 学生だと思います.

**〜んじゃないでしょうか is the useful one for disagreeing:**

ちょっと高いん**じゃないでしょうか**。 — Isn't it a bit expensive?

It raises the point as a question, which lets the other person concede without being contradicted.

**Disagreeing outright:**

そうですね、でも… — Yes, but…
確(たし)かにそうですが… — That's certainly true, but…
おっしゃることは分かりますが… — I see what you mean, but…

**The pattern is always agree-then-turn.** Leading with いいえ or でも alone reads as combative. そうですね as an opener does not mean you agree; it buys the turn.

**気がする — "I get the feeling"** — is heavily used and is weaker than と思う:

違(ちが)うような気がします。 — I get the feeling that's not right.

**Practice.** Give an opinion three ways, increasingly softly: that the film was boring. Answers: つまらなかったです。 · つまらなかったと思います。 · ちょっとつまらなかったような気がします。
Aizuchi: how to listen out loud:
相槌(あいづち) — the noises a Japanese listener makes while the other person is talking. They are not interruptions; they are required, and a silent listener reads as uninterested or hostile.

**The set:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| はい · ええ · うん | yes, go on (formal to casual) |
| そうですか | is that so |
| そうですね | indeed |
| なるほど | I see |
| へえ | oh really (surprise) |
| ほんとう(に)？ | really? |
| それで？ | and then? |
| たしかに | certainly |
| わかります | I understand |

**The frequency is the surprise.** A Japanese listener produces one roughly every few seconds, far more often than an English listener says "mm" or "right". On the telephone it is essential — without it the speaker will stop and ask もしもし？ to check you are still there.

**うん and ええ are not agreement.** They mean "I am receiving this", and a listener can うん their way through something they completely disagree with. English speakers routinely misread this as consent, and Japanese speakers routinely misread English silence as disagreement.

**Match the register.** はい with a superior, ええ in neutral conversation, うん with friends. うん to your boss is too casual; はい to a close friend is oddly stiff.

**Nodding goes with it**, and more of it than feels natural.

**へえ is the surprise one** and carries real interest — it is the sound of being told something worth hearing, and using it makes a speaker feel listened to.

**What not to do:** finishing the other person's sentences, which is normal in English conversation and reads as impatient here.

**Practice.** Watch any Japanese interview and count the aizuchi in one minute. Then listen to a podcast and practise producing them aloud at the right moments — it feels absurd alone and it is the only way to build the reflex.
Fillers and buying time:
What to say while thinking, and what to say when you have not understood. Both are vocabulary, and a learner without them falls silent at exactly the wrong moments.

**Fillers:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| えーと · えー | um, let me see |
| あのー | er — also used to get attention |
| そうですね | well now… (buying a turn) |
| なんか | like, sort of |
| まあ | well |
| ちょっと | a moment / a bit |
| そのー | that is to say |

**そうですね is the most useful** because it is a complete and polite way to take two seconds before answering a question. It is what everyone says.

**なんか is the Japanese "like"** and is extremely common in casual speech. Overused it sounds vague, which is also true of "like".

**When you have not understood:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| すみません、もう一度お願いします。 | Once more, please. |
| もう少しゆっくりお願いします。 | A bit slower, please. |
| 〜って、どういう意味ですか。 | What does ~ mean? |
| 〜ってことですか。 | Do you mean that…? |
| すみません、ちょっと分かりませんでした。 | Sorry, I didn't catch that. |

**〜ってことですか is the best of them**, because it checks your understanding rather than asking for a repeat, and it keeps the conversation moving: 明日は休みってことですか。

**Do not pretend to understand.** Nodding through something you did not catch is the single most expensive habit in language learning: the conversation moves on, the misunderstanding compounds, and you learn nothing. Asking is normal, and native speakers ask each other constantly.

**Practice.** Have a conversation — or shadow one — and deliberately use そうですね before answering, なんか once, and 〜ってことですか to check something.
Reading: native material for children:
The first material written for Japanese people rather than for learners. It is a real step and it is where the graded readers were leading.

**The ladder:**

1. **絵本(えほん)** — picture books. All kana, simple structures, pictures carrying meaning.
2. **児童書(じどうしょ)** — children's books with furigana on every kanji. 青い鳥文庫 and 角川つばさ文庫 are the big series.
3. **Manga for children** — こどもの日 titles, and anything with full furigana.

**ふりがな is the thing to look for.** Material aimed at primary-school readers prints the reading above every kanji, which removes the single biggest obstacle. 小学生向け, 全ルビ or 総ルビ on a listing means exactly this.

**Where to get it free:**

- **青空文庫** has children's classics — 宮沢賢治(みやざわけんじ) especially — out of copyright.
- **Public libraries** in Japan; **Kindle** samples otherwise.
- **ehonnavi.net** has free picture books to read online.

**What changes from Tadoku.** The vocabulary is no longer controlled, so you will meet words you do not know in a way graded readers avoided. The sentences are natural rather than simplified, which means they are often *shorter* and easier than a graded reader's careful explanations.

**Keep the extensive-reading rules**, with one amendment: you may now look up a word that appears three times, because real material repeats its own vocabulary and those repeats are the words worth having.

**宮沢賢治's 注文の多い料理店** is a common first real story — short, strange, and genuinely good.

**Practice.** Read one 絵本 today. Then find one 児童書 with full furigana and read the first page, and notice how much the furigana does.
Reading: manga, and why it is harder tha:
Manga is the material every learner wants and it is not the easy option it appears to be.

**Why it looks easy:** pictures, short lines, lots of furigana in shōnen titles.

**Why it is hard:**

- **It is nearly all casual speech**, with every contraction from the earlier lesson, particles dropped, and sentences left unfinished.
- **Role language.** Characters speak in exaggerated registers — old men, tough guys, little girls — that nobody uses. Learning from it is how you end up sounding like a cartoon.
- **Onomatopoeia** everywhere, hand-drawn, not in any dictionary you can search.
- **Slang and invented vocabulary**, especially in fantasy.

**What to pick.** Slice-of-life over fantasy, modern over historical, and anything aimed at 小学生, which will have full furigana. **よつばと！** is the standard recommendation: everyday vocabulary, full furigana, and genuinely funny.

**What to avoid at this stage:** anything historical, anything with invented terminology, and 少年ジャンプ action titles, which are full of shouting in forms you will not meet again.

**How to read it.** Picture first, then the line. The art is carrying context and using it is not cheating — it is what makes manga comprehensible input rather than decoding.

**Mine from it**, by the usual rule: words that appear more than once.

**Digital with Yomitan** removes the lookup problem entirely for anything with selectable text, which is most legally purchased digital manga.

**The pay-off.** Manga is the first native material most learners actually enjoy rather than endure, and enjoyment is what produces volume. Volume is what produces fluency.

**Practice.** Read ten pages of よつばと！ today. Note how many lines end without a verb — that absence is what casual speech does, and getting used to it is half of this.
Listening: drama, variety and anime:
Native television, which is the hardest listening there is and the most rewarding.

**In order of difficulty, easiest first:**

1. **News** — stage 4 covered it. Slow, standard, repetitive vocabulary.
2. **Documentaries** — NHK's are excellent, narrated clearly, subject vocabulary repeats.
3. **Drama** — scripted, clear, but fast and full of implication.
4. **Anime** — fast, slangy, role language, sound effects over dialogue.
5. **Variety** — the hardest. Overlapping speech, regional accents, in-jokes, on-screen text you must read while listening.

**Anime is not the easy option**, and putting it fourth surprises people. Its speech is quick, exaggerated and full of forms nobody uses; the fantasy vocabulary is useless elsewhere; and the reputation it has as learner material comes from enthusiasm rather than from difficulty.

**That said, watch it.** Interest beats optimality — 50 episodes of something you love is worth more than 5 of something you should.

**Subtitles: the rule.** **Japanese subtitles are good; English subtitles are useless.** With English on, you read and hear nothing. With Japanese on, you are doing listening and reading at once and they reinforce each other. With nothing, you are doing pure listening, which is hardest and most valuable.

The honest sequence for one episode: watch with Japanese subtitles, then again without.

**Where Japanese subtitles come from.** Netflix has them for most Japanese content. **asbplayer** syncs external subtitle files and allows mining directly from a video with Yomitan, which is the standard setup for immersion learners.

**What to expect.** The first episodes of anything will be 20% comprehensible, and that is correct. The number climbs slowly and then suddenly.

**Practice.** Watch one episode of a slice-of-life anime with Japanese subtitles, then the same episode without. Note how much more you catch the second time — that gap is the thing you are training.
以上, 以下, 未満, 以内 — bounds:
Precise words for ranges, which appear on every form, sign and legal notice.

| | Means | Includes the number? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 以上(いじょう) | ~ or more | **yes** |
| 以下(いか) | ~ or less | **yes** |
| 未満(みまん) | under ~ | **no** |
| 以内(いない) | within ~ | **yes** |
| 超(こ)える | over ~ | no |

**18歳以上** — 18 and over, including 18.
**18歳未満** — under 18, excluding 18.
**三日以内** — within three days, including the third.

**That inclusivity is the whole point** and it is legally load-bearing: 20歳未満は飲酒禁止 means under-20s may not drink, and a 20-year-old may.

**以上 also means "that's all"** at the end of a list or an order — 以上です — which was in stage 4's restaurant lesson. Same word, from the sense of "the above".

**Other range words:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 約(やく) | approximately |
| およそ | roughly |
| ほぼ | nearly, almost entirely |
| 〜ぐらい / 〜くらい | about |
| 〜前後(ぜんご) | around, give or take |
| 〜から〜まで | from ~ to ~ |

**約 goes before the number**, くらい after: 約三十分 and 三十分くらい are the same, the first written and the second spoken.

**〜ずつ — each, apiece:**

一人二つ**ずつ**ください。 — Two each, please.
少し**ずつ**覚(おぼ)えます。 — I'll learn it bit by bit.

**少しずつ is very common** and is the honest answer to how language learning goes.

**〜おきに and 〜ごとに — intervals:**

- 三日**おきに** — every third day (two days between)
- 三日**ごとに** — every three days

おきに counts the gaps and ごとに counts the units, which is a distinction native speakers also get confused about. ごとに is safer.

**Practice.** Read: 20歳未満お断り · 三日以内にご返信ください · 約1,000円 · 一人一つずつ. Then say: Within a week. · About thirty minutes. · Little by little.
自分, and the words for I and you:
Japanese has many words for "I" and almost no usable word for "you", and both facts matter.

**For "I":**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 私(わたし) | neutral; formal for everyone |
| 私(わたくし) | very formal |
| 僕(ぼく) | men, soft |
| 俺(おれ) | men, casual to rough |
| うち / あたし | women, casual |
| 自分(じぶん) | oneself; also "I" in some male speech |

**For "you" — avoid all of them.**

- **あなた** is in textbooks and is rarely used. Between strangers it can be cold; a wife may use it for her husband. Using it on someone you have just met is a small mistake.
- **君(きみ)** is downward — a superior to a junior, or a man to a close partner.
- **お前(まえ)** is rough and can be an insult.
- **あんた** is rude.

**Use their name plus さん instead.** 田中さんはどう思いますか — "what do you think, Tanaka" — where English would say "you". This is the normal solution and it is used even when the person is standing right there.

**Or drop it entirely**, which is better still: どう思いますか is a complete question and the subject is obvious.

**自分 — oneself.** It refers back to the subject, whoever that is:

**自分**の部屋で勉強します。 — I study in my own room.
彼は**自分**の間違(まちが)いを認(みと)めました。 — He admitted his own mistake.

**自分で** — by oneself: 自分でやります, I'll do it myself.
**自分の** — one's own.

**In some male speech 自分 means "I"**, particularly in sport and the military, and in Kansai it can mean "you", which is a genuine source of confusion.

**Practice.** Rewrite without あなた: あなたはどこに住んでいますか。 · あなたの本ですか。 Answers: どこに住んでいますか。 · [name]さんの本ですか。 Then say: I'll do it myself.
話し言葉 and 書き言葉:
Spoken and written Japanese differ more than spoken and written English do, and mixing them is one of the clearest markers of a learner.

**The paired vocabulary:**

| Spoken | Written |
| --- | --- |
| でも | しかし |
| だから | したがって · そのため |
| けど | が |
| すごく · とても | 非常(ひじょう)に · 大変 |
| だんだん | 次第(しだい)に |
| ちょっと | 少々 · やや |
| いろいろ | 様々(さまざま) |
| もっと | さらに |
| ぜんぜん | まったく |
| やっぱり | やはり |

**Grammar differs too:**

- Written Japanese uses **だ・である**, not です・ます.
- Contractions do not appear: 〜ている, not 〜てる.
- Particles are not dropped.
- 〜なければならない, not 〜なきゃ.

**である is the formal written copula**, more formal than だ and standard in essays and reports:

これは重要(じゅうよう)な問題**である**。 — This is an important problem.

**Mixing is the error.** A report that says しかし in one paragraph and でも in the next reads as carelessly as an English essay that says "however" and then "but, like". Pick one register per text.

**Email is its own thing** — polite です・ます with formal vocabulary, because it addresses a person.

**What takes which:**

| | Register |
| --- | --- |
| Essay, report, article | だ・である, written vocabulary |
| Novel narration | だ・である |
| Email, letter | です・ます, formal vocabulary |
| Blog, casual writing | です・ます or だ |
| Dialogue in fiction | spoken register |

**Practice.** Rewrite in written register: でも、それはちょっと難しいです。だから、すごく時間がかかると思います。 Answer: しかし、それはやや難しい。したがって、非常に時間がかかると考えられる。
Reporting what someone said:
Three ways to pass on speech, differing in how exactly you are quoting.

**1. Direct quotation, with 「」 and と:**

田中さんは「明日行きます」**と**言いました。 — Tanaka said "I'll go tomorrow."

**2. Indirect, with the plain form and と:**

田中さんは明日行く**と**言いました。 — Tanaka said he'd go tomorrow.

**と always takes the plain form** — 行くと言いました, never 行きますと言いました. That is a firm rule and a common error.

**Tense inside the quote is relative to the quoting.** 行くと言いました is "he said he would go" — the 行く is future relative to his saying it, not to now.

**3. Hearsay, with そうです or ということです:**

田中さんは明日行く**そうです**。 — I hear Tanaka is going tomorrow.

**The reporting verbs:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 〜と言う | said |
| 〜と話す | told, spoke |
| 〜と聞く | heard |
| 〜と思う | thought |
| 〜と書いてある | it is written that |
| 〜と呼(よ)ぶ | call, name |

**〜と書いてあります** is how you report what a sign or document says, and it uses てある from stage 3: here ここは禁煙だと書いてあります.

**Indirect requests take ように**, from the earlier lesson: 早く来るように言われました.

**In casual speech, って replaces と:**

明日行く**って**言ってた。 — He said he's going tomorrow.

**って言ってた is extremely common** and is what you will hear, rather than と言っていました.

**Practice.** Report: "I'm busy" — as a direct quote, indirectly, and as hearsay. Answers: 「忙しいです」と言いました。 · 忙しいと言いました。 · 忙しいそうです。
～と思われる and the impersonal voice:
Written Japanese avoids naming who thinks something, and the passive is how it does it.

**〜と思われる — "it is thought that".**

この問題は解決(かいけつ)できる**と思われる**。 — It is thought that this problem can be solved.

**〜とされている — "it is held to be":**

これは世界最古(せかいさいこ)の木造建築(もくぞうけんちく)**とされている**。 — This is held to be the world's oldest wooden building.

**〜と言われている — "it is said that":**

日本人は働きすぎだ**と言われている**。 — Japanese people are said to work too much.

**〜と考(かんが)えられる — "it can be considered":**

原因(げんいん)は三つある**と考えられる**。 — There are thought to be three causes.

**Why the passive.** Academic and journalistic Japanese does not say 私は〜と思う. Attributing the claim to nobody in particular is the convention, exactly as English academic writing prefers "it is argued that" to "I argue that" — but Japanese does it far more thoroughly.

**This is the single clearest marker of written style**, and reading news or essays without recognising it leaves you wondering who is speaking.

**〜によると — "according to":**

天気予報(てんきよほう)**によると**、明日は雨だそうです。 — According to the forecast, it'll rain tomorrow.

**によると pairs with そうです or らしい** at the end — the source at the front, the hearsay marker at the back. That pairing is fixed and worth learning as a unit.

**Practice.** Rewrite impersonally: 私はこれが一番いいと思います。 Then say: According to the news, the typhoon is coming. Answers: これが最も良いと思われる。 · ニュースによると、台風が来るそうです。
JLPT: what it is, and whether to take it:
The 日本語能力試験 — the standard external measure. Worth understanding whether or not you sit it.

**Five levels, N5 easiest to N1 hardest.** It tests **reading and listening only**: no speaking, no writing, no production of any kind. Multiple choice throughout.

**Roughly where you are.** By the end of stage 4 you are around N4; stage 5's grammar is N3 with some N2. N2 is the level employers ask for; N1 certifies reading "logically complex and abstract writings" and following news and lectures at natural speed.

**Held twice a year**, July and December, in Japan and worldwide. Registration closes months ahead.

**The case for taking it:**

- A **deadline**, which is the main thing. A fixed date produces more study than an open-ended intention.
- **Employers ask for it** — N2 or N1 on a CV is a real credential in Japan.
- Some **visas** award points for it.
- It gives a **measurable number** in a process that otherwise has none.

**The case against:**

- It tests **recognition, not production**. You can pass N1 and be unable to hold a conversation, and plenty of people have.
- **Studying for it distorts** what you study — JLPT grammar lists contain forms that are rare in real Japanese and omit things that are everywhere.
- It is not needed if nobody is asking for it.

**The honest position.** If you want the deadline or the credential, take it. If you want to speak Japanese, the test measures almost none of that, and the thing it measures is produced by the curriculum anyway.

**If you do take it:** 日本語能力試験 公式問題集 (official practice papers, free as PDFs on jlpt.jp) is the only study material you need beyond ordinary study. Do one paper, under time, to find out which section is weak.

**Practice.** Read the official N3 level description on jlpt.jp and decide honestly whether you are near it. Then decide whether you want to sit anything, and write the answer down.
Writing: an opinion piece:
The step from describing to arguing, in written register.

**The shape, which is conventional and worth following:**

1. **序論(じょろん)** — introduce the question and state your position.
2. **本論(ほんろん)** — reasons, one per paragraph, with examples.
3. **結論(けつろん)** — restate, briefly.

**The connectives this needs**, in written register:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| まず · 第一(だいいち)に | first |
| 次に · 第二に | second |
| また · さらに | also, moreover |
| 例(たと)えば | for example |
| 一方 | on the other hand |
| しかし | however |
| したがって · そのため | therefore |
| つまり | in other words |
| 以上(いじょう)のように | as described above |
| 結論として | in conclusion |

**Stating a position without claiming authority:**

〜と考える。 — I consider that…
〜のではないだろうか。 — Is it not the case that…?
〜べきである。 — ought to be…

**〜のではないだろうか is the standard academic hedge** and is far more common than a flat assertion.

**だ・である throughout.** No です, no ます, no でも, no けど, no contractions. The register lesson applies in full.

**Length.** 400–600 characters is a sensible target — about two screens, three or four paragraphs.

**Subjects that produce real writing:** something you actually have a view on. 日本語学習に教科書は必要か. 在宅勤務(ざいたくきんむ)についてどう思うか. なぜ外国語を学ぶのか.

**Getting it corrected.** HiNative takes a text this long. An italki tutor will correct writing between lessons, which is the best value in the whole enterprise — written errors are systematic and a single correction fixes a pattern.

**Practice.** Write 400 characters in だ・である arguing a position, using at least five of the connectives above. Then read it aloud and check that no です has crept in.
Speaking: holding a longer conversation:
From transactions to conversation — the step where you stop completing scripts and start sustaining something unscripted.

**What makes it hard.** A transaction has a shape and ends. A conversation has to be kept going, and keeping it going is a skill separate from knowing the language.

**The four things that sustain it:**

**1. Aizuchi**, constantly, from the earlier lesson. Silence kills a Japanese conversation faster than a mistake does.

**2. Follow-up questions.** The single most useful habit:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| どうしてですか。 | Why is that? |
| 例えば？ | For example? |
| それで、どうなりましたか。 | And then what happened? |
| 〜はどうですか。 | How about ~? |
| 私もです。 | Me too. |

**3. Returning the question.** 〜さんは？ — "and you?" — is a complete sentence and hands the turn back.

**4. Buying time** rather than falling silent: そうですね, えーと, なんていうんだろう ("how do I say it…"), which is what native speakers do too.

**When you do not know a word**, describe it rather than stopping:

〜みたいなものです。 — It's like a ~.
名前は分からないんですが、〜するものです。 — I don't know the word, but it's a thing that ~.

**That skill — talking around a gap — is worth more than vocabulary**, because the gap will always be there and the vocabulary will always be finite.

**Where.** A weekly italki conversation lesson is the most efficient option and is cheap. HelloTalk voice calls are free. A language exchange means half the time is in English, which halves the value but makes it sustainable.

**Thirty minutes a week, consistently**, beats three hours once a month. The gain is in frequency.

**Practice.** Have one 30-minute conversation this week with the rule that you may not switch to English. Afterwards write down three things you could not say, and learn them.
Review: the intermediate grammar:
The end of stage 5. A checklist to find what did not stick.

**For each, produce a sentence aloud.** Recognition is not the test.

**Aspect and compound verbs**
- 〜ところ in all three forms
- はじめる, だす, つづける, おわる
- きる, きれない, かける, なおす, あう, こむ
- がち, ぎみ, っぽい

**Certainty and modality**
- はず, はずがない, はずだった
- に違いない, おそれがある, かもしれない
- わけだ, わけではない, わけがない, わけにはいかない
- べきだ, ものだ, しかない, ざるを得ない

**Conditions and concession**
- ても / でも, いくら〜ても
- ば〜ほど, につれて
- ものの, 一方で, 反面, くせに
- さえ〜ば, こそ

**Connecting**
- について, に関して, に対して, にとって
- によって, として
- せいで, おかげで, ために
- うちに, 間に, たとたん, 次第, たびに
- ばかりか, だけでなく, 上に

**Voice and request**
- causative-passive, and its contraction
- させていただく
- the request ladder to いただけないでしょうか

**Register**
- 話し言葉 and 書き言葉 pairs
- だ・である
- contractions, recognised
- aizuchi, produced

**Expression**
- かどうか and embedded questions
- ばよかった, ところだった
- たらいい, たらどう
- と思われる and the impersonal voice

**What stage 6 does.** Native material as the main diet rather than an exercise: novels, television, podcasts made for Japanese people. The grammar is largely in place; what follows is volume, and the vocabulary that only volume gives.

**Practice.** Go down the list. Three sentences for each heading, aloud. Mark the headings where you hesitated, and reread those lessons this week.
～ようとする and ～たがる:
Two forms about attempting and about wanting, both of which solve a problem with other people's inner states.

**〜ようとする — to try to, to be about to.** The volitional plus する:

出かけ**ようとした**とき、電話が鳴りました。 — Just as I was about to go out, the phone rang.
開け**ようとしました**が、開きませんでした。 — I tried to open it, but it wouldn't.

**It is an attempt that fails or is interrupted.** A successful try is just the plain verb.

**〜ようとしない — refuses to, won't:**

誰も手伝(てつだ)**おうとしません**。 — Nobody will lift a finger.
子供が野菜を食べ**ようとしない**。 — The child won't eat vegetables.

That one carries real exasperation and is very useful.

**〜てみる is the other "try"** — trying something to see what happens, which usually succeeds:

食べ**てみて**ください。 — Give it a taste.

ようとする is attempting; てみる is experimenting. Confusing them produces sentences that sound either defeatist or glib.

**〜たがる — a third person's wanting.** From stage 3: たい is only for yourself, because you cannot know another's desires. たがる solves it:

子供がアイスを食べ**たがって**います。 — The child wants ice cream.
彼は行き**たがらない**。 — He doesn't want to go.

**It is the ます stem plus たがる**, and it is usually in the ている form — たがっている — because it describes observable behaviour: they are *showing signs of* wanting.

**It is slightly distancing** and is not used about someone present and senior. For them, 〜たいですか asks directly, or 〜たいそうです reports.

**Practice.** Say: I tried to open the window but it wouldn't open. · He won't listen (聞く). · My child wants to go to Japan. Answers: 窓を開けようとしましたが、開きませんでした。 · 話を聞こうとしません。 · 子供が日本に行きたがっています。
～がする, 見える, 聞こえる:
Verbs of perception that take が, and the difference between seeing and being able to see.

**〜がする — a sensation reaches you:**

いい匂(にお)い**がします**。 — There's a nice smell.
変(へん)な音(おと)**がします**。 — There's a strange noise.
寒気(さむけ)**がします**。 — I feel chilly.
めまい**がします**。 — I feel dizzy.

**The set is fixed:** 音, 匂い, 味(あじ), 気(き), 感(かん)じ, and the medical sensations from stage 4. It is a state that arrives, not something you do, which is why が and not を.

**〜気がする — "I get the feeling"**, from the opinion lesson, is this same construction.

**見える and 聞こえる — able to be seen and heard, without trying:**

ここから富士山が**見えます**。 — You can see Fuji from here.
音楽が**聞こえます**。 — I can hear music.

**Against 見られる and 聞ける**, the potential forms:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 見える | it is visible — passively, naturally |
| 見られる | I am able to see it — circumstances allow |
| 聞こえる | it is audible |
| 聞ける | I am able to listen to it |

ここから海が**見えます** — the sea is in view. 明日なら映画が**見られます** — tomorrow I can watch the film. The first is about the world, the second about your opportunity.

**Both take が**, like all the potential-flavoured verbs.

**できる belongs to the same family** and is the potential of する, taking が: 日本語ができます.

**Practice.** Say: There's a strange smell. · You can see the sea from the window. · I can't hear anything. · Tomorrow I can go. Answers: 変な匂いがします。 · 窓から海が見えます。 · 何も聞こえません。 · 明日なら行けます。
～限り, ～上で, ～次第で:
Three expressions for scope and condition, all common in writing and formal speech.

**〜限(かぎ)り — as far as, as long as.**

私の知る**限り**、彼は来ません。 — As far as I know, he isn't coming.
できる**限り**早く行きます。 — I'll go as soon as I possibly can.
生きている**限り**、諦(あきら)めません。 — As long as I live, I won't give up.

**私の知る限り is a very useful hedge** and is the Japanese "as far as I know".

**〜ない限り — unless:**

雨が降らない**限り**、行きます。 — Unless it rains, I'll go.

**〜限りでは** narrows it to a source: 見た**限りでは**大丈夫そうです — from what I saw, it looks fine.

**〜上(うえ)で — after doing, as a basis for.**

よく考えた**上で**、決めます。 — I'll decide after thinking it over properly.
面接(めんせつ)の**上で**判断(はんだん)します。 — We'll judge on the basis of the interview.

**It implies the first step informs the second**, which is more than 後で. 相談した上で決めます is "I'll decide having consulted", not merely afterwards.

**〜上で also means "in the process of":** 生きていく**上で**大切なこと — things that matter in living.

**〜次第(しだい)で — depending on.**

天気**次第で**、中止になるかもしれません。 — Depending on the weather, it may be cancelled.
あなた**次第です**。 — It's up to you.

**〜次第です is "it's up to"** and is a complete, very usable sentence. Note this is a different 次第 from 〜次第 ("as soon as") earlier in the stage — same characters, different construction.

**Practice.** Say: As far as I know, he's fine. · Unless it rains, we'll go. · I'll decide after talking to her. · It depends on you. Answers: 私の知る限り、彼は元気です。 · 雨が降らない限り、行きます。 · 彼女と話した上で決めます。 · あなた次第です。
～向け, ～向き, ～だらけ, ～ばかり:
Four suffixes about suitability and excess.

**〜向(む)け — intended for, aimed at.**

子供**向け**の本 — a book aimed at children
初心者(しょしんしゃ)**向け** — for beginners
海外(かいがい)**向け**に作られた — made for export

**It is about intention** — somebody designed it for that audience.

**〜向(む)き — suited to, facing.**

子供**向き**の本 — a book suitable for children
初心者**向き** — well suited to beginners
南(みなみ)**向き**の部屋 — a south-facing room

**向け is design; 向き is suitability.** A book written for adults may still be 子供向き if it happens to suit them. The distinction is fine and natives are not rigorous about it, but 向き also means "facing", which 向け never does — 南向き, 上向き.

**〜だらけ — covered in, full of (unpleasant).**

間違(まちが)い**だらけ** — riddled with mistakes
泥(どろ)**だらけ** — covered in mud
借金(しゃっきん)**だらけ** — up to the eyes in debt

**It is always negative** and always about something unwelcome spread all over.

**〜ばかり — nothing but**, from stage 3, is the near neighbour: ゲームばかりしている. ばかり is about exclusivity of activity; だらけ is about being covered in a substance or a fault.

**〜まみれ is stronger than だらけ** and strictly physical: 血(ち)まみれ, 汗(あせ)まみれ — covered in blood, in sweat.

**Practice.** Say: a book for beginners · a south-facing room · covered in mistakes · he does nothing but sleep. Answers: 初心者向けの本 · 南向きの部屋 · 間違いだらけ · 寝てばかりいます。
～を通じて, ～に基づいて, ～をもとに:
Three formal expressions about means and basis, all common in writing.

**〜を通(つう)じて / 〜を通(とお)して — through, by means of, throughout.**

友達**を通じて**知り合いました。 — We met through a friend.
一年**を通じて**暖かいです。 — It's warm throughout the year.
経験(けいけん)**を通して**学びました。 — I learned it through experience.

**The two are nearly identical.** を通じて leans towards a medium or intermediary; を通して towards a process you went through. Either is usually acceptable.

**〜に基(もと)づいて — based on, in accordance with.**

事実(じじつ)**に基づいて**書かれています。 — It is written based on fact.
法律(ほうりつ)**に基づいて**処理(しょり)します。 — It will be handled in accordance with the law.

**It implies a foundation that constrains** — a law, a rule, data. Formal and common in official writing.

**〜をもとに — on the basis of, using as material.**

この映画は実話(じつわ)**をもとに**作られました。 — This film was made based on a true story.
アンケート**をもとに**分析(ぶんせき)しました。 — I analysed it using the survey as a basis.

**をもとに is looser than に基づいて** — it is raw material you worked from, not a rule you obeyed. A film based on a true story takes をもとに; a decision made under the law takes に基づいて.

**〜によって, from earlier**, is the general "by" and overlaps with all three. The specific ones are chosen when the relationship is worth naming.

**Practice.** Say: We met through a friend. · It's based on a true story. · It will be handled according to the rules. · It's cold all year round. Answers: 友達を通じて知り合いました。 · 実話をもとにしています。 · 規則(きそく)に基づいて処理します。 · 一年を通じて寒いです。
Listening: podcasts made for Japanese pe:
The last rung of the listening ladder before television, and the most practical daily habit available.

**Why podcasts rather than TV.** They are audio only, so there is no picture to carry you — which makes them harder than drama and better training. They are long, free, abundant, and they repeat presenters, so you get used to specific voices.

**Where to start**, roughly in order:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **バイリンガルニュース** | two hosts, Japanese and English mixed, long and unscripted |
| **COTEN RADIO** | history, clearly spoken, genuinely interesting |
| **NHKラジオニュース** | five minutes, hourly, standard |
| **ゆる言語学ラジオ** | linguistics, fast, very chatty |
| **Rebuild.fm** | technology, two engineers, lots of English loanwords |

**Rebuild.fm is unusually approachable for a programmer** — the subject vocabulary is largely katakana English, which means a large share of the content words are already known.

**How to use them.** Twenty to thirty minutes a day, while walking or cooking. Accept that you will lose the thread. The gain is cumulative and comes from hours rather than from attention — this is the one place where volume genuinely beats intensity, because the ear needs exposure more than it needs analysis.

**One episode twice** is better than two episodes once, early on.

**The measure.** Every month, listen to an episode you heard a month ago. The difference is the only reliable feedback, and it is striking.

**Transcripts**, where they exist, turn a podcast into reading practice as well. COTEN RADIO and several others publish them.

**Practice.** Pick one podcast and listen to the same episode three times this week: once passively, once with attention, once passively again. Note what you caught the third time that you missed the first.
Kanji 11 · 高 安 新 古 多 少 長 短:
Eight more, continuing down the frequency list. Each with the readings it takes and the words those readings appear in.

The adjectives, in pairs of opposites. Each has a kun reading used as an adjective and an on reading used in compounds, which makes them a clean demonstration of the split.

| Kanji | Strokes | Readings | In words |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 高 | 10 | コウ / たか-い | 高い takai · 高校 kōkō · 最高 saikō |
| 安 | 6 | アン / やす-い | 安い yasui · 安心 anshin · 安全 anzen |
| 新 | 13 | シン / あたら-しい | 新しい atarashii · 新聞 shinbun · 新幹線 shinkansen |
| 古 | 5 | コ / ふる-い | 古い furui · 中古 chūko · 古本 furuhon |
| 多 | 6 | タ / おお-い | 多い ōi · 多分 tabun · 多数 tasū |
| 少 | 4 | ショウ / すく-ない・すこ-し | 少ない sukunai · 少し sukoshi · 少年 shōnen |
| 長 | 8 | チョウ / なが-い | 長い nagai · 社長 shachō · 長所 chōsho |
| 短 | 12 | タン / みじか-い | 短い mijikai · 短期 tanki · 短所 tanshō |

**高 means both "tall" and "expensive"**, which is why 高いビル and 高い本 use the same word. 最高(さいこう) — "the highest" — is also the everyday word for "brilliant".

**安 is "cheap" and also "at ease"** — 安心 is a settled heart, 安全 is safety. The sense of cost came later.

**長所 and 短所** — long point and short point — are strengths and weaknesses, and they are what a job interview asks about.

**多い and 少ない cannot go before a noun** in the ordinary way. 多い人 does not mean "many people"; you say 人が多い or たくさんの人. This is a genuine irregularity in two very common adjectives.

**社長 is the company president** — 社 from 会社 plus 長, the head of something. The pattern recurs: 部長, 課長, 校長, 駅長.

**Writing.** Watch each on Jisho once, trace it, then write it from memory before checking.

**Practice.** Write every word in the table by hand, then cover the readings and read them back.
Kanji 12 · 東 西 南 北 山 川 田 町:
Eight more, continuing down the frequency list. Each with the readings it takes and the words those readings appear in.

Directions and landscape — and most of the characters in Japanese place names and surnames.

| Kanji | Strokes | Readings | In words |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 東 | 8 | トウ / ひがし | 東 higashi · 東京 Tōkyō · 東口 higashiguchi |
| 西 | 6 | セイ・サイ / にし | 西 nishi · 西口 nishiguchi · 関西 Kansai |
| 南 | 9 | ナン / みなみ | 南 minami · 南口 minamiguchi · 南米 Nanbei |
| 北 | 5 | ホク / きた | 北 kita · 北口 kitaguchi · 東北 Tōhoku |
| 山 | 3 | サン / やま | 山 yama · 富士山 Fujisan · 火山 kazan |
| 川 | 3 | セン / かわ | 川 kawa · 河川 kasen |
| 田 | 5 | デン / た | 田んぼ tanbo · 田中 Tanaka · 水田 suiden |
| 町 | 7 | チョウ / まち | 町 machi · 下町 shitamachi |

**The compass order in Japanese is 東西南北** — east, west, south, north — not the English north-first order. 東西 means "east and west" and also "the whole world".

**東京 is "eastern capital"** and 京都 is "capital city". Reading a place name is often reading a description.

**These eight make a large share of Japanese surnames**: 山田, 田中, 山本, 川口, 北川, 西田, 中山, 山口. A surname you cannot read is usually made of characters you can.

**山 and 川 are three strokes each** and are among the oldest pictographs — a mountain and flowing water.

**〜口 on a station** is the exit, from stage 4's signs: 東口, 西口, 北口, 南口. Knowing which one you want is the difference between a five-minute walk and a twenty-minute one.
