**Writing.** Watch each on Jisho once, trace it, then write it from memory before checking.

**Practice.** Write every word in the table by hand, then cover the readings and read them back.
Kanji 13 · 天 気 雨 風 空 海 花 色:
Eight more, continuing down the frequency list. Each with the readings it takes and the words those readings appear in.

Weather and the natural world — the vocabulary of small talk from stage 4.

| Kanji | Strokes | Readings | In words |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 天 | 4 | テン | 天気 tenki · 天国 tengoku · 天ぷら tenpura |
| 気 | 6 | キ・ケ | 気 ki · 天気 tenki · 元気 genki · 気持ち kimochi · 気をつけて ki o tsukete |
| 雨 | 8 | ウ / あめ | 雨 ame · 大雨 ōame · 梅雨 tsuyu |
| 風 | 9 | フウ / かぜ | 風 kaze · 台風 taifū · 風邪 kaze |
| 空 | 8 | クウ / そら・あ-く | 空 sora · 空気 kūki · 空港 kūkō · 空いている aite iru |
| 海 | 9 | カイ / うみ | 海 umi · 海外 kaigai |
| 花 | 7 | カ / はな | 花 hana · 花見 hanami · 花火 hanabi |
| 色 | 6 | ショク / いろ | 色 iro · 茶色 chairo · 顔色 kaoiro |

**気 is one of the most productive characters in the language** and is nearly impossible to translate. It covers air, spirit, mood, intention and attention: 天気 weather, 元気 well, 気持ち feeling, 気をつけて take care, 病気 illness, 人気(にんき) popularity, 気がする to have a feeling.

**風(かぜ) and 風邪(かぜ) are the same sound, different characters** — wind and a cold. The illness is written with 邪, "evil", from an older theory of how one caught it.

**空 is "sky", "air" and "empty"** — 空 そら the sky, 空気 くうき air, 空いている empty or free. The seat-is-free sense from stage 4's booking lesson is this character.

**梅雨 is read つゆ**, which neither character suggests — "plum rain", the June rainy season, and a completely irregular reading.

**海外(かいがい) is "overseas"** — literally beyond the sea — and is the standard word for abroad in a country that is an island.

**Writing.** Watch each on Jisho once, trace it, then write it from memory before checking.

**Practice.** Write every word in the table by hand, then cover the readings and read them back.
Kanji 14 · 立 休 待 持 作 使 住 知:
Eight more, continuing down the frequency list. Each with the readings it takes and the words those readings appear in.

Eight more common verbs, all of which have been used in kana since stage 2.

| Kanji | Strokes | Readings | In words |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 立 | 5 | リツ / た-つ | 立つ tatsu · 立派 rippa · 国立 kokuritsu |
| 休 | 6 | キュウ / やす-む | 休む yasumu · 休み yasumi · 休日 kyūjitsu |
| 待 | 9 | タイ / ま-つ | 待つ matsu · 期待 kitai · 待合室 machiaishitsu |
| 持 | 9 | ジ / も-つ | 持つ motsu · 気持ち kimochi · 持参 jisan |
| 作 | 7 | サク・サ / つく-る | 作る tsukuru · 作品 sakuhin · 作家 sakka |
| 使 | 8 | シ / つか-う | 使う tsukau · 使用 shiyō · 大使館 taishikan |
| 住 | 7 | ジュウ / す-む | 住む sumu · 住所 jūsho · 住民 jūmin |
| 知 | 8 | チ / し-る | 知る shiru · 知識 chishiki · 知人 chijin |

**休 is a person 亻 beside a tree 木** — resting in the shade — and is the clearest compound in the set.

**待 and 持 differ by one radical**: 待 has 彳, the "going" radical, and 持 has 扌, the hand. Waiting is about movement; holding is about the hand. They are otherwise identical and are confused constantly.

**住 is also a person 亻**, with 主 for the sound. 住所(じゅうしょ) is an address, from stage 4's paperwork.

**知る is irregular in the ている form**, as stage 3 noted: 知っています for "I know", but 知りません for "I don't". The negative does not take ている, and nothing explains it.

**立派(りっぱ)** — splendid, fine — is a な-adjective and a common compliment, and it has nothing obvious to do with standing.

**Writing.** Watch each on Jisho once, trace it, then write it from memory before checking.

**Practice.** Write every word in the table by hand, then cover the readings and read them back.
Kanji 15 · 店 駅 道 車 電 社 事 方:
Eight more, continuing down the frequency list. Each with the readings it takes and the words those readings appear in.

Places, transport and work — the characters on signs and business cards.

| Kanji | Strokes | Readings | In words |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 店 | 8 | テン / みせ | 店 mise · 書店 shoten · 喫茶店 kissaten · 開店 kaiten |
| 駅 | 14 | エキ | 駅 eki · 駅前 ekimae · 東京駅 Tōkyō-eki |
| 道 | 12 | ドウ / みち | 道 michi · 道路 dōro · 北海道 Hokkaidō · 柔道 jūdō |
| 車 | 7 | シャ / くるま | 車 kuruma · 電車 densha · 自転車 jitensha · 車両 sharyō |
| 電 | 13 | デン | 電気 denki · 電車 densha · 電話 denwa |
| 社 | 7 | シャ / やしろ | 会社 kaisha · 社会 shakai · 神社 jinja · 社長 shachō |
| 事 | 8 | ジ / こと | 事 koto · 仕事 shigoto · 事故 jiko · 大事 daiji |
| 方 | 4 | ホウ / かた | 方 hō · 方法 hōhō · 夕方 yūgata · あの方 ano kata |

**会社 and 社会 are the same two characters reversed** — company and society — and mean quite different things. Japanese does this often, and the order matters absolutely.

**道 is "road" and also "the way"** in the sense of a discipline: 柔道 the gentle way, 書道 calligraphy, 茶道 the tea ceremony. 北海道 is "north sea road", the old administrative name.

**方 has two readings doing two jobs.** ほう is the "side" from the comparison lesson — こちらのほうが — and かた is a polite word for a person: あの方 is a respectful あの人. It also makes a noun from a verb: 読み方(よみかた), the way of reading, 使い方, how to use.

**〜方(かた) is extremely productive**: 作り方 how to make, 行き方 how to get there, 書き方 how to write. The ます stem plus 方.

**事 is "thing" in the abstract** — the こと nominaliser of stage 3, in its character — and in 仕事, work. 大事(だいじ) is important, and 大事にしてください is "take care of it".

**That is 119 characters**, and the frequency curve is beginning to flatten: the next hundred will each do less work than the last hundred did.

**Writing.** Watch each on Jisho once, trace it, then write it from memory before checking.

**Practice.** Write every word in the table by hand, then cover the readings and read them back.
The transition to native material:
The hardest step in the whole route, and the one most learners stall at.

**What makes it hard.** Graded material was written so you could understand it. Native material was written for someone who already knows the language, and it does not accommodate you at all: no controlled vocabulary, no simplified grammar, no consideration of what you have studied.

**The gap is real and it is temporary.** Going from Tadoku level 4 to a novel is not a step, it is a cliff, and the first month on the other side is unpleasant. Everyone's is.

**The three things that get you across:**

**1. Lower the bar for comprehension.** Understanding 70% of a page is reading. Waiting until you understand 95% means waiting forever, because the only thing that gets you to 95% is reading at 70%.

**2. Choose by interest, not by level.** Something you want to finish will be finished. Something at the perfect level that bores you will not. Interest beats optimality every time at this stage.

**3. Use the tools.** Yomitan on a screen removes the lookup cost almost entirely, and that changes what is possible. Reading a novel on paper with a paper dictionary at this level is a choice to make it twenty times slower.

**What to expect, honestly:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| First book | A month. Painful. Perhaps 60% understood. |
| Second | Two weeks. 70%. |
| Fifth | A week. 85%. |
| Tenth | Days. Enjoyable. |

**The curve is steep because vocabulary repeats.** An author reuses their own words, a genre reuses its own words, and the language reuses its commonest 3,000 constantly. The first book is paying for the next ten.

**Do not abandon graded material entirely.** NHK Easy and Tadoku stay useful as the thing you read when you have no energy for the hard thing. Reading something easy is better than reading nothing.

**Practice.** Pick one piece of native material you actually want to read, today. Not what you should read — what you want to. Read two pages and note the percentage you understood.
Yomitan, and reading on a screen:
The single tool that most changes what is possible at this stage.

**What it is.** A free browser extension — the successor to Yomichan — that shows a word's reading and meaning when you hover over it. No typing, no copying, no leaving the page.

**Why it matters so much.** The cost of a lookup falls from fifteen seconds to half a second. A page with thirty unknown words goes from a ten-minute slog to a readable page. That difference decides whether native material is possible now or in two years.

**Setting it up:**

1. Install Yomitan in Firefox or Chrome.
2. Import a dictionary — **JMdict** is the standard English one, free.
3. Add **JPDB** or **Kanjium** frequency data, so common words are marked.
4. Optionally add a **monolingual** dictionary — 三省堂 or 大辞泉 — for later.

**Mining from it.** Yomitan sends a card straight to Anki with one keypress — and for this site, the Add card form takes the same information by hand. The word, the reading, the meaning, and **the sentence you met it in**.

**The sentence is the point.** A word with its sentence is a card you can learn from; a word with a gloss is a card you will forget.

**What to read with it:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **青空文庫** | out-of-copyright literature, free, HTML |
| **NHK News** | the real version, not Easy |
| **note.com** · **はてなブログ** | blogs, every register |
| **Wikipedia 日本語版** | dense but endlessly available |
| Digital manga and novels | if the text is selectable |

**10ten Reader** is the alternative extension and works on iOS via Safari, where Yomitan does not.

**The warning.** Hovering over every word is not reading — it is decoding with a crutch. Use it for the words that block a sentence, not for every word you are unsure of. If you are hovering more than a few times a line, the text is too hard.

**Practice.** Install Yomitan, import JMdict, and read one NHK article — the real one, not Easy. Note how many hovers a paragraph takes.
Intensive and extensive reading:
Two different activities with different purposes, and doing one while thinking you are doing the other is the commonest waste of effort at this stage.

**Extensive reading — volume, speed, no stopping.**

- Material well within your level.
- No dictionary.
- Skip what you do not know.
- Measure: pages, and speed.
- Purpose: fluency, automaticity, the reflex of taking meaning off the page.

**Intensive reading — depth, analysis, full understanding.**

- Material slightly above your level.
- Dictionary and grammar reference open.
- Nothing skipped.
- Measure: comprehension, and words mined.
- Purpose: new vocabulary, new structures, precision.

**Both are necessary and they do not substitute for each other.** Extensive reading without intensive gives fluent comprehension of what you already know and no growth. Intensive without extensive gives a large vocabulary you cannot read at speed.

**The mix.** Roughly 80% extensive, 20% intensive, by time. Most learners invert that and then wonder why reading is still slow.

**What to use for each:**

| | Extensive | Intensive |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Now | Tadoku 4–5, children's books, easy manga | NHK News, one novel, blog posts |
| Later | Novels you can read comfortably | Anything genuinely hard |

**A practical rhythm:** one hard page with Yomitan and mining, then ten easy pages with nothing. The easy pages consolidate the hard one.

**The sign you have the mix wrong:** if reading always feels like work, there is no extensive reading in your week. If your vocabulary is not growing, there is no intensive reading.

**Practice.** This week, time your reading and split it. Aim for four parts easy to one part hard, and notice which one you have been avoiding.
Your first novel: choosing one:
The choice matters more than the method, because the wrong book ends the attempt.

**What makes a book easy:**

- **Modern** — pre-war Japanese is a different language in places.
- **Dialogue-heavy** — spoken Japanese is simpler than narration.
- **Contemporary setting** — no historical or invented vocabulary.
- **Short chapters** — a finishable unit.
- **Something you know the story of** — a translation you have read, or a film you have seen.

**What makes a book hard:** literary prose, historical settings, fantasy terminology, dense narration, long sentences, and anything praised for its style.

**Commonly recommended first novels:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **コンビニ人間** (村田沙耶香) | modern, short, simple prose, genuinely good |
| **キッチン** (吉本ばなな) | short, contemporary, gentle |
| **魔女の宅急便** (角野栄子) | children's, furigana, the film helps |
| **ハリー・ポッター** translated | you know the plot; the vocabulary is odd |
| **ライトノベル** | dialogue-heavy, furigana, simple prose |

**Light novels are genuinely easier** than literary fiction and are not a lesser choice. They are mostly dialogue, they carry furigana, and the prose is plain.

**Reading a translation of something you know** is the biggest shortcut available: the plot carries you through the sentences you do not understand.

**Where to get them.** Kindle's Japanese store, with a Japanese account or not depending on the title. **青空文庫** is free but out of copyright, so pre-1970 — harder language. Bookwalker sells digital with selectable text, which matters for Yomitan.

**Buy the digital version** if you intend to use a lookup tool. A paper book at this level is a slower path by a wide margin.

**Practice.** Choose one book today. Read the first page and count your unknown words. Under 10 per page is comfortable; 10–25 is a stretch worth taking; over 25 means pick another.
Reading a novel: the method:
How to actually get through the first one.

**Before you start.** Read the blurb and, if you can find one, a Japanese summary. Knowing the premise means the first chapter is about language rather than about working out what is happening.

**The daily shape:**

1. **A fixed amount, not a fixed time.** Five pages. Ten if it is going well. The number matters because "read for an hour" becomes "read for ten minutes and feel bad".
2. **Read a page without looking anything up.** Get the gist.
3. **Read it again with Yomitan**, looking up what blocked you.
4. **Mine two or three words.** Not all of them. The ones that blocked you, or appeared twice.
5. **Move on.**

**Do not look up everything.** A page with forty unknown words and forty mined cards is a page that produces a backlog and ends the habit. Three a page is 600 words over a 200-page novel, which is a great deal.

**Mark and move on.** If a sentence will not resolve after two attempts, mark it and continue. Nine times out of ten the next page explains it, and the tenth does not matter.

**Re-read the first chapter after finishing.** This is the single most encouraging thing available: the chapter that took a week will take twenty minutes, and the difference is visible.

**Keep a count.** Pages per day, words mined, days read. Not for discipline — for evidence. Progress in reading is invisible day to day and obvious over a month.

**Audiobooks alongside** — Audible has a Japanese catalogue — turn a novel into listening practice as well, and hearing a sentence you have read is a strong reinforcement.

**Expect to abandon one.** Starting a second book is not failure; forcing the first is how people stop reading entirely.

**Practice.** Read five pages today by the five steps. Write down the number of words you mined, and the time it took.
Monolingual dictionaries:
The step from Japanese-to-English to Japanese-to-Japanese, and when to take it.

**Why it matters.** A bilingual dictionary gives you an English word that is close. A monolingual one gives you the actual boundaries of the Japanese word, which are never the same as the English one's. 寂しい is not "lonely"; もったいない is not "wasteful"; 遠慮 is not "restraint".

**When to switch.** Not yet, entirely — but start now, in parallel. The usual advice is around 2,000–3,000 known words, which is roughly where stage 6 begins. The method:

1. Look a word up in English, as usual.
2. Then look at the Japanese definition.
3. Notice what the English missed.

**The dictionaries:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **三省堂国語辞典** | concise, modern, the usual first choice |
| **大辞泉** | fuller, with examples |
| **明鏡国語辞典** | strong on usage and common errors |
| **weblio.jp** | free online, aggregates several |
| **goo辞書** | free online |

**Yomitan takes monolingual dictionaries** as imports, so both can be shown at once — English first while you need it, Japanese underneath.

**A monolingual definition is itself reading practice**, and that is half the point. Definitions use a restricted, careful register and the same words recur, so they get easier quickly.

**類語(るいご) — synonym dictionaries** — are the other half: 寂しい against 悲しい against 切ない is a distinction no English gloss will give you.

**The sign you are ready to switch fully:** when the English definition tells you less than the Japanese one did. That happens sooner than expected for concrete words and much later for emotional ones.

**Practice.** Look up 寂しい, もったいない and 遠慮 in both an English and a Japanese dictionary. Write down what the Japanese definition says that the English did not.
News: the structure of an article:
Japanese news is written to a formula, and knowing the formula makes it far easier to read than its vocabulary suggests.

**The shape:**

1. **見出し(みだし) — the headline.** Compressed: particles dropped, verbs nominalised, often ending in a noun. 首相(しゅしょう)、来週訪米(ほうべい)へ — "PM to visit US next week".
2. **リード — the first paragraph.** The whole story in two sentences: who, what, when, where.
3. **本文(ほんぶん) — the body.** Detail, then background, then quotes.

**Read the lead and you have the article.** If the lead is clear, the body is elaboration and can be skimmed. This is the single most useful habit for news reading.

**Headline grammar is its own dialect:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 〜へ | will / heading towards |
| 〜か | possibly |
| 〜も | as many as |
| 〜巡(めぐ)り | regarding |
| noun + か | is it ~? |

Particles and verbs vanish: 政府、支援(しえん)策(さく)を検討(けんとう)か — "Government may be considering support measures".

**Dates and attribution come at the end of the sentence**, as everything does:

〜と、〇〇社が発表した。 — ~, Company X announced.
〜と見られる。 — it is thought that ~ (the impersonal voice from stage 5)

**Quotes are marked with 「」 and と**, and the verb follows: 「〜」と述(の)べた.

**The register is 書き言葉 throughout** — だ・である, written connectives, no contractions. Stage 5's register lesson is what makes it parseable.

**Practice.** Take one NHK article. Read only the headline and the lead, and write the story in one English sentence. Then read the body and check whether you missed anything that mattered.
News vocabulary: the recurring set:
News uses a closed vocabulary, and a few hundred words unlock most of it. This is the highest-return vocabulary in the language after the first thousand.

**Government and politics:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 政府(せいふ) | government |
| 首相(しゅしょう) | prime minister |
| 大臣(だいじん) | minister |
| 国会(こっかい) | the Diet |
| 選挙(せんきょ) | election |
| 法案(ほうあん) | a bill |
| 制度(せいど) | a system |
| 政策(せいさく) | policy |

**Reporting verbs:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 発表(はっぴょう)する | to announce |
| 明(あき)らかにする | to reveal |
| 述(の)べる | to state |
| 指摘(してき)する | to point out |
| 検討(けんとう)する | to consider |
| 判明(はんめい)する | to come to light |

**Change and quantity:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 増加(ぞうか) / 減少(げんしょう) | increase / decrease |
| 上昇(じょうしょう) / 下落(げらく) | rise / fall |
| 過去(かこ)最高(さいこう) | a record high |
| 前年(ぜんねん)比(ひ) | compared to last year |
| 約〜 | approximately |

**Consequence:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 影響(えいきょう) | effect, impact |
| 対応(たいおう) | response |
| 可能性(かのうせい) | possibility |
| 懸念(けねん) | concern |
| 見通(みとお)し | outlook |

**Disasters, which Japanese news covers constantly:**

地震(じしん) · 津波(つなみ) · 台風(たいふう) · 被害(ひがい) damage · 避難(ひなん) evacuation · 警報(けいほう) warning · 注意報(ちゅういほう) advisory

**Nearly all of these are 漢語** — Sino-Japanese compounds — which means they are made of kanji you know, read with on'yomi. 増加 is "increase-add"; 減少 is "decrease-few". Once you have the characters, the compounds are often guessable, which is exactly the pay-off the kanji track promised.

**Practice.** Read one NHK article and mine every word from the lists above that you did not know. Then read a second article tomorrow and count how many recur.
Blogs, forums and short-form Japanese:
Where most written Japanese actually is, and a register the textbooks do not cover.

**Blogs — note.com, はてなブログ, Ameba.** Every register from careful essay to diary. The useful thing about blogs is that they are written by one person at one level, so finding a writer you can read means finding an unlimited supply at that level.

**X/Twitter — the hardest short text there is.** 140 characters forces compression: particles dropped, abbreviations, slang, and context assumed. A tweet can be harder than a paragraph of news.

**The internet register:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 〜w / 〜www | laughter (from 笑) |
| 草(くさ) | also laughter — www looks like grass |
| 〜なう | right now (from "now") |
| マジ | seriously |
| ヤバい | amazing / terrible — context decides |
| エモい | moving, nostalgic |
| 〜すぎる | too ~ (used as emphasis) |
| 乙(おつ) | thanks / good work (from お疲れ) |
| 〜ニキ / 〜ネキ | bloke / lass (2ch slang) |

**ヤバい deserves a note.** Originally "dangerous", it now means both "excellent" and "awful" and is used constantly by anyone under forty. Context and tone decide entirely.

**Reviews — Amazon, 食べログ, 価格.com** — are excellent reading: short, opinionated, repetitive in structure, and full of ordinary adjectives used naturally.

**5ch and its descendants** are the deep end: dense slang, in-jokes, and an argumentative register. Interesting, and not where to start.

**What to take from this.** Read blogs for volume at your level. Read reviews for natural adjectives. Treat Twitter as advanced material rather than as easy material, which its length suggests and its compression denies.

**Practice.** Find one blog whose author you can read comfortably and read three posts. Then read five reviews of a product on Amazon.co.jp and notice how much structure they share.
Grammar you meet only in reading:
Forms that are common in writing and rare in speech, collected because you will not meet them any other way.

**〜ては — repeated or conditional action:**

書い**ては**消し、書い**ては**消しした。 — I wrote and erased, wrote and erased.

**〜ようでは — if this is how it is:** そんなことを言う**ようでは**だめだ。

**〜やいなや / 〜が早(はや)いか — the instant:**

着く**やいなや**、電話が鳴った。 — No sooner had I arrived than the phone rang.

Literary versions of たとたん from stage 5.

**〜つつ — while, and although:**

悪いと知り**つつ**、やってしまった。 — Knowing it was wrong, I did it anyway.

**〜つつある — in the process of:**

状況(じょうきょう)は改善(かいぜん)し**つつある**。 — The situation is improving.

**〜までもない — there is no need to:**

言う**までもない**。 — It goes without saying.

**〜ないことはない — it's not that it can't be done:**

できない**ことはない**。 — It's not impossible.

A double negative used to concede reluctantly, and very Japanese in its indirectness.

**〜とは限(かぎ)らない — not necessarily:**

高いものがいい**とは限らない**。 — Expensive doesn't necessarily mean good.

**〜にすぎない — is nothing more than:**

それは言い訳(わけ)**にすぎない**。 — That's nothing but an excuse.

**〜どころか — far from it:**

安い**どころか**、とても高かった。 — Far from cheap, it was very expensive.

**〜からには / 〜以上(いじょう)は — now that, given that:**

約束した**からには**、守(まも)ります。 — Having promised, I'll keep it.

**These are reading vocabulary.** Recognise them; do not force them into speech, where they will sound bookish. That asymmetry — knowing far more than you use — is normal and correct at this stage.

**Practice.** Find three of these in something you read this week and write down the sentences.
和語 and 漢語: the two vocabularies:
Japanese has two layers of vocabulary for almost everything, and choosing between them is register.

**和語(わご) — native Japanese words**, usually kun readings, often with okurigana:

話す · 食べる · 大きい · 始める · 会う · 終わる

**漢語(かんご) — Sino-Japanese compounds**, on readings, usually two kanji:

会話 · 食事 · 巨大(きょだい) · 開始 · 面会(めんかい) · 終了(しゅうりょう)

**They pair up:**

| 和語 | 漢語 | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 始める | 開始する | to begin |
| 終わる | 終了する | to end |
| 집める → 集める | 収集(しゅうしゅう)する | to collect |
| 選ぶ | 選択(せんたく)する | to choose |
| 使う | 使用する | to use |
| 住む | 居住(きょじゅう)する | to reside |
| 作る | 製作(せいさく)する | to produce |

**The 漢語 is always more formal.** This is almost exactly the Anglo-Saxon/Latinate split in English: *begin* and *commence*, *use* and *utilise*. A sign says 使用禁止; a person says 使わないで.

**Which to use.** 和語 in speech, 漢語 in writing and in anything official. Using 漢語 in conversation sounds stiff; using 和語 in a report sounds childish.

**漢語 + する makes a verb**, which is how Japanese absorbs new concepts: 勉強する, 説明する, 確認する, コピーする. The last shows the same machinery applied to a loanword.

**外来語(がいらいご) is the third layer** — katakana loanwords — and is often the most casual or the most technical, depending. ミーティング and 会議 are the same meeting; the first is a startup and the second is a ministry.

**Reading benefit.** Once you have the characters, a 漢語 you have never seen is often guessable: 増加 from 増える and 加える. That compounding is why the kanji track pays off so steeply in reading.

**Practice.** For each, give the other register: 始める · 終了 · 選ぶ · 使用 · 会話. Answers: 開始 · 終わる · 選択 · 使う · 話。
Compound nouns, prefixes and suffixes:
How Japanese builds long words out of short ones, and how to read one you have never met.

**Noun + noun compounds** are read right to left into English:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 自動販売機(じどうはんばいき) | automatic-sell-machine = vending machine |
| 新幹線 | new-trunk-line |
| 消費税(しょうひぜい) | consumption tax |
| 外国人登録証 | foreigner registration card |

**Long compounds break into two-character units.** 自動 / 販売 / 機. Reading them as pairs is the trick; reading them character by character is not.

**Common prefixes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 不〜(ふ) | un-, dis- — 不安, 不便, 不可能 |
| 無〜(む) | without — 無料, 無理, 無職 |
| 非〜(ひ) | non- — 非常, 非公式 |
| 未〜(み) | not yet — 未成年, 未定 |
| 再〜(さい) | re- — 再開, 再生 |
| 大〜(だい) | big — 大成功, 大問題 |
| 超〜(ちょう) | super- — 超高速; also casual "really" |
| お〜 / ご〜 | polite — お金, ご飯 |

**Common suffixes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 〜的(てき) | -ical, -ive — 経済的, 具体的 |
| 〜性(せい) | -ness, -ity — 可能性, 安全性 |
| 〜化(か) | -isation — 国際化, 電子化 |
| 〜者(しゃ) | person — 記者, 医者, 学者 |
| 〜家(か) | specialist — 作家, 画家, 専門家 |
| 〜員(いん) | member, staff — 会社員, 駅員 |
| 〜料(りょう) | fee — 送料, 入場料 |
| 〜費(ひ) | expense — 交通費, 生活費 |
| 〜中(ちゅう) | in the middle of — 営業中, 工事中 |
| 〜以上 / 〜以下 | from stage 5 |

**〜的 is the most productive of all** and attaches to almost anything to make an adjective: 一般的 general, 基本的 basic, 個人的 personal. It is a な-adjective: 具体的な例.

**This is how to read a word you have never seen.** 不可能性 is 不 + 可能 + 性 — impossibility. 国際化 is 国際 + 化 — internationalisation. The parts are known even when the whole is not.

**Practice.** Break down and guess: 無料体験 · 再利用 · 具体的 · 国際化 · 交通費. Answers: free trial · reuse · concrete/specific · internationalisation · transport costs.
Reading names:
Japanese names are the hardest reading problem in the language, and there is no complete solution.

**Why they are hard.** Name kanji take readings that appear nowhere else — 名乗り(なのり) readings — and the same characters can be read several ways with no rule to choose between them.

**生 in a surname** can be read お, い, ぶ, き, しょう, せい, なり, ふ, み and more. 一 can be read はじめ, かず, いち, ひとし. A surname written 東海林 is read しょうじ.

**Common surnames worth knowing on sight:**

佐藤(さとう) · 鈴木(すずき) · 高橋(たかはし) · 田中(たなか) · 伊藤(いとう) · 渡辺(わたなべ) · 山本(やまもと) · 中村(なかむら) · 小林(こばやし) · 加藤(かとう) · 吉田(よしだ) · 山田(やまだ) · 佐々木(ささき) · 松本(まつもと) · 井上(いのうえ)

Those fifteen cover a large share of the population.

**Place names are worse**, because many predate the characters used to write them: 日本橋 is にほんばし in Tokyo and にっぽんばし in Osaka. 秋葉原 is あきはばら and was once あきばはら.

**What to do about it.**

- **Ask.** お名前は何とお読みしますか — how do you read your name? — is a normal question and Japanese people ask each other constantly.
- **Furigana on forms.** Every official form has a ふりがな line above the name field, precisely because this problem exists for natives too.
- **Yomitan has a names dictionary** — JMnedict — which is worth importing.
- **Accept the gaps.** A name you cannot read is a name you refer to by its characters, which is what Japanese readers do too.

**In fiction**, names usually carry furigana on first appearance. Note it down; it will not be repeated.

**Practice.** Read: 田中, 山本, 小林, 中村, 井上. Then look up how 東海林 and 月極 are read, and notice that there was no way to work it out.
Listening: drama, and the method:
Scripted television is the first native listening that rewards close work, and there is a method that makes it pay.

**Why drama over anime.** Drama is adults speaking at normal speed about ordinary situations, in registers you will actually use. Anime is fast, exaggerated and full of role language. Drama is harder in the moment and more useful afterwards.

**The method, for one episode:**

1. **Watch it through with Japanese subtitles.** Do not pause. Get the story.
2. **Watch it again, pausing**, and look up what blocked you. Mine three to five things.
3. **Watch a third time with no subtitles.** This is the one that counts — the measure of what you gained.

**Three passes on one episode beats one pass on three.** The second and third passes are where listening actually improves; the first is comprehension, which is not the same skill.

**Japanese subtitles are essential and Netflix has them** for most Japanese originals. **asbplayer** syncs external subtitle files to anything and lets you mine directly from the video, capturing the audio and the screenshot with the card — which makes an extremely good flashcard.

**What to watch.** Modern, contemporary, dialogue-driven. 深夜ドラマ — late-night drama — tends to be short, cheap and talky, which is exactly right. Historical drama (時代劇) uses archaic speech and should wait.

**What to expect.** 40–60% on the first episode of anything. It climbs within the same series as you get used to the voices, which is why finishing a series beats sampling five.

**Variety shows** are the hardest native listening there is — overlapping speech, regional accents, and on-screen text you must read while listening. They are also where the language is most alive. Leave them until drama is comfortable.

**Practice.** Take one episode of one drama and do the three passes. Note what you caught on the third pass that you missed on the first.
Shadowing native material:
Stage 2 introduced shadowing with graded audio. Doing it with native material is a different and harder exercise, and it is the most efficient speaking practice available without a partner.

**What changes.** Native speech is faster, less clearly articulated, and full of reductions. You will not keep up at first, and that is the training.

**The method:**

1. Pick 30 seconds of audio you understand — a drama scene, a podcast segment.
2. Listen three times without speaking.
3. Shadow it, half a second behind, without stopping.
4. Repeat until you can keep up.
5. Record yourself and compare.

**Thirty seconds, done properly, takes ten minutes** and is worth more than an hour of loose repetition.

**What to copy.** Not just the words — the **rhythm, the pitch, the pauses, the hesitations**. Copying a native speaker's うーん and えーと is not silly; it is how the prosody gets in.

**This is where stage 1's pitch accent work pays.** Shadowing without attention to pitch trains the segments and leaves the melody English. Listening specifically for where the voice drops, and copying that, is the difference.

**オーバーラッピング is the easier variant** — reading the transcript aloud in time with the audio — and is a good step before true shadowing, which has no text.

**Material that works well:** drama scenes with one speaker, podcast monologues, NHK news, and Irodori dialogues you already know.

**Material that does not:** anything with overlapping speakers, singing, or heavy accents.

**The measure.** Record the same 30 seconds in week one and week four. The difference is audible, which is rare in language learning and worth the effort of recording.

**Practice.** Take 30 seconds of a podcast you have already listened to. Shadow it ten times. Record the first and the tenth, and listen to both.
Sentence mining at scale:
Mining was introduced in stage 3 as a habit. At this stage it becomes the main source of vocabulary, and the discipline matters more as the volume rises.

**The i+1 principle.** Mine from sentences where **one** thing is unknown. A sentence with one gap teaches that gap; a sentence with four teaches nothing and takes four times as long.

**That principle also chooses your material.** If you cannot find i+1 sentences, the material is too hard — not a reason to mine harder, a reason to read something else.

**What makes a good card:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Front** | the word, or the sentence with the word in it |
| **Back** | a short meaning, not a list of glosses |
| **Reading** | always |
| **Extra** | **the sentence you met it in** |

**The sentence is the card.** A word alone is abstract; a word in the sentence where you met it has a context, a register and a grammatical shape attached.

**How many.** Ten new a day is a reasonable ceiling and is the default on the cards page. Twenty is sustainable for a while and then is not. The limit is not how many you can learn, it is how many reviews they generate three months from now — ten a day is about 150 reviews a day at steady state, which is twenty minutes.

**What to mine:**

- Words that **blocked** a sentence you otherwise understood.
- Words you have met **twice**.
- Words marked **common** by a frequency dictionary — Yomitan shows this.

**What not to mine:** proper nouns, words from a genre you will not read again, anything you can work out from its parts.

**Deleting is allowed.** A card you have failed eight times and still do not care about should go. The deck is a tool, not a record.

**Practice.** Read for 20 minutes and mine exactly three words by the rules above, each with its sentence. Then look at your last twenty cards and delete any that are not worth their reviews.
Vocabulary: the 10,000 word mark:
A number worth understanding, because it sets expectations for how long the next part takes.

**Roughly what each level buys:**

| Words known | What it gives |
| --- | --- |
| 1,000 | the commonest 70–75% of running text |
| 2,000 | ~82% |
| 3,000 | ~86% |
| 5,000 | ~90% |
| 10,000 | ~95% |
| 20,000 | ~98% — an educated native |

**The curve is brutal.** The first thousand words buy three quarters of everything; the tenth thousand buys about one percent. That is not a reason to stop — the last percent is where all the precision is — but it explains why progress feels fast at the start and slow later.

**95% coverage is one unknown word in twenty**, which is about one per sentence. That is comfortable reading with occasional lookups, and it is roughly where a novel becomes enjoyable rather than effortful.

**Where you are.** Stage 4's end is perhaps 2,000–3,000. Stage 6 is the span from 3,000 to 6,000 or so, and it comes almost entirely from reading rather than from lists.

**Why lists stop working.** Past the first 2,000, word frequency flattens: the 4,000th most common word is barely more common than the 6,000th. Which words matter next depends on what you read, and mining from your own material is therefore strictly better than any list.

**Counting is optional.** jpdb.io will track it if you want the number; the honest measure is whether the thing you are reading is getting easier.

**Known words are not the same as usable words.** You will recognise far more than you can produce, permanently, and that is normal in a first language too.

**Practice.** Estimate where you are — jpdb's test takes ten minutes. Then calculate how many days at ten words a day it would take to add a thousand, and decide whether that is the right rate for you.
Writing: summarising what you read:
The best writing exercise available at this stage, because the content is given and all the effort goes into the language.

**The exercise.** Read something — an article, a chapter, an episode — and write 200–300 characters summarising it **in Japanese, without looking back at the text**.

**Why it works:**

- The vocabulary is fresh and you will reach for exactly the words you just met.
- Not looking back forces production from memory rather than copying.
- It is self-marking: compare your summary with the original and see what you could not say.

**The shape of a summary:**

この記事(きじ)は〜について書かれている。
まず、〜と述べている。
次に、〜。
最後に、〜と結論(けつろん)づけている。

**The reporting constructions from stage 5** are what this uses: 〜と述べている, 〜とされている, 〜によると. A summary is almost entirely indirect speech.

**Written register throughout** — だ・である, written connectives, no contractions.

**Variations:**

- **An episode of a drama**, in plain past.
- **A chapter of a novel**, which forces narrative vocabulary.
- **A conversation you had**, which forces reported speech.

**Getting it corrected.** A summary is short enough for HiNative and ideal for an italki tutor — and because the tutor can read the original, they can tell you not only whether the Japanese is right but whether the summary is.

**Keep them.** Twenty summaries over two months, read back, show the vocabulary growing in a way nothing else does.

**Practice.** Read one NHK article and write a 200-character summary without looking back. Then compare and note the three things you wanted to say and could not.
Speaking: explaining something complex:
The step beyond conversation: holding the floor for two minutes on something that needs structure.

**The task.** Explain, in Japanese, something you know well — how your work works, why you chose to learn Japanese, how a thing you built does what it does. Two minutes, no notes.

**Why it is harder than conversation.** Conversation is turn by turn and the other person carries half of it. An explanation is yours alone, needs a structure, and exposes every gap at once.

**The structure that works:**

1. **まず、〜** — the frame: what it is, in one sentence.
2. **例えば、〜** — an example.
3. **理由(りゆう)は三つあります。** — a numbered list, which buys you time and keeps you on track.
4. **つまり、〜** — the summary.

**Numbering is the trick.** 理由は三つあります commits you to three and gives the listener a map — and gives you a structure to hang sentences on while you think.

**Talking around a gap**, from stage 5, matters more here than anywhere:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 〜みたいなものです | it's like a ~ |
| 名前は分からないんですが | I don't know the word, but |
| 簡単(かんたん)に言うと | to put it simply |
| うまく言えないんですが | I can't put it well, but |

**Record yourself.** Two minutes, once a week, on a different subject. Listening back is uncomfortable and is the fastest feedback available — you will hear the hesitations, the repeated grammar, and the places you gave up.

**Then do it again, the same subject, a week later.** The second attempt on the same topic is always far better, and the gain transfers.

**Practice.** Record two minutes explaining what you do for a living, in Japanese, with the four-part structure. Listen back and write down three things to fix. Record it again tomorrow.
Review: reading real Japanese:
The end of stage 6. The checklist here is about habits rather than knowledge.

**Reading**
- Can you read a page of a novel at 70%+ without stopping?
- Is Yomitan set up, with a frequency dictionary?
- Are you reading both extensively and intensively, four to one?
- Have you finished one native book?
- Can you read an NHK headline and lead and say what the story is?
- Do you look at a monolingual definition after the English one?

**Listening**
- Can you follow a drama with Japanese subtitles at 60%+?
- Have you done the three-pass method on an episode?
- Are you shadowing native audio weekly?
- Is a podcast part of your week?

**Vocabulary**
- Are you mining from your own material rather than from lists?
- Is every card carrying the sentence you met it in?
- Is the daily number sustainable — are reviews getting done?

**Output**
- Have you written a summary of something you read?
- Have you recorded yourself explaining something for two minutes?
- Are you having a conversation at least weekly?

**Anything answered "no" is the work of the next month**, and the first four reading questions matter most: everything in stage 7 assumes reading is a habit rather than an exercise.

**What stage 7 does.** Advanced grammar — the forms that appear in essays, literature and formal speech — and the precision that separates "understood" from "understood exactly". It is the first stage where the gains are invisible from outside and real from inside.

**Practice.** Answer the checklist honestly in writing. Pick the two weakest and decide what changes this week.
Reading speed, and how it grows:
Speed is the measure that matters at this stage, and it grows differently from comprehension.

**The three bottlenecks**, in the order they are removed:

1. **Character recognition.** Having to work out a kanji stops everything. Removed by volume, not by study.
2. **Word recognition.** Knowing the characters and assembling the word. Removed by meeting the word often.
3. **Parsing.** Knowing the words and working out the structure. Removed by meeting the structure often.

**All three are removed by reading, and only by reading.** No amount of grammar study makes parsing automatic; it makes it possible, which is different.

**What to measure.** Characters per minute, roughly, on material you can read comfortably. A rough ladder:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 100–200 字/分 | decoding |
| 300–400 | comfortable intermediate |
| 400–600 | fluent reading |
| 600+ | native adult |

**Subvocalising is fine** and natives do it too. The thing to eliminate is *translating* — converting each phrase into English in your head. That is the single biggest brake and it is removed by reading faster than you can translate, which is why timed easy reading works.

**A drill that works:** read an easy page as fast as you can without losing the thread, then reread it. The second pass is noticeably faster, and the sensation of reading at that speed is the thing to get used to.

**Reading aloud is slower than silent reading** and does a different job — it is pronunciation practice, not speed practice. Both are worth doing; do not confuse them.

**The plateau.** Speed climbs, stalls, and climbs again, and the stalls are long. The only thing that moves it is more pages.

**Practice.** Time yourself on one page of something easy. Note the characters per minute. Do it again in a month on a comparable page.
Furigana, and reading without it:
A crutch worth using and worth putting down, and knowing when is the skill.

**Where furigana appears:** children's books, manga for younger readers, textbooks, newspapers for rare characters, and the first appearance of a name in fiction.

**Where it does not:** adult novels, news, signs, menus, forms, email, and essentially all of adult life.

**The trap.** Reading with furigana is reading kana with pictures above them. You will recognise a word you have met ten times with furigana and fail it the first time it appears without, because you learned the sound and not the shape.

**The fix: cover it.** Read the kanji, then check. On paper, a strip of card. On a screen, browser settings or a Yomitan option can hide ruby.

**The ladder off it:**

1. Furigana on everything (children's books).
2. Furigana available, covered, checked after.
3. No furigana, Yomitan available.
4. No furigana, lookup only when blocked.
5. No lookup.

**Stage 6 is steps 2 to 4.** Nobody reaches 5 for everything, including natives — a Japanese adult meets unfamiliar names and technical terms and looks them up.

**総ルビ(そうルビ) means furigana on everything** and is marked on book listings. 小学生向け material always has it.

**Where furigana is genuinely necessary**, even for natives: names, place names, and 当て字 — characters used for their sound rather than meaning. Those keep furigana permanently and are not a weakness in you.

**Practice.** Take a page with furigana, cover it, and read. Count the characters you could not get. Those are the cards to make.
Official documents and forms:
The hardest everyday reading there is — dense 漢語, legal phrasing, and consequences for getting it wrong.

**The vocabulary of forms:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 氏名(しめい) | full name |
| 生年月日(せいねんがっぴ) | date of birth |
| 住所(じゅうしょ) | address |
| 連絡先(れんらくさき) | contact details |
| 記入(きにゅう) | to fill in |
| 署名(しょめい) | signature |
| 捺印(なついん) | to apply a seal |
| 該当(がいとう)する | applicable |
| 添付(てんぷ) | attachment |
| 提出(ていしゅつ) | submission |
| 期限(きげん) | deadline |
| 備考(びこう) | remarks |
| 必須(ひっす) | required |
| 任意(にんい) | optional |

**The instruction phrasing:**

〜してください。 — please do
〜すること。 — do (imperative, in writing)
〜しないでください。 — please do not
〜に限(かぎ)る — limited to
〜を除(のぞ)く — excluding
〜の場合(ばあい) — in the case of
該当するものに○をつけてください。 — circle what applies

**〜すること, with a full stop, is an instruction** and appears throughout official writing. It is not a question of politeness; it is the written imperative.

**Dates use the era system** — 令和8年 — on nearly every government form, alongside or instead of the Western year.

**The bounds words from stage 5** matter here absolutely: 以上, 以下, 未満, 以内. A form that says 18歳以上 and one that says 18歳を超える are different rules.

**What to do.** Read it twice, slowly, and ask. 役所 staff are used to explaining forms and will do it. すみません、ここは何を書けばいいですか is a completely normal question.

**Practice.** Find any Japanese form online — a city office form, a job application — and read it. Note every word above that appears.
Literary Japanese: what changes:
Novels are not news, and the differences are worth naming before they surprise you.

**Narration is in plain form**, and often in the present tense for immediacy even about past events. A paragraph can switch between past and present within itself, which is normal and is not an error.

**Dialogue is unmarked by speech verbs.** Japanese fiction frequently gives a line in 「」 with no 〜と言った at all — the speaker is identified by their register, their pronoun, their sentence-final particles. This is why 役割語 exists in fiction: it is how you know who is talking.

**That means stage 5's register lesson is load-bearing here.** A line ending in だぜ and one ending in わね are different characters, and nothing else says so.

**Subjects are omitted far more than in speech**, and across longer stretches. A paragraph may run without naming who is acting, and the reader is expected to track it.

**Literary vocabulary**, which is 漢語-heavy and often has a plainer everyday equivalent you already know: 眺(なが)める for 見る, 佇(たたず)む for 立つ, 微笑(ほほえ)む for 笑う.

**Older texts bring older grammar.** Anything pre-war has 歴史的仮名遣い — historical kana usage — where は is read わ in more places, ゐ and ゑ appear, and verb endings differ. 青空文庫 is full of it, which is why free does not mean easy.

**〜である and 〜であった** where speech would have だ and だった.

**What to do.** Start with contemporary fiction, not classics. 青空文庫's free catalogue is tempting and is mostly pre-1970, which is a harder language than the one you have learned.

**Practice.** Read one page of contemporary fiction and one page of 夏目漱石 from 青空文庫. The difference is the gap between stage 6 and stage 10.
Technical and academic writing:
Dense, formulaic, and far more approachable than literature once you know the frame.

**Why it is easier than fiction.** The vocabulary is specialised but finite and repeats constantly; the grammar is restricted; nothing is implied; and there is no register play. A paper in your own field may be easier than a novel.

**The frame of a paper:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 要旨(ようし) / 概要(がいよう) | abstract |
| はじめに / 序論 | introduction |
| 先行研究(せんこうけんきゅう) | prior work |
| 方法(ほうほう) | method |
| 結果(けっか) | results |
| 考察(こうさつ) | discussion |
| 結論 | conclusion |
| 参考文献(さんこうぶんけん) | references |

**The recurring constructions**, nearly all from stage 5's impersonal voice:

〜と考えられる — it is considered that
〜と思われる — it is thought that
〜ことが分かった — it was found that
〜を明らかにする — to clarify
〜について検討する — to examine
〜に基づいて — based on
〜に対して — in contrast to
〜という点で — in terms of
〜すなわち — that is to say
〜とはいえ — that said

**Technical writing in your own field is a shortcut.** Programming documentation in Japanese is largely katakana loanwords plus a thin layer of grammar — メソッド, 引数(ひきすう), 戻(もど)り値(ち), 実装(じっそう), 型(かた). If you already know the concepts, you are reading grammar rather than content.

**Where to find it:** Qiita and Zenn for programming, J-STAGE for academic papers, and Japanese documentation for any tool you use.

**Practice.** Read one Qiita article on something you already understand technically. Note how much of the difficulty is vocabulary you already know in English.
Films, YouTube and the rest:
The listening material that is not drama, each with its own difficulty.

**Films.** Harder than drama: less dialogue, more implication, worse audio, and no episodic repetition of voices to get used to. A two-hour film is also a large commitment to something you may follow at 40%.

**Start with films you have seen.** Knowing the plot removes the comprehension burden and leaves the language. Studio Ghibli with Japanese subtitles is the standard recommendation and is genuinely good for this — clear speech, familiar stories.

**YouTube is the best value in listening** at this stage, because the range is unlimited and the level varies by creator.

| Kind | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **Vlogs** | one voice, everyday vocabulary, visual context |
| **Cooking** | highly visual, repetitive vocabulary, slow |
| **Gaming** | long, casual, one voice, lots of reaction |
| **Educational** | clear speech, structure, often subtitled |
| **Interviews** | two voices, natural speech, aizuchi |

**Automatic subtitles on YouTube are usable** for Japanese and reasonably accurate for clear speech, which makes almost any video into subtitled material.

**Variety shows** — バラエティ — remain the hardest: several people talking at once, regional accents, and on-screen text you must read while listening. They are also where the most natural, fastest Japanese is, so they are the real target rather than the starting point.

**Accents and speed.** Standard Tokyo is what you have learned. Kansai you met in stage 5. Tōhoku and Kyushu accents in variety and drama can be genuinely opaque, and subtitles exist on Japanese television precisely because natives struggle too.

**Practice.** Find one YouTube channel at your level — vlog or cooking — and subscribe. Watch one video a day for a week. Note how much easier the fifth is than the first.
Listening without subtitles:
The end state, and a skill that must be trained separately from subtitled listening.

**Why it is separate.** With subtitles you are reading and listening, and the reading carries you. Remove them and the listening has to do everything — parsing word boundaries, catching particles, holding a sentence in memory while its verb arrives at the end.

**That last point is the hard part of Japanese specifically.** The verb is last, so you cannot know what the sentence is doing until it ends. Holding the whole thing in working memory until the verb lands is a trained skill, and it is why Japanese listening lags Japanese reading for most learners.

**The progression:**

1. Known material, no subtitles — an episode you have already watched twice.
2. Audio-only of material you have seen.
3. New material, subtitles available but unused unless stuck.
4. New material, no subtitles.

**Step 1 is undervalued.** Rewatching an episode you understood with subtitles, without them, is the single most efficient exercise here: the comprehension is already there, so all the effort goes into hearing.

**Audio-only is harder than video** and therefore better training. A podcast has no faces, no gestures and no scenery to carry meaning.

**Train the memory**, not just the ear. A useful drill: listen to one sentence, pause, and repeat it aloud before thinking about meaning. Reproducing a sentence you did not understand proves you heard it, and hearing is the bottleneck.

**Expect slow progress and sudden jumps.** Listening improves in steps rather than smoothly, and the steps come after periods where nothing seems to change.

**Practice.** Take an episode you have already watched with subtitles and watch it again without. Note the percentage. Then do the sentence-repetition drill for five minutes on a podcast.
Writing: a review:
A short, opinionated text with a conventional shape, and one of the most useful things to be able to write.

**Why a review.** It is short, it has a structure, it needs opinion vocabulary and hedging, and there are thousands of native examples to read first. Amazon, 食べログ and 価格.com are a free corpus.

**The shape:**

1. **What it is**, in a sentence.
2. **What was good** — 良かった点(てん).
3. **What was not** — 気になった点.
4. **Who it suits** — 〜な人におすすめです.

**The vocabulary:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| おすすめ | recommended |
| 満足(まんぞく) | satisfied |
| 期待(きたい)以上 / 以下 | better / worse than expected |
| コスパがいい | good value |
| 使いやすい / 使いにくい | easy / hard to use |
| 気になる点 | points of concern |
| 残念(ざんねん)ながら | unfortunately |
| 総合的(そうごうてき)に | overall |
| 星(ほし)〜つ | ~ stars |

**The hedging from stage 5 is what makes it sound Japanese:** 〜と思います, 〜ような気がします, 〜かもしれません. A review that states everything flatly reads as aggressive.

**Criticism is indirect.** 気になった点 — "points that bothered me" — is the standard heading, and it is softer than 悪かった点. ちょっと〜かなと思いました is how a complaint is made.

**Length.** 150–300 characters. Native reviews are short.

**Read twenty before writing one.** The conventions are obvious after twenty and invisible before.

**Practice.** Read ten Amazon.co.jp reviews of something you own. Then write your own, 200 characters, in the four-part shape.
Speaking: discussing what you read:
The exercise that joins the reading strand to the speaking strand, and the most natural subject for conversation practice.

**Why it works.** You have just read something, so the vocabulary is loaded and the content is ready. Conversation practice usually fails on "what shall we talk about"; this removes that.

**The shape of the conversation:**

最近(さいきん)、〜という本を読みました。
〜についての話です。
一番面白かったのは、〜です。
〜と思いました。
〜さんはどう思いますか。

**Summarising aloud is harder than in writing** because there is no time to choose words. That pressure is the exercise.

**The useful constructions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 〜という本 / 記事 | a book/article called ~ |
| 〜についての話です | it's a story about ~ |
| 要するに | in short |
| 簡単に言うと | to put it simply |
| 〜と書いてありました | it said that ~ |
| 〜らしいです | apparently |
| 個人的には | personally |

**Disagreeing about something you read** is good practice for the softening from stage 5, because it is low stakes: 私はちょっと違うと思いました。

**With a tutor**, send the article in advance. Thirty minutes discussing a piece you both read is worth several hours of unstructured conversation, because the vocabulary is shared and the corrections land on things you were trying to say.

**Alone**, record yourself summarising what you read, for two minutes, once a week. It is the explaining exercise from the previous stage with the content provided.

**Practice.** Read one article today and record yourself summarising it aloud in Japanese for two minutes. Listen back and note what you reached for and could not find.
Abbreviations, acronyms and numbers in t:
Small things that stop a sentence dead when unfamiliar.

**Shortened words.** Japanese abbreviates by taking the first two mora of each element:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| スマホ | スマートフォン |
| パソコン | パーソナルコンピューター |
| エアコン | エアコンディショナー |
| コンビニ | コンビニエンスストア |
| リモコン | リモートコントロール |
| 就活(しゅうかつ) | 就職活動 — job hunting |
| 婚活(こんかつ) | 結婚活動 — looking for a spouse |
| 東大(とうだい) | 東京大学 |
| 高校(こうこう) | 高等学校 |
| 国連(こくれん) | 国際連合 — the UN |

**〜活 is productive**: 就活, 婚活, 終活 (preparing for one's death), 朝活 (early-morning activity).

**Roman acronyms are read as English letters:** JR (ジェイアール), NHK (エヌエイチケー), ATM, PC, AI. They are extremely common in writing.

**Numbers in text:**

- **Vertical writing uses kanji numerals**: 三十五年.
- **Horizontal uses Arabic**: 35年.
- **Counting large amounts switches to 万 and 億** rather than grouping by thousands: 1億2千万人 — 120 million people.
- **〜割(わり)** is tenths: 3割 is 30%, and it is used for percentages constantly in news and sport.
- **〜倍(ばい)** is times: 2倍 double, 3倍 triple.
- **第〜(だい)** makes an ordinal: 第1回, 第二次世界大戦.

**約, 以上, 以下, 前後** from stage 5 appear in every statistic.

**Symbols:** 〒 postcode · ㎡ square metres · ℃ degrees · ※ note · 〜 range · ○ correct · × wrong · △ partial.

**※ is extremely common** and marks a footnote or caveat — ※税込, ※一部店舗を除く.

**Practice.** Read: 約3割の人が賛成。※ただし、18歳未満を除く。 Then expand: スマホ, 就活, 国連, 東大.
Counters, and the rest of them:
The long tail of counters, collected for recognition rather than production.

**Already covered:** つ, 個, 人, 本, 枚, 匹, 冊, 台, 杯, 回, 歳, 階, 度, 番.

**The rest you will meet:**

| | For |
| --- | --- |
| 軒(けん) | houses, shops |
| 件(けん) | cases, matters, emails |
| 通(つう) | letters, documents |
| 着(ちゃく) | items of clothing |
| 足(そく) | pairs of footwear |
| 頭(とう) | large animals |
| 羽(わ) | birds, rabbits |
| 隻(せき) | ships |
| 機(き) | aircraft |
| 両(りょう) | train carriages |
| 室(しつ) | rooms |
| 名(めい) | people, politely |
| 品(ひん) | dishes, items |
| 皿(さら) | plates of food |
| 粒(つぶ) | grains, pills |
| 束(たば) | bundles |
| 組(くみ) | sets, pairs, groups |
| 巻(かん) | volumes of a series |
| 話(わ) | episodes |
| 曲(きょく) | pieces of music |
| 点(てん) | points, items, artworks |

**巻 and 話 matter for manga and anime**: 第3巻, 第12話.

**件 is the email and business counter**: 3件のメール, その件について.

**Abstract counters:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 〜つ | ideas, points, reasons |
| 〜点 | points in an argument |
| 〜項目(こうもく) | items in a list |

理由は三つあります, from the explaining lesson, uses the simplest one — which is usually the right choice for anything abstract.

**When you do not know the counter**, ～つ works for almost anything concrete up to ten, and nobody minds. That remains true at every level.

**Practice.** Count: three shops · two letters · five birds · volume seven · episode twelve · two matters. Answers: 三軒 · 二通 · 五羽 · 第七巻 · 第十二話 · 二件。
Classical traces in modern Japanese:
Fossils of older grammar that survive in set phrases, signs and formal writing. You do not need classical Japanese to read modern Japanese, but you do need these.

**〜ず — the old negative**, surviving in adverbs and set phrases:

必(かなら)**ず** — without fail
思わ**ず** — unintentionally
相変(あいか)わら**ず** — as always
知ら**ず**知らずのうちに — without realising

**〜ざる** is the attributive form of the same: 許(ゆる)さ**ざる** — unforgivable. And ざるを得ない from stage 5 is this.

**〜べき** — from the classical べし, met in stage 5.

**〜き / 〜し — old adjective endings:**

良(よ)**き** 時代 — the good old days
悲(かな)**し** — sad (in poetry and titles)

**〜なり, 〜たり, 〜り** in proverbs and names: 時は金なり — time is money.

**〜れ / 〜よ — the imperative**, which survives in signs and shouting:

止(と)ま**れ** — STOP (on road signs)
見**よ** — behold
注意(ちゅうい)せ**よ** — take care

**〜まじ / 〜べからず — prohibition**, on old signs:

立入(たちいり)**禁止** is modern; 入る**べからず** is the old form and still appears.

**Why these survive.** Set phrases, signs, proverbs and titles preserve old grammar in every language. The Japanese ones are more visible because the writing system did not change around them.

**Stage 10 does classical Japanese properly.** This lesson exists so that 必ず and 思わず and 止まれ are not mysteries in the meantime.

**Practice.** Identify the classical element: 相変わらず忙しい。 · 止まれ。 · 言わざるを得ない。 · 良き友。 Answers: ず negative · れ imperative · ざる negative + を得ない · き adjective ending.
～における and ～にあたって:
Formal replacements for に and で, and the first of the written-only constructions.

**～における / ～において — "in", "at", "regarding".** The formal equivalent of で for a setting:

日本**における**教育制度 — the education system in Japan
会議**において**議論(ぎろん)された — it was discussed at the meeting

**における modifies a noun; において modifies a verb.** That is the only difference: 日本における問題 and 日本において起きた問題.

**It is not usable in speech.** 日本で is what anyone says; 日本において belongs in a report.

**～にあたって / ～にあたり — "on the occasion of", "when doing".**

開会(かいかい)**にあたって**、一言(ひとこと)申し上げます。 — On the occasion of the opening, allow me to say a word.
就職(しゅうしょく)**にあたり**、必要な書類(しょるい)です。 — These are the documents needed when taking up employment.

**It marks a significant occasion**, not an ordinary time. 食事にあたって is absurd; 結婚にあたって is normal. That weight is the whole of its meaning.

**～に際(さい)して is nearly identical** and slightly more formal still:

利用(りよう)**に際して**は、規約(きやく)をお読みください。 — On using the service, please read the terms.

**These three are the register of ceremonies, contracts and announcements.** You will meet them constantly in reading and should not reach for them in conversation — doing so sounds like a public address.

**Practice.** Rewrite formally: 日本で教育の問題がある。 · 結婚する時に必要な書類。 Answers: 日本における教育の問題。 · 結婚にあたって必要な書類。
～をめぐって and ～に先立って:
Two more formal connectives, both common in news.

**～をめぐって / ～をめぐる — "concerning", "over".** Used when there is a dispute or discussion around something:

その問題**をめぐって**議論が続いている。 — Debate continues over the issue.
相続(そうぞく)**をめぐる**争(あらそ)い — a dispute over an inheritance

**It implies contention.** について is neutral; をめぐって says people are circling the thing and disagreeing. News uses it constantly for exactly that reason.

**～をめぐる modifies a noun**, をめぐって modifies a verb — the same split as における and において.

**～に先立(さきだ)って / ～に先立ち — "prior to", "in advance of".**

開会**に先立って**、黙祷(もくとう)が捧(ささ)げられた。 — Prior to the opening, a silent prayer was offered.
発売(はつばい)**に先立ち**、試写会(ししゃかい)が行われた。 — Ahead of release, a preview was held.

**It is for formal sequence**, where 前に would be the plain version. The event before must itself be significant.

**～を皮切(かわき)りに — "starting with", "beginning from".**

東京**を皮切りに**、全国(ぜんこく)でツアーが行われる。 — Starting in Tokyo, a tour will be held nationwide.

**It implies a series follows.** A single event does not take it.

**All three are reading vocabulary.** Recognise them in news and reports; producing them is for formal writing only, and stage 7's writing lesson is where that belongs.

**Practice.** Identify what each implies: 問題について議論する vs 問題をめぐって議論する。 Then rewrite formally: 開会の前に挨拶があった。 Answer: 開会に先立って挨拶があった。
～を問わず and ～にかかわらず:
Two ways of saying something does not matter, plus their near relatives.

**～を問(と)わず — "regardless of", "irrespective of".** Takes a noun:

経験(けいけん)**を問わず**、どなたでも参加(さんか)できます。 — Regardless of experience, anyone may take part.
年齢(ねんれい)**を問わず** — irrespective of age
昼夜(ちゅうや)**を問わず** — day or night

**It appears in job adverts and notices** more than anywhere else, and the nouns it takes are a small set: 経験, 年齢, 性別(せいべつ), 国籍(こくせき), 有無(うむ).

**～にかかわらず — "regardless of".** Takes a noun, or a pair of opposites:

天候(てんこう)**にかかわらず**、開催(かいさい)します。 — It will be held regardless of the weather.
行く行かない**にかかわらず** — whether you go or not

**～にもかかわらず is a different thing** — "despite", "even though":

雨**にもかかわらず**、たくさんの人が来た。 — Despite the rain, many people came.

**That も changes it entirely.** にかかわらず is "it doesn't matter which"; にもかかわらず is "and yet". One syllable, two meanings, and it is a reliable exam question and a reliable misreading.

**～によらず is close to を問わず**: 理由(りゆう)によらず — for whatever reason.

**～はともかく — "leaving aside":**

味(あじ)**はともかく**、安いです。 — Taste aside, it's cheap.

That one is conversational and useful, where the others are not.

**Practice.** Translate: Regardless of experience. · Despite the rain. · Whether it rains or not. · Taste aside. Answers: 経験を問わず。 · 雨にもかかわらず。 · 雨が降る降らないにかかわらず。 · 味はともかく。
～はもとより and ～はおろか:
Two ways of saying "let alone", differing in whether what follows is positive or negative.

**～はもとより — "not to mention", "to say nothing of".** Neutral or positive:

漢字**はもとより**、ひらがなも書けます。 — He can write hiragana, to say nothing of kanji.
国内(こくない)**はもとより**、海外でも有名です。 — Famous abroad as well as at home.

**～はおろか — "let alone", always with a negative:**

漢字**はおろか**、ひらがなも読めません。 — He can't read hiragana, let alone kanji.

**The second clause must be negative.** おろか with a positive is wrong, and that constraint is the difference between the two.

**Both put the more obvious case first**, which is the reverse of English. 漢字はおろかひらがなも読めない reads as "kanji — never mind that — he can't even read hiragana". Reading it backwards into English is the habit.

**～どころか, from stage 6**, is the conversational version and works both ways:

安い**どころか**、とても高かった。 — Far from cheap, it was very expensive.

**～も～も, with a negative**, is the plain way to say it: 漢字もひらがなも読めません.

**～さえ, from stage 5**, overlaps: ひらがな**さえ**読めません。

**Which to use.** さえ or も in speech, はもとより in formal writing, はおろか when the thing is genuinely surprising and negative. おろか is strong and slightly literary.

**Practice.** Say: He can't read hiragana, let alone kanji. · Famous abroad as well as at home. · Far from cheap. Answers: 漢字はおろか、ひらがなも読めません。 · 国内はもとより、海外でも有名です。 · 安いどころか高いです。
～ならでは and ～ずにはいられない:
Two expressions of distinctiveness and compulsion.

**～ならでは(の) — "unique to", "only possible with".** Always positive, always praising:

この店**ならではの**味 — a flavour you'll find only here
日本**ならでは**の文化 — a culture unique to Japan
プロ**ならでは**の技(わざ) — skill only a professional has

**It is the language of advertising and travel writing** and is almost always complimentary. The structure is [noun] + ならでは + の + [noun].

**～ずにはいられない — "cannot help but".**

笑(わら)わ**ずにはいられなかった**。 — I couldn't help laughing.
心配せ**ずにはいられません**。 — I can't help worrying.

**Formation: the ない form with ない replaced by ずにはいられない.** する becomes **せ**ずにはいられない, irregular as always.

**It is about an emotional compulsion**, not a practical necessity. なければならない is obligation; ずにはいられない is being unable to stop yourself.

**～ないではいられない** is the same thing, slightly more colloquial.

**～てやまない — "to ~ endlessly", formal and warm:**

ご成功(せいこう)をお祈(いの)り**してやみません**。 — I wish you every success.
彼を愛し**てやまない**。 — She loves him endlessly.

**てやまない is restricted to a small set of verbs** — 祈る, 願う, 愛する — and is the register of speeches and letters.

**～を余儀(よぎ)なくされる — "to be forced to", formal and unhappy:**

中止(ちゅうし)**を余儀なくされた**。 — We were forced to cancel.

That one is news vocabulary and extremely common in reports of disruption.

**Practice.** Say: a flavour unique to this shop · I couldn't help laughing · We were forced to cancel. Answers: この店ならではの味 · 笑わずにはいられなかった · 中止を余儀なくされた。
～べく, ～べからず, ～んがため:
Classical forms surviving in modern formal Japanese.

**～べく — "in order to", from べし.**

問題を解決(かいけつ)す**べく**、会議が開かれた。 — A meeting was held in order to resolve the problem.

**する becomes すべく** — not するべく — which is the same irregularity as すべき.

**It is literary**, and ために is the ordinary version. べく appears in reports and formal narration.

**～べからず — "must not", on signs:**

入る**べからず** — do not enter
初心(しょしん)忘る**べからず** — never forget your beginner's mind

**The second is a famous proverb**, from Zeami's writing on Noh, and is quoted constantly.

**～べからざる — the attributive**: 許す**べからざる**行為(こうい) — an unforgivable act.

**～んがため(に) — "for the purpose of", strongly literary:**

生き**んがため**に働く。 — To work in order to live.

**Formation: the ない form, with ない replaced by んがため.** する becomes **せ**んがため.

**～がゆえ(に) — "because of", formal:**

若い**がゆえに**、失敗(しっぱい)した。 — He failed because he was young.
それ**ゆえ** — therefore

**ゆえ is the classical reason-marker** and survives in それゆえ and 〜がゆえに. Both are written-only.

**Why learn these at all.** They appear in editorials, literature, formal speeches, signs and proverbs — all material you will read. You will never need to produce them, and producing them in conversation would be absurd.

**Practice.** Read and translate: 立入るべからず。 · 初心忘るべからず。 · 問題を解決すべく努力する。 · 若さゆえの失敗。
～たる and ～なる — the classical attributives:
Two forms that look like ordinary words and are not, and that appear constantly in formal writing and titles.

**～なる — the classical attributive of なり**, equivalent to modern な or の:

偉大(いだい)**なる**人物 — a great figure
単(たん)**なる**偶然(ぐうぜん) — a mere coincidence
いかなる理由があっても — whatever the reason

**単なる and いかなる are the two you will meet most**, and both are completely standard in modern formal writing. 単なる means "mere" and いかなる means "whatever".

**～たる — classical, meaning "being, in the capacity of":**

教師(きょうし)**たる**者(もの)、模範(もはん)であるべきだ。 — One who is a teacher ought to be an example.
堂々(どうどう)**たる**態度(たいど) — a dignified bearing

**～たる者 is the common pattern** — "one who is a ~" — and carries a sense of the obligations that come with the role.

**Many adjectives exist only in たる form**: 堂々たる, 確固(かっこ)たる, 錚々(そうそう)たる, 漠然(ばくぜん)たる. They are adjectives that never became な-adjectives, and they are frozen that way.

**〜と / 〜として is their adverbial form**: 堂々**と** — proudly, 漠然**と** — vaguely. You already use 堂々と without having known it was classical.

**～ともあろう — "someone as ~ as":**

先生**ともあろう**方(かた)が、そんなことを…。 — That a teacher of all people should do such a thing…

**It carries reproach** — the role makes the behaviour worse — and is a fixed pattern.

**Practice.** Translate: 単なる偶然 · いかなる場合も · 堂々とした態度 · 教師たる者. Answers: a mere coincidence · in any case · a dignified manner · one who is a teacher.
～なりに, ～ばかりに, ～あまり:
Three expressions about degree and consequence.

**～なりに / ～なりの — "in one's own way", within one's limits:**

子供**なりに**考えた。 — The child thought about it in his own way.
私**なりの**答(こた)えです。 — It's my own answer, such as it is.

**It is modest and accepting.** It acknowledges that the effort was limited by the person's capacity and values it anyway. 私なりに頑張りました — I did my best, for what that is worth — is a common and rather Japanese thing to say.

**～ばかりに — "simply because", with a bad outcome:**

一言(ひとこと)言った**ばかりに**、喧嘩(けんか)になった。 — Just because I said one word, it turned into a row.

**It always regrets.** から is neutral; ばかりに says the cause was small and the consequence was disproportionate and unwelcome.

**～あまり — "out of too much", "so ~ that":**

心配の**あまり**、眠(ねむ)れなかった。 — I couldn't sleep out of sheer worry.
驚(おどろ)いた**あまり**、声も出なかった。 — I was so startled I couldn't speak.

**It takes an emotion**, usually, and the consequence is involuntary. Formation: a noun with の, or a verb in plain past.

**～のあまり is the noun form** and is the commoner one.

**All three are about disproportion** — effort smaller than hoped, cause smaller than effect, emotion larger than control — which is why they sit together.

**Practice.** Say: I did my best, in my own way. · Just because I was late, I missed it. · I was so worried I couldn't eat. Answers: 私なりに頑張りました。 · 遅れたばかりに、見られませんでした。 · 心配のあまり、食べられませんでした。
～ないまでも, ～までだ, ～たりとも:
Three expressions of limit and minimum.

**～ないまでも — "even if not quite":**

毎日**とは言わないまでも**、週に三回は練習したい。 — Not every day perhaps, but I'd like to practise three times a week.
完璧(かんぺき)で**ないまでも**、だいたいできた。 — Not perfect, but mostly done.

**It concedes a lower standard** while insisting on something. The structure is [the higher standard] + ないまでも + [the lower one].

**～までだ / ～までのことだ — "then I'll just":**

だめなら、やめる**までだ**。 — If it's no good, I'll simply stop.
歩く**までのことです**。 — Then I'll just walk.

**It is resolve, not resignation** — a statement that the fallback is acceptable and no fuss is required.

**～たりとも — "not even one", with a negative:**

一日**たりとも**忘れたことはない。 — I have not forgotten for even a single day.
一円**たりとも**払(はら)わない。 — I won't pay a single yen.

**It takes a counter of one** — 一日, 一円, 一人, 一瞬(いっしゅん) — and requires a negative. It is emphatic and literary.

**～すら is close to さえ** and more formal:

子供**すら**知っている。 — Even a child knows.

**～だに — "not even", very literary:**

想像(そうぞう)**だに**しなかった。 — I never even imagined it.

**These last three are reading vocabulary**, and たりとも and だに especially belong to speeches and literature.

**Practice.** Translate: 一日たりとも休まなかった。 · 完璧でないまでも、よくできた。 · だめなら、やり直すまでだ。
～ともなると, ～とあって, ～こそあれ:
Three connectives of circumstance, all formal.

**～ともなると / ～ともなれば — "when it comes to", "once you reach":**

大学生**ともなると**、責任(せきにん)も増(ふ)える。 — Once you're a university student, responsibilities increase too.
夏**ともなれば**、観光客(かんこうきゃく)が増える。 — Come summer, tourists increase.

**It marks a threshold** — a stage or a season at which things change — and the second clause is a consequence that follows naturally.

**～とあって — "given that", "because of":**

連休(れんきゅう)**とあって**、道が混(こ)んでいる。 — Being a long weekend, the roads are busy.

**It is news register** and gives the reason for an observable situation. The cause is usually a circumstance rather than an action.

**～こそあれ / ～こそすれ — "though there may be", formal concession:**

多少(たしょう)の違いは**こそあれ**、基本(きほん)は同じだ。 — There may be slight differences, but the basics are the same.
感謝(かんしゃ)**こそすれ**、恨(うら)むことはない。 — I feel only gratitude, certainly no resentment.

**こそすれ denies the opposite emphatically** — "gratitude yes, resentment no" — and is a formal rhetorical move.

**All three belong to editorials and reports.** Meeting them is the point; producing them is for stage 7's writing lesson and nowhere else.

**Practice.** Translate: 連休とあって、新幹線は満席だ。 · 冬ともなると、雪が降る。 · 多少の問題はこそあれ、成功だった。
～に相違ない, ～とみえる, ～んばかり:
Three ways of inferring, two formal and one vivid.

**～に相違(そうい)ない — "without doubt".** The formal に違いない:

彼が犯人(はんにん)**に相違ない**。 — He is without doubt the culprit.

Same meaning, higher register. 相違 means "difference" and the construction is "there is no difference from this".

**～とみえる / ～とみえて — "it appears that":**

疲れている**とみえて**、すぐ寝てしまった。 — He seems to have been tired — he fell asleep at once.

**It infers from evidence**, and とみえて leads into the evidence's consequence. More literary than ようだ.

**～とみられる is the news version** — "is seen as", "is believed to be" — and is the impersonal voice from stage 5:

原因(げんいん)は漏電(ろうでん)**とみられる**。 — The cause is believed to be an electrical fault.

**～んばかり(に) — "as if about to", vivid and literary:**

泣(な)か**んばかりの**顔 — a face as if about to cry
あふれ**んばかりの**笑顔(えがお) — a smile overflowing

**Formation: the ない form with ない replaced by んばかり.** It describes an appearance taken to its extreme without actually happening.

**～とばかりに — "as if to say":**

早く帰れ**とばかりに**、時計を見た。 — He looked at his watch as if to say "go home".

**It reports an unspoken message** conveyed by behaviour, and it is a favourite of novelists.

**～ごとく / ～ごとき — "like", classical:**

飛(と)ぶ**がごとく** — as if flying
彼**のごとき**人物 — a figure like him

**ごとき after a person can be dismissive**: 私ごときが — "someone like me", self-deprecating, or 君ごときに — "the likes of you", insulting.

**Practice.** Translate: 疲れているとみえて、黙っている。 · 泣かんばかりの声。 · 原因は火災とみられる。
～やら, ～だの, ～なり, ～であれ:
Four ways of listing, each with its own attitude.

**～やら～やら — "what with this and that", suggesting disorder:**

掃除(そうじ)**やら**洗濯(せんたく)**やら**で忙しい。 — What with the cleaning and the washing, I'm busy.

**It implies more than listed** and a certain harassed quality.

**～だの～だの — the same, with complaint:**

高い**だの**まずい**だの**、文句(もんく)ばかり言う。 — Too expensive, no good — he does nothing but complain.

**だの is critical.** Quoting someone's words with it conveys that you found them tiresome.

**～なり～なり — "or", offering alternatives:**

電話する**なり**メールする**なり**して、連絡してください。 — Phone or email — just get in touch.

**It suggests the choice does not matter**, and it carries a slight impatience: pick one.

**～であれ～であれ / ～にしろ～にしろ — "whether ~ or ~":**

雨**であれ**雪**であれ**、行きます。 — Rain or snow, I'm going.
行く**にしろ**行かない**にしろ**、早く決めて。 — Whether you go or not, decide quickly.

**～つ～つ — classical, in fixed pairs only:**

行き**つ**戻り**つ** — back and forth
抜(ぬ)き**つ**抜かれ**つ** — overtaking each other

**There are perhaps a dozen of these** and they are frozen; you cannot make new ones.

**～といい～といい — "both ~ and ~", in praise or complaint:**

味**といい**値段(ねだん)**といい**、申し分(もうしぶん)ない。 — Both the taste and the price are beyond criticism.

**Practice.** Translate: 掃除やら料理やらで忙しい。 · 電話するなりメールするなりしてください。 · 雨であれ晴れであれ、行く。 · 味といい見た目といい、素晴らしい。
Parsing a long sentence:
Japanese sentences in formal writing can run for several lines, and they are parseable by a method rather than by intuition.

**The structure is always the same:** modifiers before what they modify, and the main verb at the very end. A long sentence is a short sentence with things stacked in front of its nouns.

**The method, in order:**

1. **Find the final verb or copula.** That is the main predicate and the sentence's spine.
2. **Find the は.** That is the topic, and it usually belongs to that final verb — not to anything between.
3. **Find the を or が just before the verb.** That is its object or subject.
4. **Everything else is modification**, and can be set aside on a first pass.
5. **Now unpack the modifiers**, from the noun backwards.

**Worked example:**

> 昨日(きのう)友達と一緒に行った店で買った本は、思ったより高かった。

- Final predicate: **高かった** — was expensive.
- Topic: **本は** — the book.
- So the frame is: 本は高かった — the book was expensive.
- Everything before 本 modifies it: 買った本 — the book I bought; 店で買った本 — the book I bought at the shop; 行った店で買った本 — at the shop I went to; 友達と一緒に行った店 — the shop I went to with a friend; 昨日 — yesterday.

**The frame first, the detail second.** Trying to read left to right and accumulate meaning is what makes long Japanese sentences feel impossible; finding the spine first makes them routine.

**Signals that a clause is subordinate:** が instead of は, a plain form where you expected polite, a て-form, or a connective like ので, たら, と, ながら.

**Commas help and are not reliable.** Japanese comma placement is looser than English and marks breath more than structure.

**Practice.** Parse this by the method: 去年の夏に京都で撮った写真を見せてくれた友達が、今度東京に引っ越すらしい。 Find the predicate first, then the topic, then unpack. (Predicate: 引っ越すらしい. Topic: 友達が. The rest modifies 友達.)
Ellipsis: what Japanese leaves out:
Japanese omits anything the listener can supply, and far more of it than English does. Reading well means reconstructing what is not there.

**What gets dropped:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Subjects** | constantly, across whole paragraphs |
| **Objects** | when obvious |
| **Particles** | in speech — を, に, へ first |
| **The second half of a sentence** | ちょっと…, 〜んですが… |
| **Repeated nouns** | replaced by の or nothing |
| **です / だ** | in casual speech and headlines |

**Subject tracking is the skill.** A Japanese paragraph can run without naming who is acting, and the reader is expected to keep hold of it. The clues:

- **は sets a topic that persists** until something changes it. Everything after it is about that topic unless told otherwise.
- **が introduces something new**, which often becomes the next topic.
- **Giving and receiving verbs mark direction.** くれた means it came towards the speaker — so the subject is someone else and the recipient is me, with neither named.
- **Honorifics mark who.** いらっしゃる is about someone senior; 申す is about me.
- **たい is first person.** A sentence ending 行きたい is about the speaker.

**That last set is why stage 3 and stage 5 matter for reading**: giving verbs and honorifics do the work that pronouns do in English.

**The unfinished sentence is a real sentence.** ちょっと…, 〜んですけど…, 〜と思いまして… are complete communications, and the listener finishes them. Translating them requires supplying what was meant, not what was said.

**When you lose the thread**, go back to the last は and work forward. The topic is almost always the problem.

**Practice.** Take a paragraph of a novel and mark who is doing each verb. Note how many have no stated subject, and what told you.
～のである, and emphasis in writing:
The written form of んです, and one of the commonest constructions in essays and literature.

**〜のである / 〜のだ — explanatory emphasis.**

彼は知っていた**のである**。 — He knew, you see.
これが問題な**のだ**。 — *This* is the problem.

**It frames the sentence as an explanation or a conclusion** — the same job んです does in speech, in written register.
