**It is overused and that is a style question.** Good Japanese prose uses のである sparingly, for the sentence that lands a point. A paragraph with four of them reads as hectoring, exactly as English with four "the fact is" would.

**〜のではないか / 〜のではないだろうか — the hedged assertion:**

問題は別(べつ)のところにある**のではないだろうか**。 — Is the problem not in fact elsewhere?

**This is the standard way to state a thesis** in Japanese academic writing. A flat assertion claims authority; the rhetorical question invites the reader to agree. It is far more common than 〜と思う in formal writing.

**〜に他(ほか)ならない — "is nothing other than":**

これは差別(さべつ)**に他ならない**。 — This is nothing other than discrimination.

Emphatic identification, common in argument.

**〜こそ, from stage 5**, in writing: これ**こそ**が本質(ほんしつ)だ — this is the very essence.

**体言止め(たいげんどめ) — ending on a noun**, with no verb:

静かな夜。遠くに響(ひび)く汽笛(きてき)。 — A quiet night. A whistle sounding in the distance.

**It is a literary device** for atmosphere and compression, common in poetry, headlines, and descriptive prose. It is not an error.

**Inversion — 倒置(とうち)** — putting something after the verb for emphasis, which modern Japanese allows in speech and in literary writing: 行ったよ、昨日。

**Practice.** Rewrite as a hedged thesis: 日本語の勉強には読書が一番大切だと思います。 Answer: 日本語の学習において、読書こそが最も重要なのではないだろうか。
四字熟語 — four-character compounds:
Fixed phrases of four kanji, usually from Chinese, carrying a whole idea in four characters. They appear in speeches, editorials, and anywhere someone is being emphatic.

**The common ones:**

| | Reading | Means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 一石二鳥 | いっせきにちょう | two birds with one stone |
| 十人十色 | じゅうにんといろ | everyone is different |
| 一期一会 | いちごいちえ | a once-in-a-lifetime meeting |
| 自業自得 | じごうじとく | you brought it on yourself |
| 以心伝心 | いしんでんしん | tacit understanding |
| 試行錯誤 | しこうさくご | trial and error |
| 臨機応変 | りんきおうへん | adapting to circumstances |
| 一生懸命 | いっしょうけんめい | with all one's might |
| 無我夢中 | むがむちゅう | utterly absorbed |
| 単刀直入 | たんとうちょくにゅう | straight to the point |
| 優柔不断 | ゆうじゅうふだん | indecisive |
| 本末転倒 | ほんまつてんとう | putting the cart before the horse |

**一生懸命 is the one you will use** — it is entirely ordinary and means "doing one's utmost". 一生懸命働く, 一生懸命勉強する.

**一期一会 is from the tea ceremony** — every meeting is unique and will not recur — and is quoted constantly.

**The structure is usually two pairs.** 試行 (trial) + 錯誤 (error); 臨機 (facing the occasion) + 応変 (responding to change). Reading them as two halves is how to guess at an unfamiliar one.

**There are thousands** and most are rare. Perhaps fifty are in common use, and those are worth knowing; the rest are dictionary material.

**They are a conspicuous register marker.** Using one in casual conversation is like quoting Latin in English — occasionally apt, usually showing off. In a speech or an essay they are entirely at home.

**Practice.** Use 一生懸命 in a sentence. Then guess from the parts: 半信半疑 · 十人十色 · 自画自賛. Answers: half believing, half doubting · ten people, ten colours · praising one's own painting.
ことわざ and 慣用句:
Proverbs and idioms — the fixed expressions that cannot be worked out from their parts.

**ことわざ — proverbs:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 猿(さる)も木から落ちる | even monkeys fall from trees |
| 石(いし)の上にも三年 | three years on a stone — persistence pays |
| 出る杭(くい)は打(う)たれる | the nail that sticks up gets hammered down |
| 七転(ななころ)び八起(やお)き | fall seven times, get up eight |
| 塵(ちり)も積(つ)もれば山となる | dust piled up becomes a mountain |
| 急(いそ)がば回(まわ)れ | if you're in a hurry, go round |
| 知らぬが仏(ほとけ) | ignorance is bliss |
| 花より団子(だんご) | dumplings over flowers — substance over style |

**出る杭は打たれる is the one most quoted about Japan**, often by outsiders, and Japanese people quote it ironically as often as seriously.

**慣用句 — idioms**, usually built on body parts:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 顔が広い | well connected |
| 手を貸(か)す | to lend a hand |
| 耳が痛い | a criticism that stings |
| 口が軽い | indiscreet |
| 気が合う | to get on well |
| 腹(はら)が立つ | to be angry |
| 頭が上がらない | to be indebted to |
| 目がない | to be mad about |
| 足を引(ひ)っ張(ぱ)る | to hold someone back |
| 猫の手も借りたい | so busy you'd borrow a cat's paws |

**気 appears in dozens of them**: 気になる, 気がする, 気をつける, 気が付く, 気を使う, 気が済む. They are among the most common expressions in the language and each has to be learned whole.

**Using them.** 慣用句 are ordinary speech and are safe to use. ことわざ are quotations and land better when they fit exactly; dropping one in loosely is conspicuous.

**Practice.** Use three 慣用句 from the list in sentences. Then explain 石の上にも三年 and say whether you believe it.
同音異義語 and 送り仮名:
Two problems the writing system creates, and both are everyday.

**同音異義語(どうおんいぎご) — words that sound identical and are written differently.**

| Reading | Words |
| --- | --- |
| こうえん | 公園 park · 講演 lecture · 公演 performance · 後援 support |
| きかい | 機会 opportunity · 機械 machine · 器械 apparatus |
| かてい | 家庭 household · 過程 process · 仮定 assumption · 課程 curriculum |
| いし | 意思 intention · 医師 doctor · 意志 will · 石 stone |
| せいか | 成果 results · 聖火 sacred flame · 青果 produce |

**Japanese has an enormous number of these** because Chinese readings collapsed many distinct syllables into few. The kanji is what distinguishes them, which is one of the strongest arguments for the writing system continuing to exist.

**In speech, context does it** — and when it does not, speakers spell it out: 機会の「き」は機械の「き」です.

**This is why typing is a selection task.** An IME offers several candidates for こうえん and you pick; picking wrong produces a sentence that is grammatical and absurd, and is a common and funny error.

**送り仮名(おくりがな) — the kana after a kanji**, which marks the inflection and often the word:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 上(あ)がる / 上(のぼ)る | to rise / to climb |
| 行(おこな)う / 行(い)く | to carry out / to go |
| 生(い)きる / 生(う)まれる / 生(なま) | to live / to be born / raw |
| 細(ほそ)い / 細(こま)かい | thin / fine, detailed |
| open 開(あ)く / 開(ひら)く | to open (by itself) / to open out |

**The okurigana is what tells you the reading.** 行う and 行く are the same character and different words, and only the kana says which.

**There are official rules** — 送り仮名の付け方, a Cabinet notification — and they have exceptions. In practice the okurigana is learned with the word.

**Practice.** Give three words read こうえん and three read きかい. Then read: 上がる · 上る · 行う · 行く · 生ける花.
Register: 硬い and 柔らかい:
A final pass on register, now that all of it is available: how to judge how formal a piece of Japanese is, and how to match it.

**The axis.** 硬い(かたい) — hard, stiff, formal — and 柔(やわ)らかい — soft, approachable. Every choice you make sits somewhere on it.

**What makes a text 硬い:**

- 漢語 over 和語 — 開始 over 始める
- である over です
- 〜における, 〜に関して, 〜をめぐって
- Long noun phrases and nominalisation
- The impersonal voice — 〜と思われる
- No contractions, no dropped particles

**What makes it 柔らかい:**

- 和語, katakana, and 〜です・ます
- Short sentences
- Sentence-final particles — ね, よ
- Direct address and questions
- Contractions

**The same content, three ways:**

> 本件につきましては、来週中に回答いたします。 (very hard)
> この件については、来週お返事します。 (polite normal)
> その件、来週返事するね。 (soft)

**Matching matters more than being formal.** Over-formal Japanese to a friend is as wrong as casual Japanese to a client, and the first is less often noticed by learners because it feels safe. It is not: 本日はお忙しい中ありがとうございます to a mate is comic.

**Reading register is the skill.** Before replying to anything, read what was sent and match it. An email that opens お世話になっております expects the same back; one that opens おはよう！ does not.

**Where learners go wrong:** mixing registers within one text, which is the most noticeable error of all. One sentence of である followed by one of です reads as carelessness.

**Practice.** Take one sentence and write it at three levels, as above. Then look at the last three Japanese things you wrote and judge where each sat, and whether it matched what it was answering.
Reading: essays and criticism:
The most demanding ordinary reading there is, and where stage 7's grammar lives.

**Why essays are hard.** Fiction gives you a story to hang on to. News gives you a formula. An essay gives you an argument built in a structure you must follow, with no narrative and no repetition.

**The Japanese essay structure — 起承転結(きしょうてんけつ):**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 起(き) | introduce the subject |
| 承(しょう) | develop it |
| 転(てん) | **turn** — introduce a complication or a different angle |
| 結(けつ) | conclude |

**転 is what surprises Western readers.** The third movement deliberately shifts — a new perspective, an apparent digression — before the conclusion ties it back. An English reader looking for a thesis-support-conclusion shape will read the turn as a derailment.

**It is not universal** — academic Japanese increasingly uses the Western shape — but it is common in 随筆(ずいひつ), the personal essay, which is a major Japanese form.

**What to read:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 新聞の社説(しゃせつ) | editorials — short, argued, daily |
| コラム | newspaper columns, 天声人語 especially |
| 随筆 | personal essays |
| note.com の長文 | modern, varied, free |

**天声人語** — the Asahi's front-page column — is 600 characters daily, dense, allusive, and used in Japanese schools for exactly this kind of practice. It is hard and it is the standard exercise.

**The method.** Read once for the shape — where is the turn, what is the conclusion. Then again for the sentences. An essay read sentence by sentence without the shape is a list of statements.

**Practice.** Read one 社説 today. Identify its four movements before translating anything. Then read it again for language.
Listening: lectures and talks:
Structured monologue — the last listening format, and the most useful for work.

**Why it is easier than conversation**, in some ways: one speaker, no overlapping, a prepared structure, and usually slides or visuals.

**Why it is harder:** it runs for a long time without a turn, the vocabulary is specialised, and losing the thread early means losing the rest.

**The structural signals to listen for:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 本日は〜についてお話しします | today I'll talk about ~ |
| まず · 次に · 最後に | first, next, finally |
| 三つのポイントがあります | there are three points |
| つまり · 要するに | in other words |
| 例えば | for example |
| 一方で | on the other hand |
| ここで重要なのは | what matters here is |
| 以上です | that's all |

**Catching the signposts is most of it.** If you hear 三つのポイント, you know the shape of the next ten minutes even if you miss sentences inside it.

**Where to find them free:**

- **TEDxTokyo** and Japanese TED talks — short, subtitled, prepared.
- **YouTube lectures** — 東京大学 and others publish them.
- **NHK高校講座** — school-level lectures on every subject, clear and free.
- **Conference talks** in your own field, where the content is already known.

**NHK高校講座 is undervalued.** It is school broadcasting: clear, slow, visual, structured, on every subject from physics to classical Japanese, and entirely free.

**Note-taking in Japanese** is the natural exercise here and is harder than it sounds — writing while listening in a second language competes for the same attention. Start by noting only the signposts.

**Practice.** Watch one NHK高校講座 episode on any subject. Note only the structural signposts, not the content. Then watch again and fill in.
Writing: a formal essay:
The output exercise for this stage: 800–1,000 characters, 起承転結, written register throughout.

**The structure.** Either the Japanese four-part shape or the Western three-part one — but choose, and be consistent.

**The register rules**, all from earlier lessons:

- だ・である throughout, never です.
- 漢語 where there is a choice.
- Written connectives: しかし, したがって, さらに, 一方.
- The impersonal voice for claims: 〜と考えられる, 〜のではないだろうか.
- No contractions, no dropped particles, no sentence-final particles.

**The opening.** Japanese essays often open with a general observation or a question rather than a thesis:

> 近年(きんねん)、外国語学習の方法は大きく変化している。

**The thesis is often at the end**, not the start, which is the reverse of English academic convention and worth deciding deliberately rather than by default.

**Paragraphing.** One idea per paragraph, and Japanese paragraphs are shorter than English ones. The first character of a paragraph is indented by one space — a full-width space — which is the convention and is noticed when absent.

**Length discipline.** 800 characters is about four or five paragraphs. Writing to a character count is a real constraint and a useful one.

**Getting it corrected.** This is long enough that HiNative will not serve; an italki tutor who teaches writing is the realistic option, or a Japanese colleague if you have one. A corrected essay is worth ten uncorrected ones.

**Subjects that produce real argument:** 外国語学習に文法は必要か · 在宅勤務は生産性を高めるか · なぜ人は物語を必要とするのか.

**Practice.** Write 800 characters in 起承転結 on a question you have a view about. Then reread specifically for register: find and remove every です and every contraction.
Speaking: the formal register:
Producing 硬い Japanese aloud — presentations, meetings, and anything with an audience.

**What changes from conversation:**

- **です・ます throughout**, with 〜ております and 〜いたします where appropriate.
- **漢語 over 和語** — 開始いたします over 始めます.
- **Fuller sentences** — no dropped particles, no trailing off.
- **Signposting**, as in the lectures lesson, because the audience cannot ask.

**The frame of a presentation:**

本日は、お忙しい中お集まりいただき、ありがとうございます。
[name]と申します。
本日は、〜についてお話しさせていただきます。
まず〜、次に〜、最後に〜についてご説明いたします。
…
以上で発表を終わります。ご清聴(せいちょう)ありがとうございました。
何かご質問はございますでしょうか。

**させていただきます, from stage 5**, is the register of presentations and is used throughout.

**ご清聴ありがとうございました closes every presentation** in Japan and is worth having as a unit.

**Handling questions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| ご質問ありがとうございます。 | Thank you for the question. |
| 確認して、後ほどご連絡いたします。 | I'll check and get back to you. |
| 申し訳ございませんが、分かりかねます。 | I'm afraid I don't know. |

**分かりかねます** uses かねる from stage 5 — a polite inability — and is far better than 分かりません in a formal setting.

**Pace and pauses.** Formal Japanese is delivered more slowly than conversation, with clear pauses at phrase boundaries. Rushing is the commonest fault and makes an accent much more noticeable.

**Practice.** Prepare and record a two-minute presentation on anything you know, using the full frame. Listen back for dropped particles and trailing sentences — both are conversation habits and both are wrong here.
Review: the advanced grammar:
The end of stage 7. Most of this stage is recognition rather than production, and the checklist reflects that.

**Recognise, when reading:**

- における, にあたって, に際して, に先立って, を皮切りに
- をめぐって, を問わず, にかかわらず — and にもかかわらず, which is different
- はもとより, はおろか, ならでは
- べく, べからず, んがため, がゆえに
- たる, なる, ともあろう
- ずにはいられない, てやまない, を余儀なくされる
- なりに, ばかりに, あまり
- ないまでも, までだ, たりとも, すら, だに
- ともなると, とあって, こそあれ
- に相違ない, とみえる, んばかり, とばかりに, ごとく
- やら, だの, なり, であれ, といい

**Produce, in formal writing:**

- だ・である throughout
- のである and のではないだろうか
- 一方で, したがって, さらに
- 起承転結, or a chosen alternative

**Produce, in formal speech:**

- The presentation frame
- させていただきます where permission is genuine
- 分かりかねます rather than 分かりません

**Use freely:**

- 一生懸命 and the common 四字熟語
- 慣用句 built on body parts
- Register matching — reading what was sent and answering in kind

**The honest position on this stage.** Almost none of it belongs in conversation. Its value is that editorials, literature, contracts and speeches stop being opaque, and that your own formal writing stops reading as translated. If you find yourself saying ならでは in a café, something has gone wrong.

**What stage 8 does.** Keigo properly — the honorific and humble systems, the verb tables, and the social reasoning underneath them. It is the last large body of grammar in the language.

**Practice.** Go down the recognition list and find five of them in something you read this week. Then write one paragraph in である and read it aloud to hear how it sounds.
The three systems of keigo:
敬語(けいご) is not one thing. It is three systems doing three different jobs, and keeping them apart is most of the difficulty.

| | Name | What it does | Applied to |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 丁寧語 | ていねいご | plain politeness | the sentence |
| 尊敬語 | そんけいご | **raises** the other person | their actions |
| 謙譲語 | けんじょうご | **lowers** you | your actions |

**丁寧語 is です and ます**, which you have used since stage 2. It is politeness towards the listener and is independent of who is doing what.

**尊敬語 and 謙譲語 are about the subject of the verb.** The same action gets a different verb depending on who performs it:

- 先生が**いらっしゃいます**。 — The teacher is here. (honorific — about them)
- 私が**参(まい)ります**。 — I will come. (humble — about me)

**Using the wrong one is the classic error**, and it is not a small one: saying 私がいらっしゃいます elevates yourself, which is the opposite of what politeness is for.

**The test is always: whose action is this?**

- Their action → 尊敬語
- My action, or my group's → 謙譲語
- Neither, or a general statement → 丁寧語 alone

**謙譲語 lowers you in order to raise them.** There is no insult in it; it is a relative measure, and the humility is formal rather than felt.

**美化語(びかご) is a fourth, minor system** — the お and ご on nouns: お茶, お金, ご飯. It beautifies the word rather than honouring anyone, which is why お金 is polite about money and not about its owner.

**Where this comes from.** Japanese grammaticalises social relationships that English handles with tone and word choice. It is not decoration: a sentence must choose, and choosing nothing is itself a choice.

**Practice.** For each, say whether it needs 尊敬語, 謙譲語 or neither: the teacher is eating · I am eating · it is raining · my boss will call you · I will call your boss. Answers: 尊敬 · 謙譲 · neither · 尊敬 · 謙譲.
尊敬語: the special verbs:
A small set of verbs has its own honorific form, and these are the ones to learn first because they are the ones you will hear.

| Plain | 尊敬語 | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 行く · 来る · いる | **いらっしゃる** | ます form: いらっしゃいます |
| 言う | **おっしゃる** | おっしゃいます |
| する | **なさる** | なさいます |
| 食べる · 飲む | **召(め)し上(あ)がる** | 召し上がります |
| 見る | **ご覧(らん)になる** | ご覧になります |
| 知っている | **ご存(ぞん)じだ** | ご存じです |
| くれる | **くださる** | くださいます |
| 寝る | **お休(やす)みになる** | |
| 死ぬ | **お亡(な)くなりになる** | |

**Five of these are irregular in the ます form.** いらっしゃる, おっしゃる, なさる, くださる and ござる drop the り: いらっしゃ**います**, not いらっしゃります. That irregularity is worth drilling because it is where learners stumble.

**いらっしゃる covers three verbs** — to go, to come, and to be — so 先生はいらっしゃいますか can mean "is the teacher in?" or "is the teacher coming?", and context decides.

**いらっしゃいませ, in every shop**, is this verb: "welcome", literally an imperative of "come".

**ご存じですか is "do you know?"** and is how you ask a superior. 知っていますか is not wrong but is flat.

**くださる is the honorific くれる**, and 〜てくださる is the honorific of 〜てくれる — which gives ください, the request form you have used since stage 2. It was keigo all along.

**Practice.** Convert to honorific: 先生が来ます。 · 社長が言いました。 · 何を食べますか。 · 知っていますか。 Answers: 先生がいらっしゃいます。 · 社長がおっしゃいました。 · 何を召し上がりますか。 · ご存じですか。
尊敬語: the regular patterns:
For every verb without a special form, there are two regular ways to make it honorific.

**1. お + ます stem + になる** — the standard pattern:

書く → **お書きになる**
読む → **お読みになる**
帰る → **お帰りになる**

**ご + 漢語 + になる** for する-verbs: ご利用になる, ご出発になる.

**2. The passive form, 〜れる / 〜られる** — lighter and very common:

書く → 書**かれる**
来る → 来**られる**
する → **される**

先生が**来られました**。 — The teacher came.

**The passive honorific is weaker and safer.** It is less formal than お〜になる, it never sounds overdone, and it is what most people use in ordinary workplace speech. Its drawback is ambiguity — 書かれた is both "was written" and "wrote (honorific)" — and context resolves it.

**3. お + ます stem + です** — a lighter honorific state:

お待ちです — you are waiting
お帰りですか — are you leaving?
お持ちですか — do you have it?

**ポイントカードはお持ちですか**, from the shop lesson in stage 4, is this pattern.

**The honorific request: お + stem + ください**

お待ちください。 — Please wait.
ご覧ください。 — Please look.
お入りください。 — Please come in.

**This is politer than 〜てください** and is what announcements and staff use.

**Do not stack them.** お書きになられる combines two honorifics and is 二重敬語 — double keigo — which gets its own lesson. Pick one.

**Practice.** Make honorific three ways: 待つ. Answers: お待ちになる · 待たれる · お待ちです。 Then: please sit (座る). Answer: お座りください。
謙譲語: the special verbs:
The humble forms, for your own actions. Learn these second, because these are the ones you will say.

| Plain | 謙譲語 | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 行く · 来る | **参(まい)る** | 参ります |
| いる | **おる** | おります |
| 言う | **申(もう)す** · 申し上げる | 申します |
| する | **いたす** | いたします |
| 食べる · 飲む · もらう | **いただく** | いただきます |
| 見る | **拝見(はいけん)する** | 拝見します |
| 聞く · 訪ねる | **伺(うかが)う** | 伺います |
| 知っている | **存(ぞん)じている** | 存じております |
| あげる | **差(さ)し上げる** | |
| 会う | **お目(め)にかかる** | |

**You already use three of these.** 申します, from stage 2's self-introduction. いただきます, before eating. ございます, which is the humble ある.

**伺う does three jobs** — to ask, to hear, and to visit — and is extremely common in business: 明日伺います (I'll visit tomorrow), ちょっと伺いますが (may I ask something).

**存じております for "I know"**, 存じません for "I don't". ご存じ is the honorific; 存じる is the humble. Same character, opposite directions.

**拝見します for looking at something of theirs** — a document, a photograph. 見ます would be flat.

**お目にかかる — "to meet"** — is literally "to have one's eyes meet" and is the formal humble for 会う: お目にかかれて光栄(こうえい)です.

**The ます-form irregularity again:** ござる and 申す behave; いたす and 参る are regular.

**Practice.** Convert to humble: 私が行きます。 · 見ました。 · 聞きたいんですが。 · 田中と言います。 Answers: 私が参ります。 · 拝見しました。 · 伺いたいんですが。 · 田中と申します。
謙譲語: the regular patterns:
For verbs without a special humble form.

**1. お + ます stem + する** — the standard pattern:

持つ → **お持ちします** — I'll carry it
送る → **お送りします** — I'll send it
知らせる → **お知らせします** — I'll let you know

**ご + 漢語 + する** for する-verbs: ご説明します, ご案内します, ご連絡します.

**2. お + stem + いたす** — more formal still:

お持ち**いたします** · ご説明**いたします**

いたす is itself humble, so this is the humble pattern plus a humble verb — and it is accepted rather than being double keigo, because it has become fixed.

**3. お + stem + 申し上げる** — the most formal:

お願い**申し上げます** · お礼(れい)**申し上げます**

This is the register of formal letters and ceremonies.

**4. 〜させていただく**, from stage 5 — doing something with permission.

**The pattern only works for actions that affect the other person.** お持ちします means "I'll carry it *for you*". A humble form of an action that has nothing to do with them — お寝(ね)します — is nonsense. This constraint catches learners who have learned the pattern and not the logic.

**謙譲語 I and II.** Modern descriptions split the humble forms:

- **謙譲語 I** lowers you *relative to the person the action is directed at* — 伺う, お持ちする.
- **謙譲語 II** (丁重語) simply lowers your action in front of the listener, with no third party — 参る, おる, いたす.

So 明日парisに参ります — "I shall go to Paris tomorrow" — is humble towards the *listener*, not towards Paris. That is why 参る works for actions involving nobody.

**Practice.** Make humble: 荷物を持ちます。 · 説明します。 · 連絡します。 Answers: お荷物をお持ちします。 · ご説明いたします。 · ご連絡いたします。
内 and 外: who counts as your group:
The rule that decides which form to use, and the one that surprises everyone.

**Keigo is not about rank alone. It is about which side of a boundary someone is on.**

**内(うち) — your group:** you, your family, your company, your team.
**外(そと) — outside it:** everyone else, in that moment.

**The rule: humble about 内, honorific about 外.**

**The consequence that catches people.** Speaking to a client about your own boss:

- 田中部長は**おりません**。 ✓ — Tanaka is not in. (humble, no title, no さん)
- 田中部長は**いらっしゃいません**。 ✗ — elevates your own boss to an outsider.

**Your own boss loses his honorific the moment an outsider is listening.** Inside the company he is 田中部長 and takes 尊敬語. On the phone to a customer he is plain 田中 and takes 謙譲語.

**The same applies to family.** To a colleague, your own mother is 母 and does not take honorifics; their mother is お母さん and does.

**The boundary moves with the conversation.** Among your department, another department is 外. Speaking to another company, your whole company is 内. It is relative, not fixed, and it is recalculated every time the audience changes.

**弊社(へいしゃ) and 御社(おんしゃ)** encode it in nouns:

| | Mine | Theirs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| company | 弊社 · 当社(とうしゃ) | 御社 · 貴社(きしゃ) |
| opinion | 私見(しけん) | ご意見 |
| name | 私ども | 皆様(みなさま) |

**御社 in speech, 貴社 in writing** — that split is fixed and is a standard business-Japanese test question.

**Practice.** You are on the phone to a client. Say: Tanaka is out at the moment. · I will pass on the message. Answers: 田中はただいま外出しております。 · 申し伝(つた)えます。
二重敬語 and over-politeness:
Keigo can be wrong by being too much, and the errors are common enough to have names.

**二重敬語(にじゅうけいご) — stacking two honorifics on one verb:**

| Wrong | Right |
| --- | --- |
| お読み**になられる** | お読みになる *or* 読まれる |
| ご覧に**なられる** | ご覧になる |
| おっしゃ**られる** | おっしゃる |
| お伺い**いたします** | 伺います *or* お伺いします |

**One honorific per verb.** お〜になる is already honorific; adding られる doubles it. It is a real error and a noticed one, although it is so widespread that some forms — お伺いします — have become accepted.

**The exception.** A few double forms are fixed by custom and are correct: お召し上がりください, お見えになる.

**バイト敬語 — the keigo of part-time staff**, widely used and widely criticised:

| Heard | Problem |
| --- | --- |
| 〜の**ほう**になります | ほう adds nothing |
| 千円**から**お預かりします | から is wrong |
| こちら、コーヒー**になります** | it does not *become* coffee |
| よろしかったでしょうか | past tense for a present question |
| 〜**させていただきます** everywhere | permission where none is involved |

**You will hear all of these constantly**, in every shop and café in Japan. They are not correct and they are completely normal, which is a useful lesson in itself: prescriptive correctness and actual usage are different things here as everywhere.

**For a learner: use the plain correct forms.** こちらがコーヒーです, 千円お預かりします. Nobody will think you wrong, and several people will think you careful.

**Over-politeness to friends** is the other failure. 恐れ入りますが to a mate is comic. Keigo is for distance, and using it where there is none creates distance.

**Practice.** Correct these: お読みになられますか。 · コーヒーになります。 · 千円からお預かりします。 Answers: お読みになりますか。 · コーヒーでございます。 · 千円お預かりします。
ございます, でございます and 美化語:
The polite copula, and the お and ご that attach to nouns.

**ございます is the polite ある:**

トイレは二階に**ございます**。 — The toilet is on the second floor.
お時間は**ございますか**。 — Do you have time?

**でございます is the polite です:**

こちらが新商品(しんしょうひん)**でございます**。 — This is the new product.
田中**でございます**。 — This is Tanaka.

**It is 丁重語** — it raises the politeness of the sentence rather than honouring a person — which is why it can be used about objects, where 尊敬語 cannot.

**Where you hear it:** shops, hotels, announcements, telephone. It is the register of service, and as a customer you do not need to produce it — ですwill do — but you must understand it.

**美化語(びかご) — the beautifying お and ご.**

**お attaches to 和語**: お金, お茶, お水, お店, お名前, お話, お元気
**ご attaches to 漢語**: ご飯, ご家族, ご住所, ご連絡, ご意見, ご協力

**That split is reliable and has exceptions**: お電話, お時間, お食事 take お despite being 漢語, because they are so common that they were absorbed.

**Some words have fused with their お** and cannot lose it: お茶, ご飯, お金 are simply the words. 茶 alone is a different, more technical word.

**When to use it.** About things belonging to or affecting the other person — お名前, ご住所, お時間 — always. About your own things, rarely: 私のお名前 is wrong. About neutral things, as a general politeness — お茶, お水 — commonly, and more so in formal or feminine-leaning speech.

**Over-applying it is a real error.** お料理をお作りになられたお母様 is three too many.

**Practice.** Add お or ご: 名前 · 住所 · 家族 · 連絡 · 茶 · 時間 · 意見. Answers: お名前 · ご住所 · ご家族 · ご連絡 · お茶 · お時間 · ご意見。
Keigo on the telephone:
The hardest keigo, because it is fast, unprompted, and you cannot see the person.

**Receiving a call:**

はい、[会社名]**でございます**。
いつも**お世話になっております**。
少々**お待ちください**。
担当(たんとう)の者(もの)に**代(か)わります**。

**担当の者 — "the person in charge"** — uses 者, the humble word for a person in your own group. Never 方(かた), which is honorific.

**Making a call:**

**お世話になっております**。[会社名]の[名前]と**申します**。
[name]様は**いらっしゃいますか**。
**恐れ入りますが**、お取り次(つ)ぎ**いただけますでしょうか**。

**Taking a message:**

申し訳ございませんが、[name]は**ただいま席(せき)を外(はず)しております**。
戻(もど)りましたら、**折り返しお電話差し上げます**。
**ご伝言(でんごん)を承(うけたまわ)りましょうか**。 — May I take a message?

**承ります is the humble 受ける** and is the standard verb for receiving an order or a message.

**The in-group rule at full strength.** Your own colleague, to an outsider:

- 田中は**おりません** ✓
- 田中さんは**いらっしゃいません** ✗

**Ending:**

失礼いたします。 — Goodbye. (said while hanging up, by both parties)

**The caller hangs up first**, and the receiver waits — a small convention that is widely observed.

**When you cannot follow:**

恐れ入りますが、もう一度**おっしゃって**いただけますか。
お電話が遠(とお)いようですが。 — "The line seems far" — the polite way to say you cannot hear, which blames the line rather than either person.

**お電話が遠いようです is worth memorising.** It is the standard face-saving phrase and is used by natives constantly.

**Practice.** Rehearse the full sequence: answer, take a call for an absent colleague, offer to take a message, close.
Keigo in email:
Written keigo, which is more forgiving than spoken because you can think — and less forgiving because it is a record.

**The frame**, extended from stage 4:

```
株式会社〇〇
営業部 田中様

いつもお世話になっております。
株式会社△△の[name]でございます。

さて、先日お話しいたしました件につきまして、
ご連絡申し上げます。

[the substance]

ご多忙のところ恐縮ではございますが、
ご確認のほどよろしくお願い申し上げます。

――――――――――
[signature]
```

**The formulas, and what they do:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| いつもお世話になっております | the universal opening |
| 〜の件につきまして | regarding the matter of ~ |
| ご連絡申し上げます | I am writing to inform you |
| 恐縮ではございますが | I am sorry to trouble you |
| 〜のほど | softens a request |
| よろしくお願い申し上げます | the universal close |
| ご査収(さしゅう)ください | please find attached and check |
| 取り急(いそ)ぎ | in haste — for a short note |

**〜のほど is a pure softener** and means nothing: ご確認のほど. It is everywhere in business email and is one of the things critics call empty. Use it; it is expected.

**Sentences are short and lines are broken manually** at natural phrase boundaries, which is a Japanese email convention and looks odd to anyone used to flowing paragraphs.

**Replying.** Keep the quoted text, answer above it, and open with ご返信ありがとうございます or お世話になっております.

**What not to do:** emoji, exclamation marks, and 了解しました to a superior — 承知いたしました is the correct form.

**Practice.** Write an email to a client confirming a meeting next Tuesday at 3pm, using the full frame.
Asking, refusing and apologising in keig:
The three hardest things to do politely, in their most formal forms.

**Asking.** The ladder from stage 5, extended upward:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 〜ていただけますか | could you ~ |
| 〜ていただけますでしょうか | might you ~ |
| 〜ていただけませんでしょうか | would it be possible ~ |
| お〜いただけますでしょうか | the honorific version |

**恐れ入りますが opens it**, or 恐縮(きょうしゅく)ですが, or お忙しいところ恐れ入りますが.

恐れ入りますが、少々お待ちいただけますでしょうか。

**Refusing.** A flat no is almost never said:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 申し訳ございませんが、〜 | I'm very sorry, but |
| 〜いたしかねます | I am unable to |
| ご期待に添(そ)えず、申し訳ございません | sorry not to meet your expectations |
| 今回は見送(みおく)らせていただきます | we will pass on this occasion |
| 検討させていただきます | we will consider it |

**検討させていただきます usually means no.** It is the standard soft refusal in business and is understood as such by everyone except the foreigner waiting for a decision. 前向きに検討します — "we'll consider it positively" — is also usually no.

**いたしかねます is かねる from stage 5** — a polite inability — and is firmer than it sounds.

**Apologising:**

| | Weight |
| --- | --- |
| すみません | everyday |
| 申し訳ありません | serious |
| 申し訳ございません | formal, serious |
| 大変申し訳ございませんでした | a real failure |
| お詫(わ)び申し上げます | formal written |

**ご迷惑をおかけして申し訳ございません** is the standard formula for having caused trouble, and it is what every delayed train announces.

**The apology comes first and the explanation second**, and the explanation should be short. Leading with a reason reads as excuse-making.

**Practice.** Write: a request to a client to check a document by Friday · a refusal of an invitation · an apology for a late delivery.
Keigo mistakes, and when not to use it:
Two lessons in one: the errors natives make, and the situations where keigo is wrong.

**Errors natives make and argue about:**

| Common | Standard |
| --- | --- |
| 〜のほうになります | 〜でございます |
| よろしかったでしょうか | よろしいでしょうか |
| 了解しました (to a superior) | 承知いたしました |
| ご苦労さまです (to a superior) | お疲れさまです |
| とんでもございません | とんでもないことでございます |
| お名前をいただけますか | お名前を伺えますか |

**とんでもございません is interesting.** とんでもない is one word, so splitting it to make ございません is technically wrong — but it is so established that the Agency for Cultural Affairs now accepts it. Prescription loses to usage eventually.

**ご苦労さま is downward only.** Saying it to your boss is a genuine mistake and is noticed.

**Where keigo is wrong:**

- **With friends and family.** It creates distance, which is sometimes the point and usually not.
- **About your own group, to outsiders**, in honorific form — the 内/外 rule.
- **In casual writing** — a blog in keigo reads as a press release.
- **When it obscures the message.** A simple instruction buried in four layers of politeness is worse than a clear one.

**The genuine modern debate.** Japanese workplaces are moving away from heavy keigo, younger speakers use less of it, and over-politeness is increasingly read as cold or sarcastic rather than respectful. Simple です・ます with correct in-group handling is safe almost everywhere.

**For a learner specifically.** Nobody expects fluent keigo from a foreigner, and attempting it and failing is received far better than not trying. But です・ます, correctly and consistently, is never wrong — and is better than ambitious keigo with the 内/外 rule broken.

**Practice.** Correct: 社長、ご苦労さまです。 · 了解しました。(to a client) · 田中部長はいらっしゃいません。(to a client) Answers: お疲れさまです。 · 承知いたしました。 · 田中はおりません。
A full business exchange:
Everything in this stage, assembled into one sequence. Work through it aloud.

**The scenario:** you telephone a client's company, speak to a colleague of theirs, leave a message, follow up by email, and attend the meeting.

**1. The call**

> 「はい、株式会社山田でございます。」
> 「いつもお世話になっております。株式会社田中の[name]と申します。恐れ入りますが、営業部の佐藤様はいらっしゃいますでしょうか。」
> 「申し訳ございません、佐藤はただいま席を外しております。」
> 「さようでございますか。では、お戻りになりましたら、お電話をいただけますでしょうか。」
> 「かしこまりました。ご伝言を承ります。」
> 「ありがとうございます。よろしくお願いいたします。失礼いたします。」

**Note:** their 佐藤 is 佐藤様 to you and plain 佐藤 to them. The 内/外 rule, from both sides at once.

**2. The email**

> 件名：お打ち合わせの件
>
> 株式会社山田
> 営業部 佐藤様
>
> いつもお世話になっております。
> 株式会社田中の[name]でございます。
>
> 先ほどはお電話にて失礼いたしました。
> 来週のお打ち合わせにつきまして、
> 15日（水）14時はご都合いかがでしょうか。
>
> ご多忙のところ恐れ入りますが、
> ご確認のほどよろしくお願い申し上げます。

**3. The meeting**

> 「本日はお時間をいただき、ありがとうございます。」
> 「こちらが資料でございます。ご覧ください。」
> 「ご質問はございますでしょうか。」
> 「確認の上、改めてご連絡いたします。」
> 「本日はありがとうございました。失礼いたします。」

**4. Afterwards**

> 本日はお忙しい中、お時間をいただき誠にありがとうございました。

**Practice.** Record yourself performing all four parts. Then do it again having identified every 尊敬語 and 謙譲語 and checked that each is pointed the right way.
Review: keigo:
The end of stage 8. The checklist is about the reasoning as much as the forms.

**The three systems**
- Can you say which of 尊敬語, 謙譲語 and 丁寧語 a sentence needs, and why?
- Do you know that the question is always "whose action is this?"

**The verbs**
- いらっしゃる, おっしゃる, なさる, 召し上がる, ご覧になる, ご存じ, くださる
- 参る, おる, 申す, いたす, いただく, 拝見する, 伺う, 存じる, 差し上げる
- The five that drop り in ます form

**The patterns**
- お〜になる, 〜れる/られる, お〜です, お〜ください
- お〜する, お〜いたす, お〜申し上げる, 〜させていただく

**The social rules**
- 内 and 外, and that the boundary moves with the audience
- Your own boss loses his honorific to an outsider
- 弊社 and 御社; 御社 spoken, 貴社 written
- 美化語 お and ご, and the 和語/漢語 split

**The errors**
- 二重敬語 — one honorific per verb
- バイト敬語, recognised and not reproduced
- ご苦労さま downward only; 了解 not upward

**The judgement**
- When keigo creates distance you did not want
- That です・ます done correctly beats ambitious keigo done wrongly

**What stage 9 does.** Native material as the whole diet, with no graded anything left: novels, television, podcasts, work. The teaching largely stops and the using begins, which is what the previous eight stages were for.

**Practice.** Perform the business exchange from the previous lesson once more, from memory. Then write down the three forms you still have to think about, and drill those.
